SCIENTIFIC NOTES. - --------------------------------- The work of removing the ruins of the Tuileries has now METELL A.'S TOMB. been completed. Every one knows that a wedding-trip to Italy is incomplete An attempt is S:eing made to obtain a pension from the without a cis t to Cecilia Metella's tomb, that colossal tower whose Civil List Fund for the widow of Dutton Coot. It is said mute eloquence has told so many centuries how an old Roman loved and honoured the wife whom he had lost.—Soniers. that Lord Houghton is taking great interest in the matter. ' The Tour de Clovis—ascribed to the King of that name, Mid crumbling tombs along the Appian way You walked with me. And while the road we trod, The by the buildings of the Lycee Henri IV., and one Dreaming of vanished years, when Rome held sway of the most interesting remains of ancient Paris—having-I And ruled all nations with an iron roc!, been allowed to fall into a deplorable state of disrepair, is to Reigning, like Heaven, supreme, we saw at length, be renovated at a cost of 15,000 francs. Lifting its head mid ruin's circling gloom The condemned portion of Peterborough Cathedral has In scorn of Time, and like a type of strength been removed, and the foundation stones of the new piers Never to be o'erthrown: Metella's Tomb have been laid in concrete on solid rock ; but it is now Great thoughts rushed o'er me as I saw that tower feared that the two western piers will also be condemned, 'Neath which a Roman laid his love to rest, as their old foundations were laid in loose earth four feet And softly to myself I said, "No power, above the rock. o time, no tyrant, from the human breast— With reference to the forthcaming new edition of Boa- Not death iteelf—immortal love can sever. With "Johnson," it will interest many people to know Yes, Rome is dead, but Love lives on for ever !" (writes the Atheneum) that some of the earliest of Dr. Reme February 2nd, 1883. T. At the time they were printed ,in Croker's edition they belonged to Miss Cave, of Read- ing, from whom they descended to the lady who now owns them. We learn from Engineering that in recent trials of the speed of working on the Jay Gould cables laid across the Atlantic from Penzance to Canso, in Nova Scotia, 1.000 cods W"-L'is were lSfr,:ml FerlslOCe anl tecetred at the Carare itelAi'?n, in '``ele 'minutes, inelnding all repetitions and corrections. The 1,000 words consisted of 7,233 letters, I which is about equivalent to 1,458 worde of five letters each, the average number for the English language. The above rate of transmission is therefore equal to 18 words of five letters per minute. The writer who contributes to the Gentleman's Magazine under the nom de plume of " Sylvanus Urban," makes the suggestion that the Griffin should be replaced by a statue of Samuel Johnson. "Next year," he says," will be the cen- tenary of the death of Samuel Johnson. The prapriety of commemorating the occasion by some form of ceremonial has already begun to be discussed. Johnson is a promising subject for a sculptor, and I cannot but think that the genius of a Woolner could be put to no better purpose than enriching London with a statue worthy of the name." Ramabhai, the Sanskrit poetess, spent several days at Oxford last week. She was the guest of Prof. Max Muller. The extraordinary power of her memory, and the fluency and correctness with which she speaks Sanskrit, and com- poses extempore Sanskrit poetry in the most difficult metres, surprised all who saw her. Pandit Shyttmaji Krishnavarma, Mr. Visvas, of Calcutta, the Rev. C. Bellairs, lately of Bom- bay, and others had been invited to meet Rarnabhai. She is probably the first learned Brahmani who has crossed the ocean. She traces her descent from the old Vedic family of Siindilya.—Atheneum. UTILISING THE SIIN'S RAM—Professor E. S. Morse, at a recent meeting of the American Association for the Advance- ment of Science, held in Minneapolis, called attention to his plan for utilising the sun's rays for warming and ventilation. The device consists mainly of a slaty surface, painted black, placed vertically on the outside wall of a building, with flues to conduct the warm air to the inside. The slates are inserted in a groove-like glass in a frame. One made last year was Bft. long by 3ft. wide and was used for warming a ' library, measuring 20ft. by 14th, and 10ft. high. By this means the room was kept comfortable throughout the winter, except on a few of the coldest days. When the sun's rays rested directly on the apparatus, the air passing through it was raised about 30 deg., and it discharged 3,206 cubic feet of warm air per hour. This was in the morning. At 11 45 a.m. the air was raised 29 deg., when 3,726 cubic feet of air were discharged; at 12 45 p.m., 29 deg., and 4,019 cubic feet; at 1 55 p.m., 24deg., and 3,062 feet; at 245 p.m., 20 deg. and 1,299 feet. As a general result of the experiments, a difference of 30 deg. can be secured during the four or five working hours of the day. SEVERAL INTERESTING DISCOVERIES were reported last month. In a little country house at Blankenheim, in Rhenish Prussia, an oil painting has been found concealed behind the wainscot, and proves to be a Raphael which be- longed to the Dusseldorf Gallery about a hundred years ago, but mysteriously disappeared. eat Berlin, Marie An- toinette's harp has come to light in an old curiosity shop ; it is richly inlaid with ivory, and bears the name of the maker, and its history has been traced since it was carried as a souvenir by one Fleury, the Queen's valet. From St. Petersburg the discovery has been announced of eighty-one original drawings by Greuze, hidden away in the attic of the Academy of Fine Arts. In the archives of the Indies at Seville, an immense collection of historic documents con- nected with the discovery of America has been unearthed and classified, and among them has been found a list of the names of all but two of Columbus's companions in his first voyage. The Italian Government has secured for £2OO the archives of the Palla-Strozzi family at Florence, contain- ing more than 500 curious parchments of the 13th, islth, and 15th centuries, chiefly relating to the Papal Court and the Spanish embassies.

BABY. Where did you come from, baby dear? Out of the everywhere into here. IS here did you get your eyes so blue? Out of the skies as I came through. What makes your forehead smooth and high? atral it as I went by. What Makes your cheek like a warm white rose? I saw something better than any one knows. Whence that three-cornered smile of bliss? Three angels gave me at once a kiss. Where did you get that coral ear? God spoke, and it came out to hear. Where did you get those arms and hands? Love made itself into bonds and bands. Whence came 'Your feet, dear little things? From the same box as the cherub's wings. How did they all first come to be you? God thought about ma, and so I grew. But how did you come to us, you dear? God thought about you, and so I am here. GEORGE MACDONALD

When a man turns over a new leaf he is too frequently near the conclusion of the book of life. The famous Boston musical association has given the Messiah 74 times. It ought to know how to Handel it by this time. "Can any one tell what the wind whistles for ?" asked a young man at a pic-nic. "It whistles for the leaves to dance by," demurely replied a young lady. Honour is like a looking-glass, which, when only sullied by an unwholesome breath, may be wiped clean again; but if once it is cracked, it is never to be repaired. All grumbling, and hill speeches, and talebearing is doing the devil's work. All disorder and laziness is doing the devil's work. All cruelty and brutality is doing the devil's work.—Kingsley. Crying at weddings has gone out of fashion. Smilipg is the thing now, and the bridegroom is not made to feel as though he was a hardhearted pirate and buccaneer, who is ruthlessly destroying a happy home. This II a big im- provement. Buchanan, a short time before he died (at the age of 76), had completed his" History of Scotland," which had occu- pied his attention for twelve years. Finding his end draw- ing nigh, he inquired of a servant how touch money he had remaining; when, finding 4 was not sufficient to defray the expenses of his funeral, he ordered it to be given to the poor —leaving the city of Edinburgh to bear the expense of his burial. Having interred his four wives together, a disconsolate widower embalmed their memory thus:— Stranger, pause and drop a tear, For Mary Jane lies buried here, Mingled in a most surprising manner With Susan, Maria, and portions of Hannah. A Par SHOT.—A Dakota schoolmistress sued three young men for breach of promise. Counsel for one of the defendants moved for a nonsuit, on the ground that she was too promiscuous. The sourt seemed disposed to grant the motion, whereapon the plaintiff asked, "Jude, did you ever go duck-shooting?" His Honour's eyes lighted up with the pride of a sportsman as he answered. "Well, I should say so; and ntany's the time that I've brought down a dozen at a shot." ".1 kaew it," eagerly added the fair plaintiff: "that's just the case with me, Judge. A dock of these fellows besieged me, and I winged three of them." The motion for a nonsuit was denied. _ .

DANIEL ROWLANDS, OF LLANGEITUO.—It is now more than ninety years since Daniel Rowlands died, but his tune lasts still. The memorial statue reeently erected at lel ea- geitho, in Cardiganshire, proves that Wales has not yet fa:- gotten one who was the greatest even among the famous preachers she cite boast. When he WAS at the height of his fame, people would come fifty or sixty miles to listen to him, and sometimes on a single Sunday he would receive 1,500 and even 2,500 communicants at the Communists. The story of his rupture with tile Church is a sad one. In his zeal he ignored the reetrictiona of the parochial system, and encroached upon the parishes of neighbouring clergy. Remonstrance was ineffectual, and in 1763 his license was revoked. Such a man, of coarse, was not to be silenced. When he left the Church his people followed him, and now they have become the largest religious body in Wales—the Calvinistic Methodists. As Bishop IVle has pointed out, no graver blunder could have been committed, and the Church in Wales has never recovered from the loss. While too many of the clergy were living lives of indifference, if not of immorality, here was a man, full of apostolic faith and fire, silenced and ejected because his passionate devo- tion to .his Master swept him beyond the boundaries of human making. An error like this cannot be retrieved, even by years of devoted labour.—Sundaji Magazine. GETTING RID OF TROUBLE.—In young persons there is usually an abundance of life, a spirit of activity, a desire to be doing something. But even to y9ung persons some kinds of labour are very distasteful. There is something at first very irksome to a young person in most kinds of regu- lar, plodding work. If he perseveres, the irksome feeling will pass away, and he will do his work easily, patiently, and even pleasantly. But if he gives way, the irksomeness of labour will be a greater and greater bugbear, and try what he may he will never succeed. It is in this way that the spirit of confirmed indolence is formed in many. In- stead of grappling with the irksome and overcoming it, it is allowed to overcome them, and they are good for nothing. Everything is such a trouble, everything bores them. They ought to be ashamed to say so. It is a token that they have been vanquished by a foe when it would have been easy for them to conquer. Let young people and all people face wholesome labour bravely, and the idea of trouble will rapidly disappear. Let them scorn the thought of their being vanquished by the mean spirit of indolence—of their being found incapable of a few hours' steady and earnest application to any form of honest labour, however humble. Let them guard against the approaches of indolence, and cultivate the habit of making good use of fragments of time. Let them "have a time for everything, and every- thing in its time;' and it is certain that a vast amount of what is called "trouble" will vanish, and the work of life will go on smoothly and steadily, bringing pleasure as well as profit. A BEGGAR DOG'S ASSISTANT.—WhiIst walking from the North Stockton Station into the town early one morning, I overtook a bright-faced healthy little girl carrying a can and a small basket. Asking her for a drink, she replied, "Nay, sir, it's my daddy's breakast." So, walking beside her, she drew my attention to a large brown retriever dog lying in front of an upholsterer's establishment, by saying, "Do you see that dog, sir? If you give it a penny it will go to that shop (nodding to a pork butcher's on the other aide of the road), and the man will give it something for it. It used to have another dog to help it, but some bad person poisoned it. Wasn't it a shame?" I said it was and bade her good morning. Some two months after this con- versation, I had occasion to pass the same place' and there was my old friend the retriever, lying exactly where he did, but this time he was not by himself, he had a fox terrior with him. No sooner did I come to a standstill than the terrior began to bark and caper about like a mad thing. The old dog got up, but it was quite painful to see how stiff and old he was, I put a penny into his month, and he took it as carefully as possible from my hand, and in company with the small dog, who never ceased to bark, walked across to the butcher's. They waited outside un- til the door was opened. The man knew what was wanted and gave them some scraps, which was equally divided between them. The most interesting part of this story seems to be the amount of instinct which enabled the old dog to teach the terrior to bark whilst he carried the money, for if he had barked the money would have dropped out of his mouth. These dogs can be seen now, and would be thankful for any and) the smallest contributions.— Cot.., Leeds Mercury, Weekly. THE Quener UORNET.—Last fall I desired to add to my rare collection a large hornet's nest. I had an embalmed tarantula and her porcelain-lined nest, and I desired to add to these the gray and airy home of the hornet. I procured one of the large size, after cold weather, and hung it in my cabin by a string. I forgot all about it until this spring. When warm weather came something reminded me of it. I think it was a hornet. lle jogged my memory in some way, and called my attention to it. Memory is not located where I thought it was. It seemed XS though whenever he touched me he awakened a memory—a warm memory With a red place all round it. Then some more hornets came and be- gan to rake up old personalities. I remember that one of them lit on my upper lip. He thought it W,i3 a rosebud. When he went away it looked like a gladiolus bulb. I wrapped a wet sheet around it to take out the warmth and reduce the swelling, so that I could go through the folding doors and tell my wife about it. Hornets lit all over and walked around on any person. I did not care to scrape them off because they are so sensitive. You have to be very guarded in your conduct towards a hornet. I remember once while I was watching the busy little hornet gathering honey and June bugs from the bosom of a rose years ago. I stirred him up with a climb, more as a practical joke than anything else, and he came and lit on my sunny hair—that was when I wore my own hair—and he walked around through my gleaming tresses quite a while, making tracks as large as a water-melon all over my head. If he hadn't run out of tracks my head would have looked like a load of summer squashes. I remember I had to thump my head agalnet the smoke-house in order to smash him, and I had to comb him out with a fine comb and wear a waste paper basket two weeks for a hat. Much has been said of the hornet, but he has an old, quaint way, after all, that is for over zew.—BiU N.Ye•

! THE GOOSEHERRY.—Where these are in poor condition it ' would be economical to uproot them and plant young ones in a fresh place. If they are doing moderately well they way be allowed to remain till the newly planted ones are established. Some err by planting fresh trees on the ground occupied by those recently pulled up, the result being a par- tial, if not a total failure. The gooseberry is such a popu- - tar fruit that we are surprised that the trees we frequently see have sash a hungry, neglected appearance. Though its fruit does not reach maturity till late in the season, it is at the same time used and appreciated months before that, and sooner than any other out-of-door fruit. It has frequently occurred to us that it might be more extensively planted without occupying much valuable space. Why should not the boundaries of gardens be defined by a gooseberry hedge instead of one of thorn? Why not farmers plant them in their newly-formed hedgerows and gentlemen in their shrub- beries? We imagine plenty would be ready to ask what about ma.' in the'hedges ? We reply that the gooseberry does not refuse to bear when closely pruned, and we re- member an old gardener who for years clipped his trees with the shears. From the nature of the gooseberry we conclude it would be as formidable -a barrier as the thorn. The tree thrives in any soil that will allow roots to pene- trate it, and prefers moist soil to a naturally dry one. In a cottage garden the trees take less room and occupy less cul- tivatable ground if planted near the sides of the paths, and the picking of a great portion of the fruit may be per- formed without treading the ground or struggling amongst the trees. The distance between the trees may vary from 5 feet upwards, and whilst the trees are small the inter- mediate spaces can be profitably cropped, providing care is taken not to dig too near the roots to destroy them. The spade should not be used round trees within the area covered by their own branches. The varieties of gooseberries are very numerous, the show varieties alone consisting of more than 300, and there are more than 30 ordinary kinds. All growers have certain favourities, so it is probable they all have their patrons. The following are amongst the best for flavour :—Reds: Red Champagne, Warrington, Rough Red, , Ironmonger, and Crown Bob. Yellows: Yellow Champagne, Leader, Perfection, and Yellow Ball. Greens: Keepsake, ' Pitmaston, Greengage, and Model. Whites: Early White, White Champagne, Bright Venus, and Whitesmith. Some of the large show varieties, though course and wanting flavour, have the merit of being ready to pick before the others, simply because they are larger. CURRANTS.—The various kinds of these may now be planted, and as they do not object to shade, they will do under larger fruit trees, providing they are not too near their stems. The plants are best with a clear stem a few inches high, and no more than two inches of it should be covered in planting. The holes should be made slightly convexed, and large enough for the roots to be laid straight out, instead of being crowded into a hole not half large enough. If the trees at planting time are rather large, it is advisable to insert a stake to steady them, and their pruning must be deferred till they commence to grow in the spring. Amongst Black .Currants, the best varieties are Black Naples and Lee's Prolific. P.aby Castle is a fine red; so is Red Dutch and Long Bunched. Of Whites, there are the Transparent White and White Dutch. THE FRONT G&RDEN.—Echeveria glanca, a succulent plant nearly related to the common houseleek, and fre- quently used with pleasing results as edgings for small beds or borders, is nearly hardy, and as it is occasionally grown in cottage gardens, we shall offer a few remarks which, if attended to, will ensure its safety through the winter. Its succulent nature enables it to exist for months without water, so that its security depends upon a light dry posi- tion. An idea of the ease with which it may be protected may be gleaned from the following. Having more plants one season than we could accommodate in the usual way, the plants were taken up and stacked against the base of a chimney, a slate being placed under the lowest row, which was brought out a few inches to admit of piling up so much higher and secure a better footing, and the packing amongst the roots was done with fine ashes. A piece of tin was nailed to the chimney, projecting over them to throw off the wet, which is their greatest enemy in winter; and in this position they remained till planting time. If taken up and placed close together in boxes, it is not necessary to place any soil round them; they may be placed on a shelf in the back kitchen, or any other light position at the cot- tager's command. THE WINDOW.—Colens, which is of the same natural order as our common dead Nettle, is a tedious plant, that tries the patience and skill of the cottager to preserve through the winter, but with care it can be successfully done. What would be considered a moderate supply of water to some plants would be certain death to these. They ' are also injured by the slightest touch of Jack Frost's cold ands; therefore they should have the warmest spot, and On frosty nights be placed on the shelf usually fixed over th .tePlace, and replaced again in the window in the to oet relative these wetibeautifullhleo Nettle, etht tel eh, foliageys bo rams ts pot apanrnot sdd produce cbe ee a crossedona le Immv iaotdhrnetishnugebi.rmhiCsasoriudvlyed of hardier plants, what a rich treat we should have. Their distant natural affinities are probably the cause of their obstinacy to this much-desired alliance.

A bald-headed man, who has heard that the hairs of a man's head are numbered, wants to know if there is not sonse place where he can obtain the back numbers. No matter how humble the individual, he has an allotted function in life, and if he honestly discharges that duty which comes first to hand he is fulfilling his mission here. "Dear Mr. Jones," said a learned woman, " you remind me of a barometer that is filled with nothing in the upper story." "Divine Amelia Brown," said he, "you Occupy my upper story."

The man that don't measure and weigh everything about a dairy can't tell what he is doing, and it's just as easy for him to lose a dollar a day as it is to fall off a log. Now, my boy, put that wrinkle on your horn; it's worth a thousand dollars to you if you don't forget it, but you are welcome to it for nothing." SountnowN SHEEP FAnms.—Col. Kingscote, who has a large home farm on his estate on the Cotswold Hills, breedsannually from 300 pure Sussex Down ewes. This flock has been in existence a great number of years, and the greatest care and judgment have been taken in retaining the pure type of this useful, hardy breed of sheep. The system of management is that generally practised in the district, which is to put the sheep on roots as soon as the seeds and grass are cleared off, which is usually ia November, upon which, with a libe- ral allowance of hay, they live and do well as long as the roots last, which is often long over lambing time. One hun- dred old ewes are drafted every year, and the same number of young ones takes their place. All the wether lambs are kept on the farm until At for the butcher; the lint draft often being dent to market soon after Christmas, always bringing the highest price. The 300 ewes have for many years shown at shearing time from 340 to 300 lambs. The ewes are allowed occasionally, through the winter, to run over a bare pasture for exercise. This system of keeping certainly answers well, as the flock has always been espe- cially healthy, and losses very trifling. Lord Moreton, who „,neio rayni; t J.!, vale of itioneester, also keeps a choice flock of pure Soutbdowns, and the system of man- agement is much the same as above described, but the land is better and the flock not so large, couseinently there is rather a better average of lambs. As long as this flock has t been in existence the drop of lambs has averaged one-third more than the number of ewes put to the rams. The Fro- tcester Court flock, belonging to Mr. Charles Chapman, is also of the pure Southdown breed. The ewes are kept a good deal on grass, three-fourths of the land being pasture, a portion of which is hilly, well calculated for sheep. The , lambs are pat on roots in the autumn, and there remain as long as they last; the wethers, having the best chance, go off fat in the spring. The roots often hold for the ewe lambs until the spring feed, rye, vetches, ,is ready to take them. Two hundred and thirty ewes are annually put to the rams, and for many years the average of lamls has been one-third over the number of ewes turned out. Very high-bred stock, whether cattle, sheep, or pigs, are not usually so productive as ordinary bred animals, and proba- bly a lower class of Downs would show a greater average of lambs than the flocks mentioned, which are of the finest quality and purity of breeding, amply proved by the success which has attended the specimens exhibited at the great agricultural shows of the country, including the "Royal" at York this year. On all three of the farms the ewes are on grass during the time the rams are with them, as, indeed, they have been for some time previous, there being a fair proportion of pasture on each of the farms. On Col. Kings- cote's farm, on the Cotswold Hills, the ewes are turned out earlier than at Lord Moreton's or Mr. Chapman's, which are vale farms—the former on the first and the latter in the end of September. The number of ewes to'each ram varies from fifty to eighty. As the ewes are not often put on roots until the end of November, the rams are usually taken away before that time.
MISCELLANEOUS.

Dr. Oakley (Dean of Carlisle) haa accepted the Deanory of Manchester, offered him by the Premier. The schooner Fanny Truss' of Chester, was on Saturday destroyed by fire in the New Harbour, Holyheal Two men were killed by a landslip on the London and South-Western Railway n-,ar Andover, on Saturday. The Marquis of Lorne has promised to visit Birmingham during the Cattle Show week, early next month, and give a lecture on Canada.

The agricultural look-out is favourable for the tinio of vear. There is plenty of grass, and the young wheats look retnarkably well. Settling day in the Liverpool Cotton Market, which had been anticipated with considerable anxiety, passed withwat any further failures;
--I.Ehe health of the Archbishop of Canterbury has greatly improved. On Saturday he mts able to take a walk for the &et time since his illness.

At Ipswich, on Monday, Walter Makens, cattle dealer, wag I dried £46 and costs for exposing 23 bullocks affected with foot-and-mouth disease at Ipswich market on the 16th of November. It is stated that there is no truth in the statement pub- lished by an evening paper that Mr. Brand is retiring from the Speakership, he having decided to retain office during Jt i-,feent Parliament, At Scarborough, ifl aurday evening., a house in the poor , part of the town was discovered on tire, and on the premises , being entered an old woman, name' Wood, aged 76, was I found burned to death. Mr. J. K. Cross, 'M.P., Under Secretary for India, has left for Marseilles, en route for Egypt, where he will have an interview with Sir Evelyn Baring on Indian affairs, re- turning home for Christmas. The sentence of death passed at Ipswich assizes upon Thomas Lyons Day, for the murder of his illegitimate child in August last, was carried into effect at Ipswich Gaol on Tuesday morning, Binns being the executioner. The only survivor from the British steamer Iris, recently wrecked on Cape Vallano, is George Chirgwin, of Penzance. The Iris was owned at Hull, and was bound from Cardiff for Port Said. She had a crew of thirty-six hands. At the Maidstone Assizes, George rebel, member of the Folkestone Town Council, and Charles Knight were charged with being concerned in the recent riot at Folkestone directed against the Salvation Army. The jury acquitted the prisoners. The PARCHL POST.—Orders have been given for the pay- ment to the railway comiAnies of the United Kingdom of a sum of £35.392, being the amount earned by them during August and September the two first months of ex'stence of the parcel post. A Cumberland policeman, namd Little, has been com- mitted for trial for the manslaughter of a prisoner named Maxwell. It was alleged that the officer deliberately " crushed " his prisoner, who was on the ground, with his knee with such violence as to cause his death.

Mr.. Radford, official auditor of the Durham Union, re- ported to the Durham Guardians, on Saturday, that although the audit of accounts of Mr. J. Moore, rate col- lector for the Union had not yet been completed, defalca- tions amounting to i 1,061 had already been discovered. The delegates from the Transvaal had an interview with Mr. Gladstone on Tuesday. The right hon. gentleman, after hearing lengthy statements from Mr. Kruger and others, is said to have expressed an opinion which was regarded as favourable to the objects which the deputation have in OIL

Several destructive fires occurred on Tuesday. The Rag- lan Music Hall, Union-street, London, was almost com- pletely destroyed; damage to the extent of about £3OOOO was done at the Old Quay Flour Mill, Runcorn; and the Orleans Mill, Old.ha,n, suffered to the amount of several hundred pounds. An extraordinary discovery has been made in a bale of cotton delivered to the Shaw Side Mill, Crotnpton, near Oldham. In the middle of the bale was found a five- chambered revolver, and two of the chambers were loaded. Strange articles have been found in bales, but never before a loaded revolver.

At the Sheffield Town Hall, on Monday, George Coggin and Ellen &mop, who eloped last month, going to Derby and Birkenhead, were committed for trial at the sessions for stealing a large quantity of wearing apparel and other things, the property of George Jessop. Coggin had lodged at Jessop's house, and the female prisoner ran away with him, leaving seven children and taking the goods. An accident occurred to a train laden with limestone

while running between Strines and Marple on Monday night, the result being that the line was blocked until Tues- day at noon. No person was injured. A train from Ayr was in collision near Paisley, on Monday, with a train from Carlisle. One man was so badly injured that he had to bs taken to the Infirmary. Three others were slightly hurt. SEVERE SrcrowsTortm.—A snowstorm occurred on Monday

throughout Dorsetshlre, the fall in some of the more ex- posed parts of the country being two or three inches deep, and in some places even more. Farming stock of all kinds has suffered considerably from the effects of the storm, par- ticularly sheep, as the present month is an especially critical period to fiock;nasters owing to the lambing season being at its height. After a trial at the Chester AFS'Z?S extending over several days, Henry Morgan, a wool dealer of Newton, Montgomery was on Monday acquitted of several charges of fraud con- nected with his bankruptcy, wherein a sum of £26,000 was involved. There were allegations that Morgan had deceived his trustee, and also set fire to his office in order to destroy his books of account and other documents. Lord Justice Baggallay thought the prosecution had been too hasty in preferring an indictment against the prisoner before ascer- taining certain questions of ownership which must be left to a court of Chancery. There are :reports of numerous casualties owing to the dense fog which prevailed generally over the kingdom during the early part of the week. Two men walked into the harbour at Glasgow and were drowned. Near Paisley two passenger trains were in collision, and several passen- gers were injured, one being removed to hospital. Con- siderable delay and inconvenience was cinsed to shipping by the fog, and at Liverpool the cross-river traffic was greatly retarded. A train of waggons laden with limestone broke down on Monday night in a tunnel near Marple, and the Midland Railway traffic between Manchester and the South was greatly disarranged. The line was not cleared until Tuesday afternoon. A collision between passenger trains also occurred at Stourbridge, but the damage was only slight. AN UNDISTURBED PRIZEFIGHT.—A most determined and well-arranged prizefight took place between ten and eleven on Monday night, adjoining one of the principal thorough- fares leading out of Nottingham, and within ten minutes' walk of the great Market-place. To show how cleverly the affair was planned, a small group, not exceeding fifty in number, fixed upon a field close to the railway, where the luggage trucks shunt and whistle. The combatants were the champion light weight of the Midland counties and a burly tradesman of Nottingham, scaling at least three stone more than his antagonist. One of Alfred Greenfield's closest friends seconded the little champion, who, during the sharp eight rounds that lasted, knocked his opponent all over the shop, gave him a severe beating, and Cams out of the affray little injured, except about the body. On a beautiful moon- light night, and undisturbed by the police, they fought for £lO aside.

ENGLISH PATENTS.—The following patents amongst others, published in the Commissioners of Patents Journal were sealed during the week ending November 10th, 18S3: —Wm. Tatham, Rochdale, machine maker, improvements in or applicable to engines for carding frame materials; Michael Guive, Leicester, improvements in machinery for making knitted under shirts; Alexander Stewart, ilradford, improvements in cupola and blast furnaces, and in appara- tus employed in the manufacture of iron and steal; Harry- Shield and William Norris Crockett, Nottingham, improve- ments in rotary screens for screening or separating grain, seeds, or other materials; William Corteeni Sheffield, im- provements in and relating to carriage brake apparatus; William Tristram and William Whitehead, Bolton, hn- provements in looms for weaving; Fred. Byron, Chester- fi dd, improvements in pencil point protectors; David Edwards and John Williams, Cardiff, improvements in the joints of drain pipes for land draining and other purposes. List supplied by Mr.. George Davies, CE., Fel. Inst. P.A., patent solicitor, 4, St. Ann's-square, Manchester. SINGULAR ABDUCTION CASE.—An English detective, who had travelled by the night mail from Dublin, proceeded on Sunday morning to a private lodging house in Tramare, a 'fashionable watering place about five miles from Waterford, and arrested a young man named Phillip Bartlett, described as a niedical student, on the charge of abduction. He also arrested the young lady he is alleged to have decoyed from her home on the charge of having stolen from her parents jewellery to the amount of £3O, also about £l5O in cash. The girl, who has just turned her .15th year, is the only child of a gentleman of independent means residing in the suburbs of Manchester. Last summer the family sojourned at Southport, and while there Brrtlett is stated to have made the acquaintance of the girl's governess, and in this way learned that when her charge became of age she would be entitled to £4,000 a year in her own right. Bartlett at once transferred his affections from the governess to the young lady, whom he managed to meet clandestinely during the stay at Southport, and after she returned to Manchester with her parents. The governess had her suspicions arouses, and, watching the girl's movements, one evening early in October, traced her to Peel Park, where Bartlett joired her. The governess reperted the occurrence that evening, and the girl's parents at once decided on send- ing her to a boarding school, which they did on November Ist. Two days afterwards the principal of the school tele- graphed to the girl's parents to kn.iw if she had returned home, as she had disappeared from the school the previous night. Her parents replied in the negative, and her mother, on searching, found that a large quantity of jewellery was missing, as well as over £l5O in bank notes and gold. Through the governess 13artlett's London address was ascertained. Inquiry there led to the disclosure that he had left on the night of the 20,1 instant, and had not returned, his whereabouts.being unknown. Informations were sworn and warrants of arrest issued against the youth and the girl, and were placed in the hands of a detective, who traced the fugitives to Dublin, and thence to the south of Ireland. He traced them to their lodgings, and at 9 o'clock arrested tkem there. They offered no resistance. All the st,len jewellery was handed to the detective. During the day they arrived at Waterford in charge of the detective, and left in;the evening for Dublin, en route to England. The Rev. Charles Richard Holme, M.A., vicar of All Souls', Halifax, committed suicide on Thursday morning by cutting his throat. Mr. Fawcett (Postmaster General) was on Thursday elected Lord Rector of Glasgow University, defeating the Marquis of Bute and Mr. Ruskin.

While waiting for the train at Lochnahen station on Tnursday, the Rev. Mr. Hill, Free Church minister, sud- denly fell on the platform and expired. Only the waters in the shin can sink the ship; but while kept outside all the heaving deep waters thundering over three-fifths of the globe can work no shipwreck. THE "SHROPSHIRE MYSTERY" EXPLODED.—The Shrop- shire mystery has at length been exploded. It is said the gitl Emma Davies threw the buckets, looking glasses, ctc., about on her own account.

Investigation has le-d-i-O-the conclusion that the recent fire at the Albart Dock warehous4s, Liverpool, was the work of an incendiary. The Dock Board, on Tnursday, decided to offer a reward of £5OO for the discovery of the offender. The trial of the charge of fraud brought against a Mac- clesfield printer named John Henry Wood in connection with the insolvency of another tradesmen in the same town has, after occupying three days, resulted in a verdict of acquittal.

At a meeting held at Chester on Thursday evening, in support of a scheme for founding a museum in the city, it wag announced that the Duke of Westminster had given a large portion of the necessary site, in addition to a sum of £4,000 towards the cost of the building. THE CLEnreAL BIGAMIST.—At the Warwick Assizes, on Thursday, Thomas Morris Hughes (43), clergyman of the Church of England, pleaded guilty to the charge of bigamy at Birminghem, and was sentenced to seven years' penal ser- vitude. Ile had been previously convicted. Fenelon, who had often teased Richelieu ineffectually for charitable subscriptions, was one day telling him that he had just seen his picture. "And did you ask it for a sub- scription?" said Richelieu sneeringly. "No, I saw there was no chance," said Fenelon, "it was so like you." Tim BIRMINGHAM BANK FRAUDS. At the Warwick Assizes, on Thursday, before Mr. Justice Stephen John Alfred Burgan, formerly manager of the Union Bank, Bir- mingham, pleaded guilty to forging two bank drafts for £4,000 and £5,000 respectively, and also to falsifying the accounts of the bank. He was sentenced to fifteen years' penal servitude. FLOODING OF A FLINTSHIRE COLLIRRY.—The whole of the men employed at the Dublin Main Coal Company's Works, Northup, Flintshire, have been thrown out of em- ployment by the sudden and alarming flooding of the works. The loss to the proprietors will be very heavy, as it is con- sideled impossible by constant pumping to clear the mine of water and for the men to resume work before January next.

A very interesting ceremony was performed on Wednes- day, at Edinburgh. Seventeen stand of colours formerly carried by Scottish regiments, had been collected from their various resting places in Scotland, and were presented by the Duke of Cambridge to the authorities of St. Gibe's Cathedral for deposit in that venerable and newly-restored edifice. The presentation W 33 signalised by a military and popular denier) stration _ _

. Upon the colliers going to work, on Wednesday morning, at the Granville Colliery, Rowley, belonging to Messrs. Swindell and Company, they discovered that a fire was raging ki the pit shaft, and it was found nec ssary to close it. A large number of men have been thown out of em- ployment, and it is feared the proprietors of the colliery witl sustain heavy losses. A fire broke out in the same colliery some six months ago, and it was closed for three months.

Sir Alexander Gordon, M.P., speaking at the annual meeting of the Scottish Chamber of Agriculture, said that in London for the past six months 37,842 of the oxen killed were healthy, and 24,386 diseased; 7,800 calves were healthy, and 2,900 diseased; and 70,000 sheep were healthy, and 33,000 diseased. Diseased animals were rejected by the Jewish community and eaten by the Christians, with the result that the average life of the Jews was ten years longer than that of the Christians. The breach of promise ease Miller v. Joy came to a con- clusion on Thursday in the Queen's Bench Court. The learned judge,' in summing up, said he thought the jury would hardly think it a case for very heavy damages unless they felt that the plaintiff had had her feelings outraged by a heartless man. After an absence of a little more than half an hour the jury found for the plaintiff, with £2,350 damages' and for the plaintiff also on the counter claim. Notice of appeal was given. CURIOUS SEQUEL TO A MAYORAL CEREMONY.—At Black- burn, on Thursday, Thomas Ainsworth, landlord of the Wheat Sheaf Inn, was fined 40s and costs for having his house open during p ohibited hours, and 25 men, including some of the local Volunteers, the w -emanry, and members of the Borough Band, were fined 5s and costs each for aiding and abetting. The 25 had taken part in the mayoral pro- cession to church, and during the service went to the public— house, which was the headquarters of the Borough Band. Speaking at the opening of the Bradford Girls' Grammar School extension on Tuesday, Mr. W. E. Forster, M.P., said one of the most satisfactory features of the age was the im- provement being made in the position of women, not merely in matters of education, but in the opening out of new spheres of employment and the bestowal of more right. With respect to the vote for women, Mr. Forster was still of opinion that in apportioning the work of the world, men had better not throw upon women the hard duty of voting or the harder duties of representation. CHARGE OF ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE. On Saturday, at the Maidstone as.sins, Mary Ann Godfrey, a respectable-looking young woman was charged with at- tempting to murder her child, Charlotte Alice Godfrey, two Years old; and she was also charged with attempting to kill herself by throwing herself into the river Medway at Gil- lingham. For the defence, evidence to the effect that the prisoner was in a hysterical condition, and hardly knew what she was doing; and it was also suggested that she might have fallen into the water by accident. The jury returned a verdict of not guilty. Mr. Justice Kay refused on Thursday to release from Hol- loway Faison a certain Captain Dawson, who was committed to gaol four months ago for "contempt." The prisoner, it appeared, had been guilty of contempt of the most flagrant kind in marrying a ward of r, Court—who was, of course, possessed of a considerable property—and his offer to make a very humble apology to the Court was scouted. Mr. Justice Kay inci— dentally remarked upon the difficult and painful duties which Chancery Judges have to discharge in protecting the interests of their "wards "

THE WORKING OF THE ARTIZANS' DWELLING ACT.—A Parliamentary paper was issued on Thursday, showing what had been done by the various local authorities under the Artizans' Dwelling Act. The Commissioners of Sewers of the Cky of London report 22 areas, and the Metropolitan Board of Works, 33, as either dealt with or in process of dealing with. At Birmingham, the estimated net cost is over £500,000; Liverpool, £62,900; Wolverhampton, £45,000; Derby, £37,000; Nottingham, £35,000; Norwich, £20,000; Newcastle, £18,000; Swansea, £11,000; Walsall, £10,000; and Devonport, £3,000. The Act is under con- sideration at live other towns.

DISORDERLY SCENE.—A scene of great disorder occurred at the Memorial Hall, Farringdon-street, Londoa, on Thurs- day night, at which place Herr Stoeker was announced to deliver an address on "Christian Socialism." Although ad- mission was 1.3- ticket, the hall was taken possession of by a large number of persons, who greeted Herr Stoeker with groans and shouts. A large Republican flag was unfurled in the body of the hall, and red Republican and other ban- ners were exhibited. The " Marseillaise " was sung, and the platform was taken possession of by the opposing party, with cheers for the next revolution. Eventually Herr Stoeker and his supporters were obliged to retire, and the meeting then dispersed. RAILWAY MYSTERIES.—An elderly man named James Lincoln was found one the Midland Railway near Green. lane Station, London, on Tuesday evening, much injured about the head. He was unable to explain how he got on the railway.—The inquest was resumed at Tottenham, on Wednesday afternoon, on Virginia Elizabeth Ball, aged 29, daughter of an independent gentlemm, of Tullington Park, Islington. Deceased was found on the Great Eastern Rail- way, her skull being fractured and a number of incised wounds on the head. She had been seen in an intoxicated condition in company of a young man on the night of the occurrence. The jury returned an open verdict—On Wed- nesday the dead body of a man named Neale was found hor- ribly mutilated on the line of the Dublin, Wicklow, and Wexford Railway, near Arllow. It is supposed that the oleceased was trespassing on the line, and was knocked down and killed by a passing train, but much mystery surrounds the affair.

DEATH OF A VETERAN MOULDER.-Mr. Jas. Birtwhistle, a man widely known and respected in his sphere of life, died at his residence in the Ring o' Bells yard, Halifax, the other night, at the advanced age of 85 years, having been born in 1798. He had therefore lived during the reign of (cur sovereigns. Mr. Birtwhistle, who was a moulder in an Iron foundry, worked at his trade for seventy years, and up to within a few weeks of his death, having for the last thirty years been employed at Mr. John Crossley's foundry at Bank- bottom, Halifax. For sixty-one years he was a member of the Moulders' Society, and was with one exception the eldest associate of that body in England. Tke oldest associate ceased work some 15 years ago. Deceased was a teetotaller of fifty years' standing, and was hale and hearty almost up to the last. Mr. Birtwistle was an efficient workman, and of the noteworthy incidents of his lengthy career it may be mentioned that it was he who made the rails for the old North Bridge, Halifax, and put them into position. He likewise made an image of the giant Goliath, of much interest to moulders, and it now stands in the grounds of a gentleman resident at Halifax. In his younger days deceased had to wander about a good deal in search of work, and it is said that during these pere- grinations he covered 900 miles, visiting different parts of England and Wales, and also Scotland. He was conse- quently wiC.ely known. Twice he walked to London and back. It is related of him that rarely was he ever in bed after four o'clock in the morning. In the young he always took a great interest, and he had the satisfaction of knowing that by his influence and advice he was the means of en- couraging in their early struggles several young men who now occupy honourable positions. His remains were in- terred at Halifax on Saturday, being followed to their last resting place by his late master, Mr. Crossley, and many sorrowing relatives and friends. It had been intended that the members of the various trade societies with which deceased was connected should have been present to pay their last tribute of respect to him, and it was only through a slight misunderstanding that the funeral was not of a more public character. div.p: NOTES ON A.GRICULTURE, CULTURE, eze. , .

POINT() GROWING.—The present is a good time to begin to prepare the land for next year's potato crop. Putatoes may be grown on almost any soil, but net with equal success. The best soil is a rich, light loam, with a gravel bottom, or a well cultivated peat soil, with good drainage; in fact,. there must be good drainage wherever they arg grown. Now where these conditions are wanting, it is well; during the autumn and winter months, by cultivation, to bring the soil as near to the required state as circumstances will allow. Where the soil has the least tendency to clay or stiff loam, or where it is slightly damp, it is well now to incorporate with it a dressing of gaslime, quicklime, fine coal ashes, or new stable litter, which must be dug into the land, and the land left in ridges for the whole winter, that the frost may get at it, and so make it friable. The more pulverised the soil becomes, the bettor adapted it is for potato growing. NORTH LAITCASHIRE.—The land is still damp, yet most operations can now be carried on. In consequence of the great depression existing in the iron trade, and most other industries, leading to much lower wages amongst artisans, prices for most produce are depressed. The foot-and-mouth outbreak has been kept within the infected area, and the animals affected are now well again. Two animals have died. This is the third outbreak that the Ulverston Suner- -1 intendant of Police has kept within the atea first dravin:andi Mr. Whiteside certaira., ueserves the thanks of the farmers for his unwearied personal supervision. The same system of police patrols is observed as in Cumberland and West- morland. The necessity was manifested by a case heard at the Ulverston Police Court, on Thursday, October 25, when a cowkeeper from out of the centre of the infected area was charged with driving a cow for service to a farm without the area. The owner pleaded guilty, bnt said he had feted in ignorance of the limits of the area. The magistrates accepted his plea, and let him off with a tine of LI and costs.

- - REGULARITY IN MitatneG.—According to the Dairy, a journal published in the interests of dairy farming in the United States, regularity in milking is very essential to the maintenance of a constant yield of milk. This will be found very apparent when a daily weighing or estimate by measuring the milk is kept. Daring two years, in a dairy of 15 cows, a record kept of each milking shows a constant loss every Sunday when the morning milking was two hours later and the evening sometimesdater and sometimes earlier. It is not difficult to understand the reason. A delay in milking not only disturbs the cows, but it has the effect of producing congestion of the milk glands, by crowding them ; and overstockeng the fine ducts by which they are drained. Every excessive mussular or nervous action produces a corresponding reaction and a weakening of the excited organs. Besides, wheu the glands and fine ducts are filled re-absorption takes place; and by delaying the milking still longer, a cow may in time be dried up and the milk production wholly stopped by this process re-absorption of the milk. There may be an increased quantity of milk at the delayed milking, but the next one and the neat to that will be decreased. When the irregularity is frequent, of course the effect is greatly increased, and the injury corre- spondingly greater. Regularity of feeding tends to the same effect, and therefore regularity should stand next in the list of essential virtues for th4proper conduct of a dairy to cleanliness. HEREFORDS V. StIORTRORNS.—A correspondent of the Rural New Yorker, writing in respect of the Herefords at the recent Chicago Show. says :—" It must have been a proud day for the Hereford breeders when the decision of the committee was made known that the white faces had drawn the grand prize of £lOO, awarded as the sweepstakes premium to the best herd of the beef breeds. And hardly less could have been their satisfaction when it became known to them previously that the Shorthorn men had (in their view) practically given up the contest, by failing to send to Chicago but three representatives among the fifty superior herds in the State and immediate neighbourhood. The total reported entries of Shorthorns were about fifty, and they were all high-bred, first-class animals; but the Herefords outnumbered them two to one, and were the choicest selections both for home and abroad that could bd obtained by skilful breeding and feeding and the lavish use of money. It is now known that the Shorthorn men, as a body, opposed the project of holding the Illinois State Fair at Chicago; but few suspected, as many do now, that fear of open competition with the Herefords, on neutral ground, may have been the motive of the opposition." The Short- horn men do not like their cattle to compete with Herefords for " sweepstakes " prizes here any better than they do in America. Ever since the signal defeat they sustained at Oxford—when the Hereford ball, Grateful, and the Hereford cow, Leonora, took the two champion prizes—the Shorthorn men have declined to " collide " with them. There have been no more "sweepstakes' prizes! HOOVE IN CATTLE.—Mr. T. Dackharn, M.P. has written a letter to the Hereford Times, giving a remedy for hoove in cattle, and it has been extensively copied. The letter was as follows :—" The numerous inquiries I have had re- specting ;the cause of death of my celebrated and grand stock bull, Prince Horace, induces me to ask the favour of your allowing me to state that it was from hoove, the result of eating some very succulent clover when wet. Unfortu- nately I was in London at ;he time, or I have no doubt I ! should have saved him; and I feel that the value of hypo- ! sulphate of soda in such cases cannot be too widely made ' known. Some 14 years ago, when foot and mouth disease was raging in this county, my friend Professor Brown, who is now at the head of the veterinary department of the Privy Council, advised me to put a little hyposulphate of soda in the water for cattle to drink should mine be at- tacked, and at the same time he told me of its value for , hoove. You subsequently favoured me by giving publicity to the remedy, which I found very beneficial in the case of ; foot and mouth disease, and also with hoove; so much eo with hoove for both cattle and sheep that I have never been 1 without a supply. As it is very deliquescent, I have kept it for several year.; in a glass jar over my kitchen fireplace. There the jar stood when my poor animal was suffering his I agonies, but there was no one to administer the relief. I know there are other remedies, but this one is:very simple, I very effectual, and has the advantage that no injury follows an overdose. I give a tablespoonsful to a sheep, dissolved in a little warm water, and a quarter of a pound to a beast in a quart of warm water, repeating the dose if requisite. I can strongly recommend it, and feel that no farmer should be without it." The above is a very useful remedy, only it is the hypo3ulphite of soda that is intended—not the hyposulphate. Its action will he greatly assisted if vege- table charcoal in powder he given very shortly afterwards. For an ox, half-a-pint of powdered charcoal, mixed with as much water as will take it up, will be about the thing; and this may be repeated so long as the cause remains. CHANGE OF SEED.—A contemporary has the following interesting exchange of opinions :—There is perhaps no pur- suit in which the opinions of practical men are so utterly at variance as in the pursuit of farming. No sooner does one man tell us that we should do so-and-so, than another tells us we should do just the opposite. Your Staffordshire correspondent says:—" The advantage which later :listricts ; derive from a change of seed imported into them from coun- tries where the harvest is early ought to be recognised more fully than it is by the generality of farmers." Your North Lancashire correspondent says :—" Now this is just the opposite to my experience. We have of late years grown our own seed for swedes, and not only have we derived a benefit from such a course in hardier and better keeping roots, but in all cases where we have supplied others from the surplus seed it has given full satisfaction. We are now trying the same experiment with cabbage and mangel seed," I know nothing about these seeds, but I have had some ex- perience for a number of years in growing oats, and I have found that "a change of seed imported from countries where the harvest is early" is with us here in North Derby- shire a sine qua non. Oats with us ;invariably deteriorate.

No matter how good and fine a sample of seed" we sow, the produce will each succeeding year be later in getting ripe, the kernel of the grain will be smaller, the husk thicker and longer. I have tried beautiful samples of seed from Scot- land, but with the same result. Indeed, my experience of Scotch oats is that they are invariably late. If the season happens to be an early one, they answer well; if it happens to be a late one, they never get ripe. And I think if your North Lancashire correspondent had come and lived here in North Derbyshire, before he had sown his own oats for ten years in succession he would be both a sadder and a wiser man. I might make similar remarks in regard to our sheep. We have to fetch our rams from a warmer climate. If we did not their wool would each year become finer and lighter, and I have no doubt the sheep would become smaller. I dare say they would be also hardier, and more able to with- stand the rigour of the climate. But, in regard to them, the question to be asked is—Which sort will pay the best? and the action has to be taken accordingly,—John Naden. IECORDINTI r ERPORMANCES.-FrOM the ba.iry we take the following amusing illustration of the necessity for keeping strict account of each cow's produce —I was milking in the barn when young Squire Lawton came in. I lifted up the pail and hung it on the spring balance. "Just 131 b.," said I, and marked it on the little board on
the wall opPosite where the cow stood. "What do you do

that for ?" said he. "Why I always count, measuie, and weigh everything on this farm," said I. "My father taught me that when I was a boy." "But what's the use here ?" said he. "You have all the milk, and no one can cheat you." "Don't you be so sure of that. Now, look here. You gee this board. That's Topsy's milk account. Here you see is 171 b., 1611 b., 181 b., and then comes 111 b. That struck me all of a heap, and I went right there and then to Topsy to see what was the matter. Her nose was hot and dry, and her mouth was slobbering, and she was not eating. I soon found out what was the matter. She had been chew- ing the fence rails, and a big splinter was jammed into her mouth, between her teeth, and her jaw was swelled badly. Now, I mightn't have found that out for two or three days if I hadn't weighed the mill. But you see I soon set her right again. I have saved a good deal of trouble by it. And then look here. Here is 13-11 b., 151 b., 171 b., 121 b., 111 b., 141 b., and here, you see, is only 41b., and all down 6ilb 71b 741 b 51b 511 b Now, look at that cow. She's pretty, ain't she? But, bless you, handsome is as handsome does, and that cow don't stay here any longer than sha is fat enough for beef, for she ain't half handsome enough for a dairyman to keep. Then you see these glasses. These are to measure the cream by. A cow that won't give 15 per cent. of cream won't pay to keep with the fced I give thcin, and a heifer that won't make 10 per cent. won't pay to raise, and is only good to sell to those who sell milk. How could I tell all this if I didn't weigh and measure? See here ; this is the feed measure; one of these goes on to the feed for every cow at every meal, and that scoop holds just two quarts. This basket holds a full bushel, and every cow gets that full every feed. And two or three get one scoopful more. You see, it's all. brought dowu to rule. No thumb

div.head: LOCAL PRISONERS AT LIVERPOOL ASSIZ ES.
div.p: LOCAL PRISONERS AT LIVERPOOL ASSIZ ES.
BURGLARY AT WIDNES.

William Furber. aged 18, sailor, pleaded guilty to a charge of having, on the 27th August, broken into the dwelling- house of Mary Sutton and stolen £47 163. 3d. in money, a gold watch guard, two silver watch guards, a diamond ring, and other property. The prisoner, who had worked for the prosecutrix, entered the premises by lifting a grid. He was sentenced to twelve months' impriscnment. • BURGLARY AT ST. HELENS.

Edward Maley, who had been out on bail, and Morris Handley, aged 23, collier, were charged with having, at Parr, on the 9th September, broken into the house of Charles Whitfield, publican, Ashcroft-street, and stolen a gold watch and chain, Mr. M`Connell prosecuted, and Dr. Commins defended. Maley was acquitted, and Handley was found guilty and sentenced to three months' imprisonment.

div.head: STEALING POST LETTERS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: STEALING POST LETTERS AT WARRINGTON.

Samuel Higginson Worrall, aged 24, letter sm.ter, pleaded guilty to two indictments charging him with having, at Warrington, stolen, on the 30:h Sept, a registered post letter containing a half-sovereign, and on the 2ad October a post letter containing a half-sovereign, two sixpenny pieces, and 24 penny postage stamps. It was stated that the prieoner, who had been eight years in the service, was the sole sup- port of a widowed mother and sister. His lordship said be had no alternative but to sentence him to five years' penal eervitude for each offence; but he directed that the sen- tences should run concurrently. EX CRAORDINARY CASE OF BIGAMY.— '

div.head: SELLING A WIFE.
div.p: SELLING A WIFE.

Betsy Wardle, aged 25, was indicted for having, at Eccleston, on the 4th September, 1382, married George Chisnall, her former husband being 'then alive. Mr. Shand prosecuted. The prisoner having pleaded guilty, Mr. Swift, who appeared on her behalf, said she instructed him that her husband sold her for a quart of beer—(laughter)—and she seemed to have been under the impression that the transaction was a legal one and enabled her to marry again. His Lordship s That is not what she said before the magis- trates. She said then that he was an idle feilow and would not work ; that when she left him she took the child, and he said if she uould let him have the child he would not trouble her any further ; and that he said he would sell her for a quart of beer.— Prisoner: He did so, my lord.—His Lordship: Is there any- body here who knows that P—Prisoner: I es; Alice Roseby and Margaret Brown.—Margaret Brown, having been called, said she was present at the second marriage. She knew that the first husband was alive. The prisoner told her that he had sold her for a quart of beer, and Chisnall showed her a paper to that effect.—His Lordship : Where is that paper ?—Prisoner : it has got away, sir.—His Lord- ship (to witness): It purported to be a paper written by Wardle, saying he had sold her for a quart ef beer P—Wit- ness : Yes.—His Lordship : And you believed it ?—Witness : Yes.—His Lordship: And you thought it right for her to marry again ?—Witness: She asked me to give her away, and I did so.—His Lordship: You helped her to commit bigamy. Take care you don't do such a thing again, or you will get yourself into troutde.—Alice Roseby was next called, and said she saw Wardle drink a glass out of the quart of beer—His Lordship: Who was the bargain matte with P—Witness : With George Chisnall.—His Lordship: I am not sure that you are not guilty ef bigamy, or of being an:accessory .before the fact. You must not do this sort of thing again. People have no right to sell their wives for a quart of beer or anything else.—George Chisnall, the second husband, a young man, having been called and asked by his lordship how he came to marry the prisoner, replied," I bowt her." (Laughter.)— His Lordship: You are not fool enough to suppose tnat you can buy another man's wife? Witness: Ay. (Laughter.) —His Lordship: How much did you give for her ? Wit- ness: Sixpence. (Laughter.)—His Lordship: You are quite as guilt' as she is. You are an accessory before the fact. You have committed bigamy yourself. Everybody has committed bigamy in this Case. (Laughter.) How long have you lived with the prisoner ? Witness: Going for three years.—His Lordship : Do you want to take her back again? Witness: Ay, and keep her if you bike. (Laughter.)—Mr. Swift, on. behalf of the prisoner, expressed the hope that his lordship would not think it a Case in which she ought to be punished severely. She seemed to have met with a bad husband in the first instance and an ignorant one in the second. In reply to his lordship, the learned counsel said she had been out on bail.—His Lordship said it was absolutely necessary that he should impose some punishment in order that people might understand that men had no more right to sell their wives than to sell other people's wives, or to sell other people's horses or cows, or anything else. It was not a legal transaction. So many of them seemsd.to be ignorant of this that it was necessary that he should inflict souse punishment in this Case, so that they might understand it. He then sentenced the prisoner to a week's imprisonment.— At a later period of the day, Mr. Swift informed his lordship that the prisoner was apprehended on the 17th of August and was kept_ in custodyill the 27th before being admitted to bail ; so that she had already undergone a longer period of imprisonment than that to which his lordattip had sen- tenced her.—His Lordship : I will consider that.
CRIMINAL ASSAULT.

John Gregson, aged s@, collier, for having,-at Ilaydock, on the Bth August, 1580, committed a criminal assault upon Mary Whittle, a woman 71 years of age, with whom he lodged, was sentenced to penal servitude for seven years.

div.p: IHE CHARGE OF MURDER AT LOWTON.
A true bill was found in the case of John Gibbons (24), labourer, charged with the murder of Joshua Rigby, at Lowton, on the 18th Sept.

The grand jury threw--; —out iie bill in the case of James Quinn (26), labourer, charged with ste v llin a silver watch, with violence, from the person of Thomas 'Foy, on the 9th Inst., at Pennington.
Lives that are always sweet conceal the bitterness of the heart.
The greatest sources of happiness and usefulness are open to rich and poor alike. ____ _
Why does a person who is out of health partly lose his sense of touch? Because he doesn't feel well.

A lovely American girl hired one of the Parisian Jehus to drive her from her hotel to the Grands Magasins du Louvre. Arrived, she tendered him his fare—one franc fifty centimes —upon which the coachman demanded three francs. The young lady refused to pay the larger amount, and told the driver that it was his legal fare. " Ah, but if one has the responsibility of driving a young lady alone, the fare is double !" was his reply. The late Mrs. Jane W— was equally remark Ale for kindness of heart and absence of mind. One day she was accosted by a beggar, whose stout and healthy appearance startled even her into a momentary doubt of the needfulness of charity in this instance. "Why," exclaimed the good old lady, "you look well able to work." "Yes," replied the supplic..nt, " but, I have bcen deaf and dumb these seven years." "Poor man, what a heavy affliction !" exclaimed Mrs. W—, at the same time giving him relief with a liberal hand. On returning home she mentioned the fact, remarking, "What a dreadful thing it is to be deprived of such precious faculties!" ",But how," asked her sister, "did you know that the poor man had been deaf and dumb for seven years ?" "Why," was the quiet and unconscious answer," he told me so."

div.head: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE,
div.p: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE,

Fears are entertained that that the steamer Francis Smith, from Collingwood to Toronto, with 100 passengers, foun- dered on Sunday, and that all on b )ard perished. A Durban telegram states that Usibepu, the conqueror of Critewayo, has himself been defeated with heavy loss in two engagements. It is not stated whether the victors are fight- ing in Cetewayo's interest. A hurricane swept over a vast extent of territory in North America on Monday, and extensive damage is re- ported. The thriving town Shenandoah, in the Pennsyl- vania coal region, has been devastated by fire. The Luther anniversary was celebrated in Germany with great pomp. The Emperor and the Court attended a special service in the capital. The most interesting ceremony, however, appears to have taken place at Eisleben, where a splendid historical procession was organised. A commemo- rative service was held on the same day in Rome. At a meeting of the Quebec branch of the Irish League, attention was drawn to the telegrams which had appeared in American and English newspapers regarding the sup- posed discovery of a dynamite plot to murder Lord Lans- downe. The reports were indignantly denounced by the meeting as unwarranted calumnies upon the Irish race. FIGHTING IN SERVlA.—lntelligence received at Vienna states that the Servian insurgents have been attacked by Lieutenant-Colonel Hadzics and Major Stretkovics in the defile of Castra Brodica, and defeated with the loss of seven killed and many wounded. Two hundred of the rebels were taken prisoners, the remainder escaping across the frontier. A despatch from Tatnatave reports the resumption of hostilities by the French fleet. Two or three of the so- called " forts of the Hovas have been shelled. The French have in Tamatave a garrison of 600. and the Hovas blockade them on the land &de with about 5,000 men: Thera is no confirmation of the report that a revolution had broken out in the capital. According to information brought by the mail steamer from the West Coast of Africa, arrangements are being made for handing over the subsidary native territories of Little Popo and Ahgwey to the British Government, in order that they may be added to our possessions on the Gold Coast. The transfer is expected to be completed this year. Severe fighting between eative tribes is reported to have taken place near Sierra Leone. TERRIBLE BOILER Exer.ostore.—A NOW York telegram states that a dreadful accident has happened on the East River. A tug with three schooners in tow put on extra steam in order to pass Hellgate against the tide, when the boiler exploded, and the tug sank instantly. Nothing could be seen of her except some fragments of wreckage. Of her crew, which numbered seven, two were picked up in an in- jured condition; aid- others have not been found. A frag- ment killed the man who was steering the nearest schooner. An account comes from Madrid of a terrible loss of jewellery, sustained by Madame Falconi, an Italian opera singer, whilst travelling on the railway. The artzste bad for some distance be.en alone in the compartment, when at Alcazar a gentleman (?) got in, who engaged in a conversa- tion with the artiste. At the next station he so persistently Defaced her refreshment that she was induced to accept a glass of -some cooling drink, which was brought to her in the carriage. The beverage must have been drugged, for Madame Falconi, on recovering consciousness, found her- self alone and divested of her jewel case and other belong- jugs. SUICIDES BY GIRLS.—Two suicides by young girls have been reported at the Paris Prefecture of Police. An orphan 01_15, who was being brought up by an uncle on thedsland of St. Denis, fired two shots from a revolver into her head. She was removed to a hospital in a dying state, while an in- vestigation was opened into the cause of this act of despair. The same afternoon a well-dressed young person, aged • about 20, was found writhing in agony on a seat in the Avenue Bretuil. She was clutching in her hand a phial which had contained strychnine. Nothing was found on her to show her identity, and she was removed to the Necker Hospital. THE DEATH OF MRS. Moss% TILE FAT BRIDE.-1 tele- gram to the .Now York Herald says :—A special guard was placed at Mount Olivet Cemetery last night to prevent the violation ot the grave of Blanche Moses, the fat bride, who WU buried there on Saturday. As it was known that several medical colleges of the city were anxious to get the body for their dissecting tables, Keeper Beckman and his assis- tants stationed themselves in an upper room of the keeper's house, armed with shotguns and revolvers ready for any ghouls that might appear. About midnight and while it BM very dark a covered waggon was drawn up the cemetery lane and four men alighted. Two of them were white men and the other two coloured. They took shovels from the waggon, and, going to the grave, at once began their work. The watchers sighted the party and fired at them. The in- truders dropped their shovels, ran with all speed to their waggon, and drove off at a rapid rate. Another party of resurrectionists made a similar attempt later in the night, but was also frightened off. It is thought that one of the ghouls of the first party was badly wounded, as he gave a ery when the guns were fired. A strict watch will be kept over the grave for several nights. Foun ENGLISHMEN STABBED IN PARIS.—A Paris tele- gram states that a very remarkable affray occurred in the Erie Traversiere late on Monday night. It appears that while four Englishmen, named Pope, Bowes, Hodge, and Forester, were quietly walking along the street in question they noticed what they first thought was a "free fight" going on, but on coming closer they saw that four ruffians were making a savage attack on a defenceless man. They at once went to the man's assistance, and handled the ruffians so severely that they took to flight. The man they rescued did not appear to have been very serioesly injures; at all events he was able to continue his way. The English- men also walked on, but they had not proceeded far before, In a dark portion of the street, the miscreants they had put to flight quietly stole ripen them, and, evidently by a pre- concerted arrangement, made a sudden rush at them, each singling out one and inflicting upon him a determined stab, either with a dagger or a huge clasp-knifo. The attack was BO sudden and unexpected, aud the EngliehmOß were taken 30 completely unawares, that the ruffians were out of reach before any of the wounded men recovered from the shock. The attack was as ferocious as it was cowardly and unex- pected, and all four of the men have received serious wounds. The injured men were employed by the Swan Electric Light Company.

IRELAND. Mr. Bentley, of county Dublin, who had been an inde- pendent Parnellite candidate for Limerick, has withdrawn from the field. Tun MEMBER FOR MAYO—At a meeting held at Irish- town, on Monday, a resolution was adopted condemning the conduct of Mr. John O'Connor Power, as senior member for county Mayo, and the meeting pledged itself to oppose him at the next election. THE FENIAN MURDER.—Tbe trial of the Fenian, Joseph Poole, for the murder of James Kenny, in Seville Place, Dublin, in July of last year, was resumed on Tuesday, at the Dublin Commisaioa .Court. Dr. Webb, for the defence, urged that the case for the Crown WAS most improbable, incoherent, ani inconclusive. The prisoner stood in the peculiar position of being avowedly a member of the Fenian Brotherhood, but he belonged to a section of the Feniane haring no sympathy with assassination, and had incurred the enmity of Curley and party, and the learned counsel suggested that Kenny was shot by them in mistake for Poole.
