THE LUTHER COMMEMORATION. WARRINGTON. WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH. In connection with the celebration of the Luther com- memoration in Warrington, the Rev. John `Vonge, pastor of the Wycliffe Congregational Church, preached on Sunday evening to a very large congregation, from Luke i., 5, these being the words, Many shall rejoice at his birth." The preacher said: This was a prediction respecting net alone the actual birth, but the subsequent life of John the Baptist. He was to be the bearer of a special commission from heaven for the spiritual arousing and welfare of his people. Born in a critical and necessitous time, he was to prove him- self the man for the age. The darkest moment is ever that whia immediately precedes the dawn. John the Baptist was born in that darkest moment of his nation's moral his- tory. Notwithstanding many previous seasons of apostasy and idolatry, never had the Hebrew nation been so spiritually dark and hopeless as in the years just antecedent to the coming of Jesus Christ. Never had the preselice and power of a moral Reformer been so eminently needed. And hence the appearance of John the Baptist was not only timely, but it was a new illustration of what had even then become an old fact, that God always has His man ready for Hi work. Perhaps nothing is more strikingly illustrated in Hebrew history than that truth. The nation's needs were ever God's occasions. Always had He shown how He had somehow in readiness the man for the moment. And the man and the moment always came punctually together. "God never is before His time; He never is behind." Moses was called from his father-in-law's flocks in the land of Midian, Elijah f o.n anmng the inhabitants of Gilead, Amos from among the herdsmen of Tekoa, just at the precise instant when peculiar need called for peculiar help. And now John the Baptist comes into the world specially consecrated, even before his birth, for high and distin- guishing ,ervice, in a crisis of peculiar momentousness. The angel who brings the promise of his birth to Zacha- rias declares in the words of this text that "many should rejoice" on account of it. So does ha intimate that John's career should be one of widespread blessing to his people. "He shall be great in the sight of the Lord, and shall drink neither wine nor strong drink, and he shall be filled with the Holy Ghost, even from his mother's womb. And many of the children of Israel shall he turn to the Lord their God. And he shall go before Him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wis- dom of the just, to make ready a people preptred for the Lord." Such was to be his character, and such his career. A. true man of God himself, unworldly, spiritual, self-deny- ing, and devoted,—he should do God's work with marvel- lous force and energy,—in such a way as should stir the people' and prepare a goodly number to receive Him of whom he came to be herald and forerunner. Events verified the prediction. When John began to preach, the multitude swiftly gathered to his feet. All classes were reached and roused. Pharisee and Sadducee, publican and soldier, re- spectable and outcast, all alike came beneath the spell of his power, until the whole country felt the thrill of moral awakening and revival, and large numbers were "baptised of him in Jordan, confessing their sins." Many did rejoice because of him, and many were doubtless led by him to "the Lamb of God who taketh away the sin of the world." Now, we may freely adopt these words to-night as having striking fitness to the case of another religious reformer,— hardly second, if second at all, to John the Baptist himself. John, indeed,—so far at any rate as his actual ministry was concerned,—was of use simply to his own land and people. No one ever connects his name with the progress of religion beyond these limits, or regards him aa having directly contributed to moral deliverance and reformation elsewhere than in the country of the Jews. But what do we find our attention arrested by to-day? All Christendom, in both hemispheres of the world, is uniting to commemo- rate the birth and life of a man who has made the whole of

it his personal debtor. Millions of people in all lands are rejoicing in the fact that Martin Luther wee born 400 years ago ; and that he lived a life which has proved in- fluential for human welfare in all subsequent ages. Germany, the land of his parentage and birth,—from the Emperor down to the humblest Protestant peasant, is now glorying in Luther's memory, and doing its utmost to reassert the principles and doctrines of the reformed faith as Luther proclaimed' them. It seems not unlikely, indeed, that by means of this celebration the German people may be once more aroused, not this time from bondage to the Papacy, but from considerable subjec- tion to indifferentism and infidelity. And it will be a blessed thing for Germany if Luther from his grave to-day should speak again with so much of his old power, as once more to turn the heart of his people to the truth. There seems to be to-day a need for this celebration in that land as real as the need for the Reformation itself four centuries ago, But it is impossible that this commemoration ehould be confined to Germany. It must be shared more or less by all Protes- tant people, and by none should it be shared with more heartiness and devout gratitude than the people of our own land. England's debt to Martin Luther is incalculable. Mr. Fronde, in his preface to his "Short Biography of Luther," truly remarks, " When the German states revolted against the Roman hierarchy,, we in England revolted also; but there is no name among the English apostles of the Re- formation which commands the same respect as Luther's. Knox holds a position something like it in Scotland. Presbyterian Scotland is Knox's pork, and the people know this and feel it. But even the Soot's do not observe Knox's birthday. Not many of them, probably, could tell either the day or the year in which he came into the world. The great English reformers, well as they deserved of as, stand in far lower esteem. For various reasons they have never been extremely honoured, and in these days seam less in favour than ever they were. Nevertheless, we are still a Protestant nation, and the majority of us intend to remain Protestant. Hence (he adds) we can join with Germany in paying re- spect to the memory of a man to whom we also, in part, owe our deliverance. Without Luther there would either have been no change in England in the sixteenth century, or a change purely political. Luther's was one of those great individualities which have modelled the history of man- kind, and modelled it entirely for good. He revived and maintained the spirit of piety and reverence, in which and by which alone real progress is ponible." We remarked just now that this commemoration of Luther seemed desir- able in Germany, on account Of the remarkable lapse of that nation in the direction of Rationalism and infidelity. I believe that the commemoration is equally desirable in Eng- land, on aeconnt of the remarkable revival in the !let half century of sacerdotal doctrine and Ritual in the Nationil Church. We can have no wish in these days to say one harsh or censorious word against our Roman Catholic fellow-countrymen. I, for one, would take no pact in this celebration if it were meant simply, or, indeed, at all, as an attack upon the Church of Rome. However widely we may and do differ, alike from the priestly pretensions and the erroneous teachings of that Church, we have learnt, I trust, a better speech than that of abuse; and we can, at least, agree to-day to go with Luther on this point :—lle maintained that "In spite of her constitution and her erroneous dogma, there was enough of the truth of God's Word taught by the Church of Rome t 3 touch men's hearts and bring them to the Saviour." This being as, and we ourselves being at liberty to worship God according to our conscience, we can cheerfully suffer Rotqanists to do the same, without criticism or attack from us. But the case alters, however, when a so-called Protestant Church. hold- ing privileged position among us through being established by law as the Protestant Church of the State, begins to re- pudiate Protestantism. Then we have a right to speak, and it becomes a duty we owe to our faith, and principles, and libertiee, that we should do so. I say that in view of the present manifestly un-Protestantiz- ing tendency of the Church of England, this Luther c?le- I bration is likely to be of great use to the nation. Men of all I classes by means of Press, pulpit, and platform are being con- fronted afresh with the truths and principles of evangelical religion. They are being taught from the history of four centuries ago somewhat of the religious disabilities and spiritual bondage which their ancestors suffered. And the story of Luther's life and work will help to show them the value of that evangelical faith and those Protestant prin- ciples which are now once more being jeopardised; jeoper- dised as we believe by teaching in the State Church which it is almost impossible not to describe as dishonest. Is there no significance in the fact that of all the churches in Protes- tant Christendom, the Church of England takes least part in this Luther celebration? Is n3t the loudest voice that we hear from the ranks of that community- a voice which decries Lather—which disowns and repudiates the title Protestant —and which stigmatizes the Refermation as the direst catastrophe that ever betel the cause of Christianity? The Times of Monday last deals with these anti-Protestants in the Establishment, and tells them that those who dislike Luther have no proper place in the Church of England or in any Protestant Church. Their place, it says, "is not with men who claim an inheritance of the freedom which Martin Luther has made possible for them," and which cm, directly or indirectly, be traced to him. Coming from such a source the rebuke will be keenly felt, but after all, the real appeal on this matter is not with these priestly pre- tenders, but with the mass of the English people. Upon them this Luther celebration must have considerable influ- ence, and if it lead them to a revived appreciation of Gospel freedom and a renewed resistance to the sacerdetalism, both of ritual and doctrine, which is rapidly spreading throughout the country, then it will achieve a needed, and useful work. But now, in order to understand properly the work 'and worth of Martin Luther, we must have before our mind some idea at least of the condition of religion, and of the nations of Christendom, at the time he was bern. It must be observed, then, that the only representation of Chris- tianity in those days was that of the Papal Church. And that repreemtation was given by the Papal Church when it was in its deepest condition of corruption. Those who are at all familiar with the history of those times will know how difficult it would be to exaggerate the extent of that corrupt condition. Doctrine was corrupt and false. The Bible was a sealed and unknown book, Jesus Christ was represented as a capricious and vindictive Being, who needed the careful propitiation of His human mother, and the me- diation of countless saints and angels, as well as sacrifices and penances and modifications by suppliants themselves, in order to render him approachable or merciful. All di- rect access to the &wick= was thus barred and blocked against men. No salvation was possible apart from obedi- ence to the church; .while yet, at the same time, so corrupt were the practices of the church that money could buy ab- solution and preserve or even deliver from purgatory. The "kingdom of heaven" was to be bought. Christ's favour, God's pity, e 'aid be bought. Furthermore, permission to commit ill 0: sins forbidden in the Decalogue could be bought. Every sin had its price; a price usually measured by the e?ealth of the purchaser. Thus men were held by one hand in a bondage which had no alleviation, and yet suffered by the other to practice all kinds and degrees of

evil. There is no denial of the fact that the Clairch of / Rome in those days was utterly worldly, and co•rupt, and untrue. And yet, sheproudly dominated all the nations of Europe, and held England a vassal at her feet. Tile condi- tion of the nations, however, at the time Luther was born was becoming one of unmistakable ferment and commotion. After a long, dark, and horrible night,light was beginning to creep up the heavens. A spirit of enterprise was spreading in Europe. Learning was beginning to revive. Men were beginning to think and investizate as they had not done for centuries. The corruptions of the church had become so manifest e scandal that m,.:n of decent morals were shocked and repelled alike by the doctrines and doings of ecclesiastics. A deep desire for liberty from a yoke which had made itself hate- ful, was spreading throughout Europe. Princes as well as people were becoming tired of the bondage of the Court and' Church of Rome. The idea was•spreading that the Bishop of Rome was after all only a mere man, and not infrequent- ly a verg bad min. And hence men were growing restive under political and tycuniary burdens imposed by Rome for its own temporal aggrandisement at their expense. A de- mand for relief was rising on every hand, and all minds, more or less avowedly, were earnestly considering how a re- j formation, civil as well as religious, might he brought about. I Such, in brief, vague outline, was the condition of religion, I and of the nations, when Luther came into the world. When matters came to their crisis, then the man came who.was , 1 able to deal with it. Thus, once again, was illustrated how : 1 God is always to His time. A great truth, marvellously ' established by all history, and one that should ever be our, 1 hope in times of difficulty and danger. God will interpose 1 at the moment when He is needed. His hand is ever on , 1 the world, guiding its course,—controlling its events,— 1 working out. in His own best way, His own righteous will.l I Nosy, the precise circumstance which ushered in the Refor- mation appears somewhat trivial when compared with all i 1 that had been endured for centuries. But, when endurance I ' has been long strained, a trifle will suffice to provoke rebel- 1 lion. Pope Leo X., on coming to the Papal throne, found ' 1 the revenues of the Church nearly exhausted by the extra- vagance of his predecessors. Not being himself by any i 1 means versed in economy, and having immense ambitions 1 to satisfy if possible, he willingly lent himself to every de- ! vice which a cunning priesehoocl could invent to repair his • finances. Among others, he had recourse to a wide and 1 general sale of indulgences: This was not a new expedi- ent; but he gave it a larger application than ever before it V had received. The theory of the Romish Church that lay at', the root of this device was this: All the good works of saints, beyond such as were needful for their own justifica- tion, were considered as deposited, along with the infinite merits of the Saviour, in one infinite treasury. Of this treasury St. Peter and his successors the Popes. held the keys; and they had the power, as they alleged, to transfer at pleasure a portion of this abounding merit to any in- dividual for a sum of money. By this means they pro- fessed to be able to remit his sins, or release from purgatory any soul in whom he might be interested. Such was the iniquitous theory which lay at the root of this equally iniquitous device. Pope Leo X granted the right to sell these indulgencies in Germany to one Albert, Elector of Metz, and Archbishop of Magdeburg; a youth of 27," a rather worse specimen than usual of the average great Churchman of that day." Albert appointed as his chief agent in Saxony one Tetzel, a Dominican friar, of bad morals, but active spirit, and eloquent tongue. Aided by his brother monks, Tetzel carried out his commission with great success for a considerable time. Presently, however, it proved that this zealous monk had over-reached himself. He made his traffic in indulgences an insufferable scandal, a scandal which he abundantly emphasized by his wildly licentious career. The princes and nobles became angry as they' saw how their people were being drained of wealth in order to fill the Papal exchequer. Good and pious men lamented that any should be subjected to such gross de- lusion, and trained by the immoral doctrines of the monks to sin with lawless hand. And hence a state of - general public indignation was engendered, which only needed some prophet of the people to enunciate, and direct in pro- test against the abase. That was the favourable condition which presented itself for Luther's first attack *upon the Papacy, and which really opened the door for the Protestant Reformation in Europe. We must turn now and look at the man whom God had raised up to lead the people in their, revolt against this corrupt and corrupting Church. And . the first thing that strikes us is that Luther himself was a man of the people. Not a prince with an army, and an alliance of armies, at his back. dot a noble, of command- ing position, with influence at royal courts. Not one of the world's great ones, for whom Rome herself, ever awake to her temporal interests, would have felt an instinctive respect, and whom she would have endeavoured by all means to meet and conciliate. Not one such as these was the agent found by Providence for the great work to be done. Luther was himself a man from the ranks. He sprang from a peasant family, whose home was in a village on the skirts of the Thuringian forest, in the electorate of Saxony. "I am apeasant's son," said Luther; "Father, grandfather, great grandfather, were all peasants." The father was a miner, first of all at Mohra, afterwards at Eisleben. He married a peasant woman' and from that marriage, 400 years ago yesterday, came Martin Luther, their first-born son. The miner steadily rose in the world, becoming owner of a couple of smeltinf furnances, and BO accumulating some slender means enabling him to give his son Martin an edneation which should fit him for the pro- fession of law. Martin from early boyhood was earneetiv religious; having caught the spirit from his father who was in the habit of praying by his childrens' bedside. But it was when 14 years of age, at a school in Eisenach, that his mind began really to open, and he asked himself seriously as to the meaning of life. Still, religions though he thus showred" himself to be, Martin was a merry lad, fond of music, and quick at mirth. He had, indeed, a passion for music: a quality which enabled him in after years wonder- fully to spread his reformed doctrines by means of hymns and tunes of his own composition. At 18 years of aee his father sent him to Erfurt University, then the best in Germany. There Luther rose rapfidly to the degnes of bachelor and master, and gained lilgh scholastic distinction. , Now, it was here, in the library of this university that he ' came, accidently, as men would say—Providentially, as must more truly be said, upon a latin Bible. Little did he imagine whet would flow from his visit that day to that library I Little did he think as he turned, from mere curiosity, the covers of this book, that in it he would find what would cause revolution in his heart, and moral revolution, by his agency, through the Church and the world! Never before had he seen or touched a complete Bible. All, indeed, he had known of were the portions ex- tracted for use in the church services. With interest keenly excitcd he read as his first portion the story of Hannah and Samuel, returning daily thereafter to the wondrous Book as to a mine of rich wealth in which be dived and delved with earnest delight. His tutor one day saw him reading the Book. " Ah, brother Martin! what is there in the Bible? It is better to read the books of the ancient doctors. They have sucked the honey of the truth. The Bible is the cause of all the troubles in the Church ! " But, as an eloquent writer has well said, "It was this Bible that gave liberty to Luther; and Luther, with the Bible in his hand, gave liberty to the world." Here first, then, his mental eyes were opened. Two years later, when his heart was rent and torn by A con- flict of doubt and fear, of pain and penitence, his spiritual eye was opened to the light of God's blessed lamp, and he became inspired with the same spirit that breathes and burns in the Book. Luther must ever remain as a striking illus- tration of the Psalmist's words" The entrance of Thy words giveth light." We have seen already how Luther was de- signed by his father for the profession of law. God in His Providence had other designs for him. It does not need much insight to perceive how Luther the Monk could better effect the reform of religion than could Luther the lawyer. And hence we can only ascribe it to the direct leading of Providence that Luther was turned aside from the parental designation, and, by a sudden and, as it seemed, a rash im- pulse, led to take a vow of consecration to religious life. Writing to him in after days, one of Luther's University friends said, "Divine Providence foresaw what you wonlci become when the fire of heaven struck you to the ground, like another Saul to become another Paul; and, separating; you from us at the University, led you to enter the Augus- tinian Order." So indeed did God over-rule Luther's ex- periences in a violent thunderstorm in which the lightning struck him to the ground. Alarmed by that event, be vowed to become a monk. Now, our glimpses of Luther in the monastery at Erfurt, while they reveal to us the error which lay beneath the monastic life, reveal also that even in the outikely seclusion of the cloister, darkened by so much tbst is false, Koala can and do come to "the light of the world." We shall very greatly mistake if we suppose that all monasteries weri alike in evil, or all monks alike in hypocrisy and sin. Luther himself was sincere from the first, and the superior of his order, with not a few of his monkish brotherhood, were men of spirtual character and high-toned piety. There was much of heavenly grace in those austere men, an they daily walked with their Saviour amid the shadows of the cloister. Now it was in the Erfurt monastery that Martin Luther really underwent spiritual enlightenment and re- newal. He tells us himself how he went there, under the idea that if he were to get to heaven and be saved it could only be by his own efforts. Therefore, he labeured hard; submitting to all the menial discipline of the monk- ish life; and then, when his duties as porter, sexton, and , servant were done, going forth into the streets of Erfurt, , begging provisions from house to Foam. All this time he I was the subject of intense inward conflict. He was busy I painfully endeavouring to weave the robe of righteousness for himself; but he found the work a dreary task and a sorry failure." "Verily," said he afterwards, "if over a monk entered into heaven by his monkish merits, certainly I should have obtained an entrance there. All the monks who knew me would confirm this; and if it had lasted much longer I should have become a martyr." As it was, he sank into a condition in which lee really scorned to be dying. Had it not been for the loving counsel of the superior of the monastery, whose pity was aroused by the spectacle of his agony, he probably would have ended his days a victim of his resolute and intense self-discipline. But Dr. Staupitz ' had himself found the secret of Christ's peace, and willingly I sought to lead Luther to the same haven of rest. Luther I told his snperior all his sorrows, all his failure, all his sin : I not so much as confessing to a priest, but as taking counsel with a venerable father; and Staupitz told him the sweet message of the Gospel :—" Cast yourself into the arms of the Saviour; trust in Him; trust in the righteousnees of His life, trust in the atoning sacrifice of His death." " How can I dare?" asked Luther. "I must be converted before God will receive me." The venerable man revealed to him his error of belief • Lid him to accept freely from Christ what Christ rffered freely, until at last Luther's strife was ended, and lie entered into peace through trust. On May 2, 1507, Lu' her read mass, as a priest of the Church, for the first time. The Bishop of Brandenburg officiated at his con-

ecraition. When he conferred on Luther power to celebrate mass, be put the chalice into his hand, and eaid the solemn words "Receive the power ef offering sacrifice for the liv- ing and the dead 1" Luther heard that calmly then, but shuddered at it afterwards—" Tnat the eirto did not Alen open and swallew us both up," said he, " wee an instance of the patience and long sufferihg of the Lorchr7 A bishop conferring, and a nriest receiving a power, wleicli the one could not give, and the other could not receive. The fol- lowing year saw him pass from the monastery Vs the lec- ture room in the new nniversity at Wittenberg. 1`1.1.3 sub- jects were philosophy and divinity. In this last branch he lectured on the Psalms and on the Epistle to the Romatee. These lec- turee drew much notice, and the rector of the University after hearing Luther, said, " Diet monk will confound all • the learned doctors • propound a new doctrine, and reform the whore Roman Church, for he studies the writings of the prophets and evangelists; he relies on the word of Jesus Christ, and no one can subvert that, either with philosophy or with sophistry." A true prophecy, as the history showed. In 1510 Luther was sent to Rome en some business of the Augustinian Order to which he belonged. This was in his 27th year. Enlightened though he had then become, he had not yet lost his notions of meritorious service ; and so he believed that good works done in Rome, as the Holy City, would be of peculiar worth. He therefore set himself to join the crowds of pilgrims who were painfully ascending on bare knees the Scala Santa, the holy staircase, alleged to have been brought to Rome from Pilete's house in Jerusa- lem. It was a passionate impulse of his old superstitious nature, and it was banished before he reached the top by the sounding in hts soul, as by a voice from heaven, of the in- spired words, " The just shall live by faith ! " He started from his knees as by a sudden shock, and rushed from the spot to the bewilderment of all around. Now, it *seems pro- bable that Luther went to Rome hoping that there in the very centre of the Christian world, and under the very shadow of the Holy Father, he would find real religion and, a living faith. But instead of this, as Mr. Froud says, "he found a splendid city, a splendid court, good outward order, and careful political administration. He foend art on its highest pinnacle of glory. But it was Pagen Rome, not Christian. The morals of the cardinals weie a public jest. Luther himself heard an officiating priest at the altar say scornfully, 'Bread thou art, and bread thou remainest !' The very name Christian was the synonym for a fool! " Consequently he went to Germany disillusioned! His ideal of Rothe was dispelled. His last hope dissipated. He did not say then all that he mused in his soul. But he did sees some ominous words which were like the first mutterings of the thunder against Roman corruption and heresy that sheulci soon crash from his lips; " it is impossible that matters can remain in this state, things must change or break down !" And he said further, "if there be a hell, Rome is built on the top of it! Whoever lies been in Rome knows well that things are worse there than can be ex- pressed in words or believed." Notice how mirvellously and unmistakeably Luther was being prepared for the work that lay before him ! Himself a man of parts, of strong will, of fervent spirit; he had been also led through strong experiences; had had granted him peculiar access to the Lamp of Divine Truth, and powerful sense of its redeeming grace; had been brought to see the errors of doctrinal Romanism, and now the hateful evil of the entire papal system. Providence was preparing the instrument, and this visit to the city of the Pontiffs was nearly the finishing stroke in its attemperment. Deeply lie mused upon all he sew, and strongly he felt that events were at hand. With these feelings and convictions in his heart, on return- ing to Wittenberg, he gave himself to preaching. Sin, atonement, human worthlessness, the mercy and grace of God. These became his themes, and he handled them with a force and freedom that compelled attention, and created profound impeession. "This monk bee strange ideas," said his hearers. All the same ; they were Ideas that found an echo in men's souls, and wrought mighty convictions far and near. Now, it was—just when Luther was thus fully awakened to the falseness and corruption of Rome—that the Dominican Monk Tetzel entered Saxony to sell the Papal indulgences. He came in pompous state. Processions, banners, candles, choristers. Ia the nurches a red cross wee placed on the altars, a silk banner banging from it bearing the Papal arms, and an iron dish placed at the foot to ' receive the money that the deluded people should pay to escape from eternities in purgatory. Eloquent orators pro- claimed the efficacy of the indulgences, and invited all sinners, specially the most flagrant and unblushing, to seize the opportunity of blotting out past sins, and obtaining freedom to sin again. Should any sceptic dare to question this doctrine, he was menaced with ex-communication. This procedure aroused the German people. It was met with remonetrence from the Elector of Saxony. Luther tried to stir the Bishops to interfere and prevent. None of them would stir. And so, having tried all other means and failed to rouse successful opposition to this climax of sin, Luther determined himself to force a controversy, and, by by that means, expose the impious heresy,—save men's souls from a pestilent delusion, and men's temporal posses- sions from a fraudulent misuse. Mr. Froude calls the 31st October, 1517, "the most memorable day in modern European history." "Luther, being then 34 years old, fixed 95 theses on the door of the Wittenberg Church, calling in question the Papal theory of indulgences, and the Pope's right to sell them." It may be explained that that was, in those days. a common method of forcing a discussion and a settlement of disputed points in morals or theology ; and hence, seeing that this matter of indulgences had never been settiea oy any churcn Council, leuaue. ~.... ..e.oz- a:- ' and no one could object to his proceedure. Providentially, again, the printing press was of recent invention. By its help Luther's propositions on this matter, translated into German were scattered broadcast; and while they found a host of German, they raised also a storm of controversy wh;ch soon gathered hotly around Luther himself. The Pope presently interfered, and sent a Legate into Germany to put matters straight. This meant, of course, the silencing, by fair means or foul, the audacious monk who had kindled so rampant a tire. A Diet of the Empire was summoned at Angsberg in August, 1513, at which atjetan, the Legate, wee to be present, and to which Luther was bidden to come. Now began personal nerils for this challenger of Rome. But he shewed himself brave against them all; and having en- tered upon his course of hostility to Rome, he never once swerved a heir's breadth from his path. Cajetan tried cejolery, and offered Luther high honour if he would with- drawe his propositions. Luther refused. Then he tried scorn and centemptuous command. Still Luther refused to retract unless his propositions were answered. Cejetan was. A failure, and Luther escaped. The Pope next sent his ' own Chamberlain, lied Von Miltitz, a subject of Saxony, to Frederick the Elector, expressing surprise that "a child of perdition " was preaching hereey in his dominions. Ile begged the elector to put this "offspring of Satan " to silence. But when this envoy reached Germany he found the greater mass of the people already in sympathy with this "child of perdition." The Pope's messenger thereupon entered Luther's presence, and besought him with tears to retract and be reconciled. Still Luther stood firm. "If you will answer me I will retract " Time passed on, filled with controversy and fierce menaces against Luther; yet still he remained un- harmed. At length, on the 16th June, 1520, the Pope issued his famous bull against "the wild boar who had broken into the Lord's vineyard. In that document 41 of Luther's theses; were condemned. By so doing Luther con- ceived that the Pope had condemned scripture itself. Thenceforward his rupture with Rome was complete, and he inhis turn began to use strong epithets, and to call ugly names. The throne of St. Peter was now to him "Satan's seat," and the man who sat thereon was beyond a doubt Anti-Christ. On the 10th December Luther solemnly burnt a copy of this famous document. " Because," said he, "thou hest troubled the Lord's saints, let eternal fire con- sume thee!' The students of the university stood round the fire and sang a loud te Aunt. "A storm has now burst," said Luther, "which will not end until the Day of Judg- ment." Tile Pepe replied by excommunicating Luther, and putting the country which sheltered him under inter- dict. Again, an Imperial Diet was called to meet at Worms. The Emperer Charles V. was to be present, and Luther was summoned. On the 21st January it assembled. Weeks were oonsumed in angry debate as to the method of proce- dure, the Emperor being resolved on vindicating Holy 1 Church, rand many of his subordinate princes equally ' resolved on shielding Luther. At last, however, the order was given for Luther's attendance. Luther was still at Wit- tenberg awaiting events. Here the Imperial messenger found him, and speedily set forth to bring him to his trial. Meanwhile the Emperor ordered his books to be burnt. Construing this into an augury of personal danger, his friends tried to dissuade him from proceeding to Worms. But he was dauntless. "I will go," said' he, "it there are as many devils in Worms as there are tiles upon the housetops." At ten, on the morning of April 16, Luther entered Worms, attended by a large company, and received by the whole populace, which had turned out to see the most notorious and power- ful man in all Germany. Friends secretly whispered in his ear words of help and encouragement, and verily he stood in need of them! For it was a terrible ordeal he had to face. Some idea of its supreme severity can be gathered from the fact that he stood utterly alone, a plain simple monk and priest of the Church, before that august imperial tribunal, in which the Emperor himself was his enemy, while the archbishops, bishops, priests of this Church, with the nobles of Charles' retinue, shared in time same animosity. In nearly every mind in that large and majestic assembly of poten- tates and priests, the conviction ruled that Luther was fit- ting fuel for the flames!! One, and- one only, of that as- sembly spoke to him as he passed through to the chamber, —" Little monk, little monk ! thou least work before thee, that I, and many a man whose trade is war, never faced the like of I If thy heart is right, and thy cause good, go on, in God's name! He will not forsake thee." He did go on. Be was asked first, if he owned his writings, and then whether he would retract them. Ho demanded space for consideration, which was granted. He returned neat morn- ing, aud said, in a brief speech, that he could not withdraw. He was told his speech was not respectful, and that he must answer straight. without circumlocution. "Answer yes or no," said his interrogator, " without horns." His spirit rose, and pouring all his sturdy manhood into his answer, he briefly said, "I will give you an answer which has neither horns nor teeth. Popes have erred, and councils have erred. Prove to me out of scripture that I am wrong, and I sub- mit! Till then, my conscience binds me!! Here I stand ! I can do no more I God help ins! ! Amen." It has been truly said that this appearance of Luther before the Diet at Worms "is one of the finest, perhaps it is the very finest, scene in human history." "..'ertainly it was a supreme illustration of what a man can do and dare who is full of the Holy Ghost! Is mess be carefully noted now in all his controversy with Rome, Luther inek his stand immoveably upon Scripture. The Book he Lead i;onnd by accident became the instrument with which he not oiely defied, but defeated, the Papal power. Against authoritative councils and infallible Popes he placed the Divine Book, and declared it ,greater than them all. To him, therefore, belongs the immortal honour of restoring the Word of God to its true piece in human regard. Nor was that all. He secured further honcur by being the first to give a German translation of the Hebrew and Greek Scriptures. 'lbis work he achieved when in retreat at Wartburg; thus splen- didly utilizing the seclunion made expedient by his circum- stances. The New Testament was issued fir -and speedily found its way into nearly every home. The Old Testament , followed, and then the German Bible completed what the the theses nailed to the church door in Wittenberg had begun. The Protestant Reformation was an established fact. We must not follow further this marvellous history. It may properly occupy our attention, however, -at a time like this and in a place like this. It was the inspiration of Luther's work that made possible and successful the true work of the reformation in this country. The bonds of the Papacy, which held in subjection the whole of the nations of Christendora, were snapped and broken at the Diet of Worms. When Luther there took his immovable stand on Holy Scripture. he freed himself, and he freed Christendom! He did it at mighty risk, in face of crushing odds, "not counting his life dear unto himself." He did it by inspira- tion of God, for love of truth, and love of man. And we can look back across the four centuries to-day and thank God for Luther. We may rejoice in the man himself, for it is a grand thing to see, whether in history past or in life present, how individual men can wield influences that bene- fit the world. It is inspiring to know that God sometimes r uses a single individual for great purposes. Men like Luther teach us what vast possibilities are wrapped up in manhood. "Lives of great men all remind us, We can make our lives sublime." And as We see how a simple, plain man of the people, true to conscience, true to God, true to his fellow, can confer world-wide good, we may well inquire whether wOre fulfilling all the designs of our life; whether there is not some work possible to us by which we can influence mankind. •While, however, we rejoice in the man—our joy must be more fully in God—the God who sent, inspired, and made Luther successful. God ever has human interest in Ills own keeping.. It has often seemed in the course of the world's history, as if God had forsaken the works of His hands, and the race of man:He had created. God knows how to keep both secrecy and silence. "Thou art a God that hidest thyself, Oh, God of Israel, the Saviour !" But however silent, or secret, God is not slumbering, nor is He heedless of human affairs. This wondrous world is ever responsive to His will. Never will He lose His sovereign hold upon mankind. He who rolled away the darkness of the middle ages; and, by Luther's hand unlocked the treasuries of truth, spreading broadcast the tidings of salva- tion-, giving joy and freedom to souls and to nations—will at last dispel all the darkness that yet overhangs the world, and tause His light to shine forth undimnied,unclouded and clear. Yes ! And God will yet complete Luther's un- flaiehed work of letting out all the light of scripture. There is more light still in this lamp of truth—light more pure and lovely than our eyes have yet beheld. God will one day burst it forth upon the nations, and then they shall learn by instinctive perception, what now they slowly and blunderingly reason out for themselves that love is the life of God, and that love is the salvation and bliss of man. Finally, Luther, the great reformer, the believer in the Bible, the defender of Christ's simple gospel,seems to speak with peculiar accent to us christians of the 19th century. He reminds us of the cost at which our spiritual liberties have been won. Ile reminds us of the bondage from which we have been delivered; and he bids us carefully defend the one, lest we become again entangled in the yoke of the other. It may possibly seem to us that any such counsel from him would surely spring from his memory of his own times, and has no justification in any- thing existing now. Many people refuse to see danger in the ktomanizing tendency now working in the Anglican Church. They are indifferent to its doctrines, and smile at Its ritual of vestments, and candles, and incense, and genu- flection. All the same, the movement is there; the very things Luther turned out of the Reformed Church—the sacramental doctrine, the priestly claims, the practice of the confessional, the vaunt of Church authority, the assertion of no salvation out of the Church—all are there; and, what is worse, it is the popular phase of respectable religion to-day! How Luther's voice echoes to us down the centuries," Hold fast the word of God," as sole authority in faith and religion, and suffer no Church, be it Anglican or Roman, or any other, to intrude its authority in conscience or belief. Hold fast the simple Gospel of salvation by faith in Ckrist alone, and allow no priest and no sacrament to coins between the sinner and the Saviour. Hold fast liberty of conscience— yes, aid grant it to everyone else; for "each man shall give —seems!' ef .hieuself to Holri 1...6, ..a ocv ei lre go, the spirit of Almighty Liod, the Supreme and Only Teacher of the Human soul. Be true to this, your inheritance. Be faithful to your responsibilities, and hand down the Reformed Faith, unalloye I, unfettered, to the generations following. Such seems to me to be Luther's appeal to the men of to-day; and it is an appeal, surely, which we of the Free Evangelical glaurches will know how to honour and obey. CAIRO-STREET UNITARIAN CHAPEL. The Rev. Richard Pilchsr, 8.A., has been giving a series of discourses upon the Reformation, of which that on Sun- day last was a sort of rescind. The subject was : " What Luther did for Man." Tue preacher contended that the justification and strength of the priestly system was found in the doctrine of original sin, which denies to man any power of conceiving of or desiring religiousness except it be put into him from without. The only motive which urged ' men to a religious making act was fear of a " wrath to come," of which he received fall description and warning. Every act of a priest-administered ritual was directed to the imparting to man a holiness he would not otherwise gain, by means of holy made and holy making things and acts, such as holy water, holy bread and wine, holy oil, holy works of penance, six, ie. Two results followed. One was, that the men who were supposed able to work this stupendous series of miracles, gained a power over their fellows which human nature could not bear. The other was, that the acts themselves, staled by repetition, and having (by the hypo- thesis of original sin) no echo in the soul itself, sank to the level of mere mechanism. This was the result of all Ritualism. This was the result is Pagan and Christian Rome alike. To Martin Luther belonged the immortal honour of having dealt a death blow to this system and its soul-deadening results. In his doctrine of faith, he went .0 extremes, as earthen vessels of the Divine treasure were

-hut too apt to do. Salvation by faith only is a doctrine just as unreasonable, unscriptural, and immoral in its logical results as the doctrine of salvation by ritualistic works only. But it must be re- an:mbered that faith, in Luther's teachings and in his best days, meant the giving up of of the whole man, of inward thought and of outward act, to God. In Luther's later years he gave it a more intellectual meaning as it were mere creed. This has been its main meaning with colder fol- lowers of Luther, and lesser natures than was his. His was the old prophetic protest of Hebrew literature, which the Master took up and made all His own. On its moral side it said "It is thy faith which saves, i.e. heals, thee, go and sin no more." On its intellectual side it said, "Why even of your own selves judge ye not what is right ?" Thus; little as Luther towards the end of his life liked it, he prac- tically recognised the conscience as the ultimate court of appeal in matters of faith, as in every other department of human knowledge. In this he was powerfully assisted by the re-discovery (for it was no less) of the Bible, which showed the people a whole nation for 2,000 years impelled and upheld by this God-seeking faculty, and in it and through it growing in insight tilt a Christ became possible. The Germans saw in the book also how that the Hebrews fought against the same kind of tyranny as that against which they had to fight in Luther's day, and that they held the life of the family in an honour withheld from it by the ascetic theories of the Church of }tome. By breaking down this practical denial of honour to the family life Luther secured that devotedness and intelligence hither- to laid-by barren in monastery and convent, were reproduced by that law of hereditary genius, of which we• have heard much of late years. Luther was a peasant, and had much of the rough, coarse energy of his race as well as of his times. He was for years in constant fear of imme- diate seizure and speedy death in the flames. His bravery and cheerful humour were marvellous in the light of this fact. He was very superstitious, and dissented much less Mau many Protestants fancy from the doctrines, rights and policies of the Church of Rome. Yet, making all de- ductions fairly called for, the words of Cardinal Cajetan seem accounted for by Luther's greatness—" I will talk no more with this animal, for he has deep eyes and wonderful speculations in his head." On his services to Germany and its literature, and through them to humanity, time did not permit the preacher t dwell. The 'Air had struck in which a higher level of the Promised Land was to be reached. The man came, and the voice of God went forth through him. The work was done through the faith of the man, "God also bearing witness "by the startling results in respect to his gifts, and by that faith to all men every- where, he being dead yet epeaketh.—ln the evening, Mr. Pilcher drew out a compatison of the likeness and unlike- ness of the teachings of Luther and St. Paul. At Otelbornesstreet Baptist Chapel the pastor, Rev. Ed. Moore, made alluoion to the life and work of the greatlte- former. The influence of Luther's work Mr. Moore said still lived in every Protestant Church and heart. This celebration brought to their minds the reasoes why they were Proteatants and Nonconformists. He thmight the dis- tinctive point, of difference between the eysteins of Popery and Protestantism shoulcrbe made known and emphasized, for though they di.' not quarrel with the Catholics as individuals, they did oppose their system. He clii not be- lieve in intoleranee, er persecution e their Catholic fellow- citizens were entitled to the same civil, political, and reli- gious rights as they claimed for themeelves, and true Non- conformists would never desire anything else. But, at the same time, they hated and opposed Popery, because they be- lieved it was the enemy of freedom,. national progress, education, prosperity, and the deadly enemy of souls. The chief points of difference were the following, which the Church of Rome taught: Reverence paid to images, mario— latory, and invocation of saints; transubstantiation, com- munion in one kind, celibacy of the clergy, purgatory, claim of absolute obedience to the Bishop of Rome, infallibility of the Pope, withholding the Word of God from the people, auricular confession, and prayers in a foreign tongue. The majority of these things the Roman Church held essential to salvation. Against these things they strenuously pro- tested and hence were Protestants. Besides these things, there were three other points of doctrine, of even more im- portance than those above mentioned, upon which also they differed. These were the supremacy of Holy Scripture, the universal priesthood of believers, and the doctrine of justi- fication by faith. Speaking of the first of thee, the preacher said that the Reformation in this respect bad a peculiar interest for them as Baptists, because he believed they were the only demomination that remained true to this great principle, the absolute authority of God's Word. They believed and practised be- lievers' baptism because they found it in God's Word, and they refused to sprinkle infants because they knew there was no such thing in the Bible. If there were, let it be pointed out, and they would practice it. Infant sprinkling I was a relic of Popery, and as they believed in the sole adthority of Scripture, they could not do with it. They tried to make the same loyalty to*God's Wbrd ran throughout all I their faith and practice. As to the priesthood, no Nencou- formist minister assumed, or desired to assume, the office and functions of priests. They Inelieved that every truly converted person was a king and priest to God. The doctrine of justification by faith, as one of their friends remarked, was the "sledge haminer " that broke the fetters which bound the Church. In conclusion let them be true to the principles of the Reformation; let them trust in Luther's God, and endeavour to carry on his work. ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH. Special sermons were preached in St. John's Pres'eyterian Church, Winwick-street, on last Sunday, in connection with I the Luther Commemoration. In the morning the Rev. Jas. Cleland occupied the pulpit, and dwelt on the "Doctrinal I Principles of the Reformation." In the evening the Rev. James Warnock preached on "Martin Luther." He said that Luther's was a name which posterity would not wil- lingly let die. He was one of

_ _ Those dead but sceptred sovereigns who still rule Our spirits from their urns. The Reformation straggle raised many questions which had not yet been brought to a final issue. The influence of that struggle on its secular side was still felt by the nations, and on its religious aids still was, or ought to be, a power in all their lives. The Reformation might be regarded as a revolt of patriotism against foreign domination. It was to it that Germany owed her present power and prosperity. The leading statesmen of Germany knew this well, knew that Luther's was a name to conjure with, and hence they took advantage of the 400th anniversary of his birth to foster a spirit of patriotism, and work out more firmly than ever the great ideal of a united Germany. Luther's translation of the Bible was his most enduring monument. That transla- tion had done for German lite,rature what our own Bible ha& done for English literature. His literary activity was mar. vellous. rims couective wriitu LlUnit-Mitt./ LIU ICCS3 1,-au Cro volumes, 67 of these volumes being written in the German, and 23 in the Latin language. His services to literature were admired by many who did not sympathise with his theological beliefs. But Luther's chief glory was what he had done for religion. The principal events in the Reformer's We were dwelt upon, showing how the great truths which he afterwards pro- claimed to others were first wi'ought out in the experiences of his own inner life. Finally attention was called to the diversified greatness of the man. As a preacher he was un- rivalled. -He was a great lover of nature. He excelled in the gift of song. He was a -mince of talkers. A letter writ- ten by him to one of his children, a little boy of four years, has been characterized by Mr. Froade as the prettiest letter ever addressed by a father to his child. He organised a Church which still bore his name—the Lutheran Church of Germany. Such a life and so great labours could not be easily forgotten. They ought to thank God for what Ile enabled Martin Luther to do, and magnify the grace of God in 'lira. Considering the issue of his life, let them imitate his faith. Dr. H. Bonar's "Hymn of Deliverance," and the hymn "Luther," by Mr. Martin F. Tupper, with music by the Rev. E. W. Ballinger, D.D., were excellently rendered by the choir.

RUNCORN. BETHESDA CHAPEL. Preaching to a large congregation at Bethesda Chapel, Runcorn, on Sunday, from the 11th verse of the 3rd chap- ter of Galatians, the Rev. J. D. Tuomas said there were good reasons for joining in this commemoration, and it be- hoved them to wrest manfully for the truths which Luther succeeded in rescuing from the dusty theological lumber- rooms of the Nledireval Church. They bad been tossed aside as of no \rake, and the accumulative dust of centuries lay upon them when Luther put his hand upon them, and brushing away the dust lifted them up into the light of day. Europe had for ages believed that "the Church" could save. It believed that salvation had beep put into the hands of the priesthood. Luther, with the voice of one who knew and felt what he was saying, denied this falsehood. "No," he said, "that cannot be." It is Christ that saves. The great salvation is wholly in the hands of Him who, his own self, "bare our own sins in his own body on the tree." This

doctrine stood out before Luther as the one great compre- hensive doStrine of revelation. He held that k was by departing from this dectriv that the Church had fallen into bondage, and had cattle to groan under penances and works of self-righteousness. In no other way, he believed, could the Church find her way back to truth and liberty than by returning to this doctrine. This was the road to true Reformation. This great article of Christianity was in a sense its fundamental article, and ' henceforward Luther began to proclaim it as eminently the gospel—the whole gospel in a single phrase. His (Mr. Thomas's) object' that evening was not only to do honour to the work and memory of Luther, but also to explain this fundamental doctrine of evangelical Protestantism. Their starting point, therefore, was the awakened conscience. It was certain that if there las not first of all an awakening to a sense of guilt, there would not be any deep and abiding in- terest in the all important question : "How shall man be just with God ? More than that, sinless there be a consciousness olltain, the need of justification would neither be felt nor seen, Luther's conscience was first awakened by the read- •Jing of the Bible. In these days, when Bibles were 90 plen- tiful, we were apt to forget that formerly they were very scarce, and that it was not at all uncommon for people even in so-called Christian lands to grow up into manhood with- out ever geeing a copy. Luther was 20. years of age before he sew one. If they could imagine with what joy a travel- ler discovered a new country, or a scientific investigator I alighted upon anew truth, they would readily understand 1 what delight the discovery of the Bible occasioned in the heart of Luther. He read and read again, and with mingled surprise and joy he still returned to read. From that moment began those struggles in his soul which were destined never to cease till they issued not morel,' in a new man, but a new age new •Eu:ope. Mr. Thomas described how Luther , resolved to wrench himself from the world and enter a monastery. It was so quiet, so holy, so near to heaven as he thought, that soon as he had crossed its threshold the world would be shut out; sin, too, would ba shut out, and that sore trouble of soul which he was enduring would be at an end. But in the solitude of It's cell and in the drud- gery of convent life his burden grew more grievous, and day by day his inward torments became more insupportable. Instead of finding heaven in the ntonastery he had found the lowest depths of hell. Formerly communicative and jovial, he had grown exceedingly taciturn. What with the drudgery of the day, the studies of the night, and the fasts and macerations he practised, he was more like a c`,rPse than a living man. He fell sometimes on the floor of his cell in sheer weakness; and the likelihood was that instead of living to do battle with error and superstition he would soon find a quiet grave somoviltere in the pr,?ctncts of the monastery. It was by means of these works and this mortifying of the flesh that he thought to buy pardon. Upon a bed of sickness he became to in the forgiveness of sins. Men persisted in payments far sin ft;it God pei- sisttd in the forgiveness of sins. He lus:tAiel the s:nner by faith without the deeds of the law. him. Still he busied himself in religious acts, that be might nourish his piety and return a holier man than he came. Under the influence of this feeling he went to the Church of the Lrteran, in which are the Holy Stairs that Christ is said to have descended on retiring from the judgment hall where 'Pilate had passed sentence upon him Luther was climbing the steps in the appointed way, on his earnine at every step a year'e iedulgence, when bi • wasetarded b n V ga suddeoice which. ipc,ic from heaven, and said, "The just shall live by fatta. " What - folly," thought he, "to seek an indulgence from the Church which c„elast me but a few years, when Got sent me in His Word Ms indulgence that will last me for ever. How idle to toil at these performances when God is Willing to acquit me of all my sins, not as so Tench wages for so much service, but freely, in the wity of believing on His Son." "The just shah, liV3 by faith." That one sentence had more efficacy in it a thonstnd timm over than all the holy treasures that Rome contained. It was the key that unlocked the closed doors of paradise ;It was the star that went..before his face and led him to the throne of a Saviour there to find a fne salvation. It eteded but to re- kindle that old light in Ole skies of the Church, and a day as clear as that of apostate times would again, shine upon her. This was what Luther nroprosed doing-. When he turned his back on Rome he turned his facs Cowards the Bible, and with that Bible be put to flight the darkness and tyranny that had long cursed the peopleof Europe.. SERVICE 07-SONG.

ST. PAULV CHURCH. "The Reformation and the principles by veleich it was won was the subject of the Rev. George Hack'e,diecourse, in the above Church, on- Sunday. The preacher said that with the exception of t-e Apoetle Paul no maii had probably been so charged with the destinies of mankind as Luther. No one could reed his life without being convinced how admirably he was stted for his great work. Gifted with a robust constitution, endowed with great intrepidity -of spirit, combined with a highly. strong emotional nature, splendidly educated, so that he could grapple with the ablest scholars Ronie tnieht oppose him, and above all saved by faith and full of God he waS just the man to battle succeesfully with Rome. After de- scribing the Reformer's work„he asked what had been the influence of Popery upon the prosperity and renown Of nations. Lord Macaulay said: "The lovelieSt and most fertile provinces in Europe have under her role been sithk in poverty and political servitude and in intellectual torpor, whileTrotestent countries, one proverbial for ster- ility and barrenness, had been turned by skill and industrry. into gardens, and can boast of a long list of heroes and Statesnien, of philosophers and poets." Mr. Hack said the influence of Popery on Government had been equally dis- astrous, and the doctrines and institutions of Popery were subversive of the very foundation of morality. Well might they venerate the name of Luther, and celebrate with enthu-- siasm the Reformation, for to him and to it they owed all. that was splendid in their position as a country, all that was valuable in the possession of the Bible, and all that was lofty in social virtue and commercial transactions. - HOLY TRINITY CHURCH.

Preaching on the Luther commentor-a-tion-O; Sunday, the Rev. W. Preston said the Papal power was an unlawful en- - croachment, and was opposed by English sovereigns from the conquest onward. Papal errors accompanied this usurpa- tion which concealed the Primitive faith. The Reforma- tion swept away these errors. No new church or new creed were formed. The corrupt creel of Rome was cast out of - the old Church, the yoke was taken off her neck, and the crown was restored to its supremacy over spiritual men and causes before Luther's faithful men, convinced of the• corrupt state of the Church, sought to work reform. The. Protestant religion was no younger than the apostles and early fathers; it embraced all that they held. The Protestant Church even in 787 protested ag tinst the image-worship of dome. The Reformation was the revolt against priestcraft, and Luther brought about the crisis. Before he aied Luther had disintegrated the Papal empire, and his name would be held in everlasting remembrance. WIDNES. PARISH CI Ult _ _

On Thursday evening the Rev J. Wright Williams, vicar of Widnes, delivered a lecture on Luther in the National Schools. Despite the boisterous state of the weather a good audience assembled, and listened attentively to the lecturer's narrative. Messrs. Kilcross and Cave:occupied seats on the platform. Mr. Williams at the outset said that in all great Lueiu airect- ing minds, and it was one of the greatest pleasures a re.en could have in looking over history to see if they could de- tect some of the master minds in these movements. And at this time very largely on the Continent and indeed through- out the world men were having their attention called to that great movement the Reformation, and to one of. the greatest if not the greatest minds in that Reformation— Martin Luther. The childhood and youth of Martin were described until he became a student at thern University of Erfurt to be educated for the life of a lawyer. There he dis- covered a Latin Bible, in which he found many truths which somewhat stir-tied gim, especially in cenneCtion with the State religion. The whole of the Christian countries in Europe were Christian, insomuch that they were connected- ' with the great city and Pope of Rome. But for hundreds of years Christianity had been becoming more and more de- based. The Popes, instead of being examples of all that was good and pure, were in many instances. eaaraples of just the reverse, and Roderigo Borgia, who was then on the Papal throne as Alexander 6th, was a man who lived In a state of considerable sin, and even manifest and open impurity. And as the Pone, So the priests in many cases were. The various orders of Monks were touched upon, and the spiritual doctrines of the whole of Christendom at the be- ginning of the 16th century was graphically described; the sudden death of Alexis; its effect upon Luther, who sub- sequently entered a monastery; and the deep heart-search- ings which followed were narrated in an interesting manner. Speaking of the Confessional, the rev, lecturer said he thought that for Christian people to go to a Christian man or a clergyman and ask him for a little Con- solation, a little comfort, or a little direction, was much the ' same as a clergyman going t' a a joiner and asking how to join a piece of wood, for it was the work of a clergyman to preach of God and relieve the conscience. The various f other important events in Luther's life were passed in re- view, and the lecturer concluded with an eloquent perora-
tien upon the ability, goodness, and courage of tile Reformer. The thanks of the meeting were accorded to the Vicar, on the motion of Mr. J. Farrant, seconded by Mr. IL N. Wharton.
POLITICAL BANQUETS.

Lord Selleorne and Mr. Shaw-Lefevre were entertained at a banquet at Reading on Wednesday, in celebration of the twentieth anniversary of Mr. Shaw-Lefevre's election for the borough. It was natural that the right hon. gentleman on such an occasion should review Liberal legislation in that period, aml he was able, in looking back upon it, to declare that, though certain things had been ptiled down by the Liberals during the last fifteen years, nothing had been uprooted that was worth preserving, and what had been done only the more clearly brought into view the lines of the constitution. Lord Selborne, in looking to the future, and having regard to the pledges of the Government said he did not think that the machinery of the constitution should be perpetually undergoing alteration; ,but these were times for improvement, and public opinion win dicate when always when such times had come. There could be no more com- plete recognition than this of the duty of legislators to obey the clearly expressed wish of the people, mad at the present time there is no room for doubt as to what legislation the country demands. Mr. Chamberlain and M. de Lesseps were present at the Trinity House banquet on Wednesday night, but M. de Les- seps, though he reiterated his desire to anticipate the reasonable demands of English commerce, and his convic- tion that he would be able to reconcile English and French Interests, did not throw much light upon the means by which he hopes to accomplish these objects. Mr. WILLIS, the Liberal member for Col- chester, has given notice of his intention to move, early in next session of Parliament, the follar'ing resolution: "That the legisla- tive power of Bishops in 'lie House of Peers in Parliament is a great hindrance to the dis- charge of their spiritual functions, prejudicial to the commonwealth, and ought to be taken away by That this moticn deserves the hearty support of every Liberal member of Parliament is, we think, abundantly proved in a little pamphlet entitled, "The votes of the Bishops in the House of Lords," just issued by the Liberation Society. The fact that in June of last year the Marriage with a. Deceased Wife's Sister Bill was rejected in the House of Lords by the votes of the bishops alone, has tended to direct public attention to the position of their lordships in that assembly. Their actions at various periods of the country's history have since been severely criticised, and probably by none more so than by Mr. Bright, who at a recent Liberation meeting showed with considerable truthfulness and force that judged by their past conduct the bishops are not likely in the future to be of any value in advancing measures which have for their object the welfare of the people at large. The pamphlet to which we have referred contains a record of the action of the bishops in regard to some of the most important public questions which have come before Parliament in recent years, and a perusal of the record impels us to the con- clusion that the interests of the bishops in legislative matters are of a purely selfish character. The pamphlet opens with a very appropriate quotation from the "Church Reform Papers" of the Rev. J. C. Ryle, now Bishop of Liverpool, who in 7870 wrote : "The notion that English Christianity would suffe; damage if the bishops were withdrawn from the House of Lords appears to me entirely devoid of foundation. I have read the debates in Parliament with considerable attention for twenty-five years, and I am un- able to see that the Church of England de- rives much benefit from its bishops being temporal peers. On the contrary, the com- plaint has been made—and with no little. show of reason—that in the debates and divisions of the Upper House the bishops are often present when they ought to be absent, and absent when they ought to be present! The little good that they do in the, House of Lords certainly does not out- weigh the harm that is done by absence from. their dioceses, and by an expensive sojourn in London. At any rate there seems no necessity for more than five bishops at most being in Parliament." The votes of the bishops lend point to these observations, and substantiate Dr. RYLE'S argument with ten-fold force. It will be of interest to our readers if we quote a few facts from the pamphlet. In 1807 the Parochial Schools Bill, which authorised magistrates to provide schools where they were wanted out of the rates, was submitted to the House of Lords,. but was rejected on the second reading without a division. The Archbishop of CANTERBURY, we are told, spoke strongly against the Bill, his main reason being that education was more widely extended than was supposed?

MERSEY SALT AND BRINE COMPANY.—It Will be een, Ola reference to our advertising c durns, that the directors of this well-known company are now prepared to issue six per Pont. debentures (convertible at the option of the holders into ordinary shares at par), in order to complete the under- taking by the erection of silt works at Runcorn. The line Of PiPes from Marbury to Runcorn is already laid, and the large reservoir at the latter place already contains more than two million gallons of brine. The Company have every confidence of success in their undertaking. Spellman, in order to avoid a distraint for rent.—From the evidence of William Carroll, it appeared that the defendant hal been a tenant of Mr. Speakman's since 1878. There had been arrears of rent for a long time, but the defendant's wife having been ill Mr. Speakman had taken pity on the man, and delayed taking proceedings. About six months ago he permitted him to leave a house, the rent of which was 4s, 6d., to go into a house in Pool-lane at 2s. Bd. per week, Mr. Speakman thinking the difference between the two sums would enable him to pay off the arrears. Instead of that being the case however, there had been a great deal of trouble to collect the 2s. Bd., and at length he removed his furniture without giving notice. The arrears amounted to £9 Is. 6d,' and the defen- dant had promised to pay 23. 03. per week if the Bench would make that order.—lt was stated by Mr. Ashton (the maeis- trates' clerk) that the Bench could only make an order with reference to the arrears of the defendant at the house in Pool-lane, and these only amounted to the sum of 198. 61— The witness asked, however, if the magistrates had not p)AvEr to make an order for double the value of the goods ; and Mr. Ashton replied in the affirmative. The goods were worth over £5.-Ihe Bench made an order for the payment of the arrears, 19s. 6d., with the costs, 10s. 6d., forthwith. THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES. With the close of the year there is the usual quietening down in the iron trade, and the unfavourable reports during the last few days from the iron centres in the north of England, and at Glasgow, have had a further tendency to check •the giving out of orders here. There was only a quiet market on Tuesday, and very little doing in pig iron. Lancashire makers are getting no new orders of 'any importance, but hold to their full rates, which nominally remain at 45s 63, less 21- for forge and foundry qualities, delivered equal to Manchester. For district brands very few inquiries are re- ported at the top prices of 44s 103 to 45s 103, less 2-1 for forge and foundry Lincolnshire delivered here, and there are one or two sellers at 6d under these figures. In the manufactured iron trade orders are running out faster than they are being replaced, and the tendency is towards an easier tone in prices. The minimum quoted rates for delivery into the Manchester district remain, however, at £6 2s 6d to £6 5s for bars, £6 103 for hoops, and £7 15s to £8 Os per ton for sheets.— Although there has not as yet been any very materially in- creased weight of actual business doing in the coal trade of this district the market during the last few days has shown rather more animation. Any advance in prices has not been obtainable from buyers, and in the present state of the market colliery proprietors are very cautious about commit- ting themselves far ahead. The better classes of round coal are moving off freely for house fire purposes, but the de- mand so far has not necessitated any very material filling up out of stocks to meet requirements; common round coals I for furnace purposes also move off without difficulty, but engine classes of fuel still only meet with a slow sale, with plentiful supplies of the common qualities of slack. Prices I are without change since the commencement of the month, ! and at the nit mouth remain about as under :—Best coals, Os 6d to 103; seconds, is 63 to Sc; common house coals, es ed to 79; steam and forge coals, 5s 6sl to 6s ; burgy, 4s fil to ss; good slack, 3s 6d to 4s and common sorts about 2s &I to 3s per ton at the pit. The demand for ship- ment during the week has been only moderate, with steam coal delivered at the Garston Decks, or the high level, Liverpool, averaging 78 6d to 7s 9d per ton. Coat con- .
