I think even now I may prophecy what will be the most interesting picture in the Academy, which is bold vaticina- tion, as not a stroke of the work has yet been put on the canvas. No painter that we have paints old age as Mil- lais does. In the treatment of it he is at least a realist. I suppose most people have seen, and, I am sure all who have seen will remember, his likeness of Mrs. lleugh—that furrowed face, and those wonderful knotted hands were a revelation to those who knew Millais only as a fashionable portrait painter. It will be interesting to see what he vriil do with Sir Mo9o3—the interest will be the greater as the finest partrait George Richmond ever painted was from the same model.

America is so completely the El Dorado of actors, opera singers, and lecturers that it will be a surprise to hear of big figures coming from an Eastern capital, and above all from such a dead and alive old city as Moscow. Russians when you meet them abroad are about the richest people you come across, and a dignity and a retenue, unknown to the Yankee millionaires, all makes in the direction of sup- posed greater wealth; but sometime ooe does not fancy them to be very nice at borne, or likely to come into collision with America in hiring the services of an opera singer. And yet I hear that Pauline Lucca goes there next month, and for singing at three concerts gets a thousand pounds down. Tnere is one thing to be said about these big fivres. The singers risk a great deal in going to a cold or unsuitable climate. The voice is a delicate organ, and is LUCCA'S stock-in-trade. Part of the thousand is in fact an insurance against cold, and the premium should beibie: to cover the risk of a De- cember in Moscow.

The sword fish seems to be almost as much of a royal fish as the whale or the sturgeon, and one has just been sent by its captors as a present to the Prince. That idea of the Sovereign being a kind of aquarium to which every species of rare marine monster should be forwarded so soon as it was caught did very well in the feudal times, but I am told that now-a-days it is a little inconvenient. There is a statute still unrepealed—if I de not mistake—certainly unrepealed a couple of years ago, under which sturgeons were royal fish, avd the property of the Crown. Wholly unconscious of the distinction they have during the last ten years propagated very fast and have been captured very freely. The law-abiding fishermen of the coasts used to firward them to Buckingham Palace, or Windsor, or Bal- moral, till at last Her Majesty round it to be more blessed to give than to receive. The Crown had waived its rights, the sturgeon belongs to its captors, and the public may buy It at is. a lb., and Not get a very good bargain at the price.

A new kind of fur for the new kind of hat. It is only just announced from Paris, and has not yet been seen in the parks or the streets. The fur is cat skin, acd the ornament is the head of the kitten; smetimes there are two heads en the same hat. It is said to create quite a sensation i• Paris, and I can readily believe it. When black capes first came into fashion there was a cheap kind made of the fur of black rabbits, and I am told that so great was the demand in one winter that those rabbits were ne irly exterminated. Are we to lose our tabbies?

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

THE CABINET COUNCILS ELECTION OF SHERIFFS—FROZEN MEAT IN PROCESSION—A NEW TENOR MRS. WELDON BBEACH OF PROMISE CASE—SUICIDES—O'DONNEL'S TRIAL —SIR MOSES AND MILLAIS—LUCCA AT MOS- COW—SWORD FISH, STURGEON, AND KITTENS. LONDON, TIIIIRMAY. Two questions before the Cabinet Councils this week re- quired consideration. It was necessary that something should be settled about the appointment •1 Speaker. The policy which, I think, not merely the Government but the whole House would wish to adopt would be pieta non movere. The present Speaker is both competent and popu- lar. There is conflance in his impartiality and in his ability. But Sir Henry had to be heard himself. He is not what he used to be, nor is the Speaker's chair what it used to be. If next session were to he like the last he would necessarily have to resign, an& resignation in the full swing of business might be very incon- venient. And so his resignation is discussed now. It is known that Sir William Harcourt cannot be spared from his present post. He makes a right good Home Secretary, and he would make a very indifferent Speaker of the House. Then there is Sir Henry James. It seems to be understood that when Parliament meets he will still be Attorney-General. There is Mr. Dodson, and there is Mr. Whitbread. Other names have been put forward, but in a conjectural way. lam told a strong appeal has been made to Sir Henry Brand, and that when Parliament meets in February he will be found—if he can at all manage it—in the enjoyment of his accustomed office. Another point that the Council settled was how the Parnellite campaign in the North was to be met. Earl Spencer had very strong views, and he was, of course, speaking on his own subject. The powers given the Executive under the Peace Preservation Act are to be resortc3 to, and the meetings will be pro- claimed.

The honourable °Mee of High Sheriff for the county seems every year to grow less popular. All sorts of ex- cuses were put forward by those whose position entitled them to have the honour of ontertaining her Majesty's jus- tices when they come down to hold their assizes. The ex- cuses were as a rule not liatened to, though one gentleman who pleaded lunacy had his claim prodaptly allowed. The court was very full, for a report had circulated that the Prime Minister would attend. Lord Coleridge has since his return been making uncomplimentary critilism in the New Courts of Justice. Certainly the old Court of Exchequer, where the late and last Chief Baron used to preside on "the morrow of St. Martin," was much better suited for the ceremony. But it's a stupid ceremony, at best. Mr. Childers, in his black and gold robes, afforded perhaps some kind of comfort to those who are only accustomed to seeing;him in that well fitting frock—his wonted wear—and Lord Derby in mufti was lombersome, without being impressive. The Judges wore their black robes, which was technically all right, but which looked all wrong. If public business is to be inter- rupted for such a ceremonial, it may as well be as Stately as possible. I think everyone will be glad to hear that there has been a disclaimer put in about the part frozen meat took in the Lord Mayor's procession. It made the whole show ridicu- lous. A great butcher's cart with a dozen carcases of fat mutton oscillating from the pegs of its frame-work was a curious property to interpose between Grace Darling's boat and my Lord Mayor's state ooach. There was a certain humourous cruelty in the notion of these corpulent alder- men bowing graciously to a jocular mob and quite uncon- scious of the mutton that looked as if it was going home with them to the banquet, I remember some years ago a ceremony used to be performed in the old Court of Ex- chequer at Westminster. The Recorder would attend with the retiring Lord Mayor, and the Chief Baron would call upon the latter to resign in favour of his successor, or certain appointMents would be held. One of these was the chief guager to the Corpora- tion. On this occasion the Chief Baron was indisposed_ or absent, and the puisne who took his place was near-sighted and unaccustomed to this duty. "And I now, my lord, I must call upon you to resign the post"— here he looked through his glasses to see the word—" to re- sign the post of chief gorger to the Corporation of this ancient city." Preceded by all that mutton, the Lord Mayor aid look last week as if be were chief gorger to the Cor- poration. lam glad to see that its apdearance in the show I was quite unwarranted. II hear of a new tenor likely 900 n to appeut on English beards, and the more welcome because he Is an Englishman Most musical Londoners have heard him in sacred music. He is the son of Cave Wade, at whose church Solis FaciiS Passion music has for many successive seasons of Lent been 'so beautifully rendered. The tenor parts used to be taken by Mr. Arthur Wade, who has now for some years been study- ing in Italy. We have so few tenors now, and so very few who can sing sacred music, that Mr. Wade will be quite an , acquisition to the stage.

Our two sensation cases have made the courts very bright and busy this week. .Mrs. Weldma has become quite a public character. She has got to be as well known to the ushers of the Divorce Court as Mrs. Gialometti Prodgers is 1 to the cabmen at Victoria Station. Certainly the pertina- cious way in which she pushed her seige of Sir James ' Hannen went far to show that such women as may be fitted for advocacy will not be restrained by any motives of false delicacy. She was as resolute as the most experienced of silks. Sir James is the most austere of all jndgesss the coldest and the most dignified; but Mrs. Weldon was not to be awed. The court had ordered that Mr. and Mrs. Weldon should live together, and the husband said he I would not do it at any price ; and so Mrs. Weldon comes in, professing the kindest feelings to her husband, and asking that she should have her rights, and that Mr. Weldon should do what was ordered, or else be punished for being in contempt. It was no use for Sir James to look dignified and to look cross, There was the law, and he was to ad- minister it. Sir James was very much like the doge in the trial scene in the "Merchant of Venice." He was bound by the letter of the law to act against its spirit. He takes time to consider. They talk of driving a coach and six through an Act of Parliament. But suppose Mr. Weldon has such an unaccountable dislike to Mrs. Weldou that he'd rather live in prison without her than at home with her, what will Sir James do? He takes time to consider, and well he may. I think young persons about to marry ought to do the same. Though really what was going on in another court at the same time makes the difficulty almost as great. In that case there was no marriage, but instead an action for the breach of it. The plaintiff certainly is a very showy woman. and there was a a great deal of mystery about her previous lover, said to be a millionare, said to be unable vcry well to read or write, and called the American. There were whisperei about the court as to who this Silver King would turn out to be, some Astor, or Stewart, oc Vanderbilt. And it was better than any play when, worried by cross-examina- tion, she came out with the name herself. I suppose to keep a secret is the one thing a woman cannot do. The whole aspect of the coin was very gay. Baron Pollock, a melan- choly kind of indge, quite cheered up, and the light comic business thrown in by counsel made this morning's per- formance a complete success. The house was filled to over- flowing, and everyone seemed in good humour.

In the meantime another poor defendant in a breach of promise case, tried only a few days before, had just com- mitted suicide. The forty shillings damages and the fact of being beaten were too much for him. It is curious that there seems to have been this week a wave of suicide, which has passed all over Europe.. There is an idea that here in Loltdon we suffer most from the epidemic in the month of November, and that the fogs have to do with it. But in Paris there have been three cases; in Venice there were also three, the sisters who sailed out to the Lido and died so romantically; in Padua there was the Roman general who had risen from the ranks, served so honourably at Sol- ferino, and was decorated with quite a museum of war medals. The three cases this week in Paris were not iso- lated. There have been more suicides in Paris during the last fortnight than have been known for years, and they sees to be chiefly of the female sex. In Ireland the tedium vital has broken out amongst the private soldiers, and yet in Italy, France, and England the first fortnight of No- vember has been exceptionally bright and sunny. Everyone has been surprised at the selection of the Judge to try the prisoner O'Donnell. Mr. Justice Denman has never put himself forward either as a criminal lawyer or as a sensation judz,e. A few years ago, whenever any notori- ous ease was in the list, if it did not fall to the lot of the Lord Chief Justice, Mr. Justice Brett had somehow the good

The MEDICAL OFFICER (I)r. Bride) reinired as follows : " I have to report that Thomas Clarke is eufferin4 from tiphoid fever at a cottage at Five Crosses, Frodsliam Lord- ship. This man worked with Thomas Parker at Kingsle:v, and it has been stilted that the men employed in laying down of conduit pipes drank freely of water taken from the Brook. I therefore must assume that the germs of the disease were conveyed to the bodies of these men by this vehicle. Further efforts must be made to discover from whence the pollution of the brook origi- nated ; therefore I shall report upon this outbreak and that of scarlet fever at Suttin more fully in a future communi- cation."—The NUISANCE INsrEcroß (Mr. Farrington) said that these men had drunk water from the brook which runs through Kingsley. He believed that men who had worked at Kingsley had left there because they found that some- thing was the matter with them, but they could not tell what it was. The men referred to in the report had not been in c-litact with each other, but they had both drunk of the water from the brook. All the inhabitants of Kingsley know that the water was not fit for drinking purposes. It seemed that these men bad set a lad to fetch them drinking water, and he had taken it from the nearest place from which he could get it, and that was the brook. He (Mr. Farrington) thought that it was clear the fever bed been ciused by the water from the brook—The CLERK said that the water varied in quality every day.—The CHAIRMAN: What if an analysis shows that the fever has been caused by the water ?—Tbe CLERK said that it would be a matter for litigation. They would have to prosecute everybody who turned any pollutiort into the water if they meant to alter the matter.—Mr. ASHTON said there was nozhing to compel the men to drink tlae water. All that the Authority could do was to prevent the contamination of the water.—The CHAIRMAN said that as far as he could see, it was the fault of the men them- selires.—Mr. ASHTON : What do we propose to do in the matter ?—The CHAIRMAN: I don't see that we can do any- thing.—The CLERK: You could not remedy the state of the brook except through very expensive litigation.—The matter then dropped. NUISANCE INSPECTOR'S REPORT.

The NUISANCE INSPECTOR reported the existence of a nuisance at the Bull's Head, Overton, and he received instructiens to serve a notice for its early removal. He also reported that be had reasonable grounds for suspecting that the water supply to the Ring O'Bells, Daresbury, and to Hillside Farm, Appleton, was polluted. He was instruc- ted to obtain samples of the water to submit them to analysis. He called the attention of the authority to a nuisance caused by a stable in Church-street, Froclsham, and to a nuisance at Wilderspool. Instructions were given him to serve notices for the removal of the nuisances. LEGAL ASSISTANCE FOR THE NUISANCE INSPECTOR. On the motion of Mr. R. ASHTON, seconded by Mr. SMITH, it was resolved that the Nuisance Inspector in pro- ceedings before magistrates should be authorised to employ where necessary, a solicitor, at a cost of not more than one guinea in each care.

div.head: POISONING MYSTERY AT IVIDSES.
div.p: POISONING MYSTERY AT IVIDSES.

THE /NQUES I' ADJOURNED. At the Angel Inn, on Monday, an inquest was held on the body of William Williams, who died on Friday morning, under circumstances which are surrounded in mystery. The acting coroner was Mr. W. Hardy, barrister, Manchester, and the foreman of the jury was Mr. Faulkner.—The first witness called was Catherine Mort, wife of George Mort, residing at 1, Davis-street, Widnes, who said the deceased was her father, and had lived with her husband since her mother died, 18 months ago. He was a master baker, and was 63 years of age. Feeling unwell about a fortnight ago, deceased gave up work. lie had often said that he did not feel well, and he wished he was lying with her mother in Runcorn Cemetery. He was a temperate men. There was no poison of any kind in the house' and they had never, to her knowledge, bought any stuff to kill vermin. On Thurs- day, althote4h for a fortnight previously the deceased had kept his bed, he got up, and about half-past two went out for , a walk. On returning at five o'clock, he said he hid bees , to see his wife's grave, and complained of being heertsich. At his request, some mussels wefe cooked for his tem. and then, still feeling eickly, he went to bed- About eleven o'clock .he was tmViCla • WOW. and Dr. M`Donnell vast sent ge,r. - • '' ' assistant prescribed for him av. ,! Ihe doctor s plied. He, howeve- remedies were ap- Witness insur. . nair-past one next morning. ..a( deceased in the Prudential Assurance Com- pany .reent lour years ago. She paid sixpence per week, and Was entitled to receive £l3 Os. 4d. Deceased had about .00 in the bank when he took the bakehouse, but he had I nothing at the time of his death, and sold his furniture when he came to live with her husband. Ile was not in- sured in any other society than the Prudential. Sarah Kinsey said she laid out the body of the deceased. He seemed in good condition, and there were no Dierks upon his hodv.—Charles Lloyd, commercial traveller for IVlessrs. Radford and Sons, Liverpool, said he had known deceased , for many years, and had done business with him About four o'clock on Thursday he met the deco teed in Runcorn, and asked him to stay to tea but he refused. Deceased said " Good night ; it will be as much as I can do to get over Runcorn Bridge; I shall not be here long." The deceased looked very poorly.—Dr. 11PDonnell deposed that on Thursday evening his assistant was hurriedly called to see the deceased. On returning to the surgery next morning he informed witness of the nature of the cas and the synipi owls deceased exhibited. Deceased was in a state of collapse and dying. He was suffering from severe abdominal pain and vomiting a bloody frothy mucous; there was severe relax ttion of the bowels, burning sensation in the throat, and cramps in the calves of the legs. The de- ceased died about two hours after the assistant's visit. His assistant had left his service, and he did not know where he was at present. On Sunday he (witness) received orders from the police to make a post-mortem examination of the body of the demeed. He had done so that raorniug. in the presence of Dr. M`Cambridge and his present as- sistant, Hugh A. Richardson. He should certainly say, from the appearance of the lining membrane of the stomach, that death had not resultecdfrom natural causes, but from the introduction of some irritant poison. He was eatistied that deceased died from irritant poisoning, but wh it particular poison, or how administered, he was not in a position to say. —The Coroner said no stone would be left untamed to die- cover the real facts, for there could be no doubt that the deceased had been poisoned. It was a most mysterious c tse. —The inquest was then adjourned for a week to allow the county analyst to analyse the viscera of the decessed.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES.

Yesterday morning James Brannon, t3O years of age, a stone breaker at Messrs. Hutchinson's Ch2tnical Works, Widnes, fell down dead whilst following his employment. He lodged at 3, Marsh-street, and during the last week. had complained of a pain in his left side.
IMPORTANT TO WIDNES BUILDERS.

An adjourned meeting of Widnes Local Board was held on Friday morning, Mr. E. Carey in the chair. There were also presont Messrs. T. Handley, J. Midwood, B. Dutton, E. Manley, R. Webster, S. Sadler, W. 11. Kershaw, Dr. O'KeeiTe, J. T. Allen (clerk.)—Various formal matters !ere attended to; and then Dr. Thorne, medical inspector to the Lieal Government Board, ant Mr. Smith, architect, had an interview with the Board with respect to the bye- laws which were passed some months ago, but had not yet received the sanction of the Local Government Board. The by-laws of the Highway Committee contained a clause. regulating the height of houses, but Dr. Thorne stid the Boatd had no power to make such a bye-law. All they could do was to make the streets broader, so as to obtain the same result—that the streets should not as it w,re be made into alleys.—ln answer to Mr. Kershaw, Dr. THORNE said that after a cottage or any building was erected with the sanc- tion of the Board, the owner, if he wished, could erect a tower of Babel upon it without asking the approval of the Board. The Board had no power over the alteration of buildings. Of course if the building was dangerous the Board could take ction.—lt was incidentally mentioned `..'- be that the old bye-laws stlted that all buildings aould put up to the F ttisfaction of the Board.—D,.. TIioRNE said the Local Government Board never passed such a clause. It really was not a bye-law. i the public could never know when they were ri.,at. If twe or three j,erry builders be- came members of the Board there was no telling :hat would be done.—A discussion on technical points followed.

DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT RUNORN. OLD QUAY MILL BURNT DOWN: DAMAGE £30,000. About half-past six on Tuesday morning a fire was dis- covered to have broken ont in the top storey of the Old Quay Mill. An alarm was at once conveyed to the fire brigade, which, under the command of Superintendent Wright, arrived on the !cane of the conflairation shortly before seven o'clock with the fire-engine. The engine was at once connected with the canal, and a stream of water was poured upon the flames. In the meantime the workmen bad attached two hose pipes to the Water Company's main, and the firemen now fixed another, at owing to the fact that• certain pipes were being repaired at the works of Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele very little pressure was obtained. The full pressure was, however, subsequently put on, and large quantities of water were thrown upon the burning building. There were also on the premises about 30 buckets, and these were brought into use in the attempt to subdue the flames, which burst through the roof and lit up with a lurid glare the foggy atmosphere around. At a distance of 40 yards, so dense was the fog, the conflagration could nit be seen, and the motions of the workers were not hampered by the assemblage of a large crowd, not more than 00 people con- gregating on the spot. The work of the firemen was both dangerous and difficult, but all concerned acted with com- mendable courage, Their efforts to save the building were only partially successful. The roof fell in with a crash, and the conflagration became more furious. The floors were formed of stone and concrete, and when they became heated they broke up with a tremendous crash, splinters fly- ing in all directions. Floor after floor, with the machinery upon them, fell in, and it was not until half-pest 10 that the flames gave any sirs of subsiding; but water was poured on to the smouldering mass until noon, when the fire appeared to be utterly extinguished About half-past eight in the morning the fire engine of the Bridgewater Navigation Company arrived on the scene in readiness to protect their warehouse, which was in the im- me Bate neighbourhood, but happily the engine was not re- quired. Daring the progress of the fire, two' members of the brigade named Fox and Joyce, who had been con- spicuous in their efforts to save property, were overcome by the smoke and became unconscious. 1)r. MacDougall was sent for and applied remedies, and the men were afterwards taken home. Marcus Ward, a foreman at the works, was also overcome in a similar manner. A young man named Comes had a very narrow escape. He was carried down with a falling floor, but miraculously escaped with only a few scratches. A force of police, under the command of Sergeants McMichael and Walley, rendered good assistance. The mill is the property of a company of which Mr. William Rathbone, M.P., and Mr. Ross T. Smythe, of Liver- poi, are large shareholders. Operationsahad only been car- ried on by them about two years, the mill having fre- quently changed hands, and about 25 Years ago it was des- troyed by fire. It was elaborately fitted up on an American system, and was considered to be "fire proof." Very little wood entered into its construction. Polished pitch pine shoots connected the top of the building, which was seven storeys high, with the bottom, and these, nearly all the woodwork in the place, burnt furiously. All the floors were of stone, supported by iron girders and pillars, while the staircases were also of iron. As the event showed, all these precautions against fire were unavailing. The floors with two exceptions, smashed up, the iron girders were bent and twisted into many fantastic shapes, and the staircases, in many instances, were cracked, and are unfit for further use. The building had only recently been fitted up with expen- sive machinery at a cost it is stated of about £12,003, and this is almost completely destroyed. Mr. Yapp, the manager, arrived at the works shortly after the alarm was given, and under his directions a large quantity of flour was Baca, and we believe the office books and part of the furniture. The engine and boiler also escaped destruction, but everything is in a more or less damaged state. How the fire originated is a mystery, but it has been suggested that the excessive friction of some of the machinery in ; he top storey, which was known as the purifying room, wag the cause. Toe damage is estimated at the sum of £30,000, which is fully covered by insurance in the following offices :—Millers and Gereral, Loadon and North-Western. Lancashire, Equitable, and Standard

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday, under the presidency of Mr. Carey. There were present Messrs. Pankhnrst, Handley, Forster, Wrigbr, Midwood, Dutton, Houghton, Manley, Webster, Sadler, Kershaw, Dr. O'Keeffe. Allen (clerk), Higginson (surveyor), Carr (gas engineer), and 'Copeland (resident engineer.)

div.head: AN OBJECTION TO THE HOSPITAL TENTS.
div.p: AN OBJECTION TO THE HOSPITAL TENTS.

The CLERK read a letter from the St. Helens Permanent Building Society, objecting to the close proximity of the hospitAl tents to their property in Egypt-street and Moor End. In consequence the tenants had intimated their de- termination to leave the neighbourhood, aad the Society bad resolved on the motion of Mr. Dickenson, seconded by Mr. Wildgoose—(lond laughter)—to rcqust the Widncs Authority to remove the tents to such a place as'would , satisfy the tenants. Mr. KERSHAW WAS strongly opposed to the present pogi- tion of the tents which he stated almost blocked the road from Widnes to Ditton. It was not creditable to the Board to have placed the tents in close proximity to a sewer, and he thought a better site could have been obtained.—Tbe CHAIRMAN: What are we to do with the letter ?-111e. KER- SHAW: You can do what you like with the letter.—Mr. Hotrowrox remarked that he had enquired how far the St. Helens Infectious Diseases Hospital was from any dwelling., and he recdived a telegram stating the distance to be 70 or 80 yards.—Mr. WRIGHT expressed the opinion that that space did not intervene.
MR. JEFFIITHS AND THB BOARD: AN ACTION THP.EAIENED.

The CLERK said he had received a letter from Mr. Jeffries, dated the 9th of November, which he had harried to Mr. Robert Davies. It stated that Mr. Jeffries was going to enter an action against the Board for various reasons, one being that the resident engineer and surveyor bad not given him proper information, and that he (the clerk) and Mr. Davies had deceived him, while some members of the Board had obstructed him. (Laughter.) He (the Clerk) had asked Mr. Davies to be prepared to meet the C. 130 on behalf of the Board, and he wished that instruction confirmed—Mr. CAREY moved a proposition to that effect, Mr. WEBSTE% seconded, and it was carried.

div.head: DEFINITION OF A PAUPER.
div.p: DEFINITION OF A PAUPER.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board sta.t- that a pauper was a person actually in receipt of poor relief, and if he was suffering from an infectious dist as it was the duty of the Guardians to provide accommodation for him. The Guardians were not compelled to provide hospital ac- commodation for any other kind of perms. It was, how- ever, much better that the Local Authority should provide hospital accommodation for a diseased pilper, and charge the Guardians with the cost.

div.head: BASIS OF THE COUNTY BATE.
div.p: THE BASIS OF THE COUNTY BATE.

The CLERK drew the attention of the Board to the fact a meeting of the vestry was to be held on Fliday to consider the basis of the county rate recently issued by the justices. lie founct that the last basis was prepared in 1870, and that they bad now increased the rateable value of Widnes about £40,000. Instead of allowing some deduction between gross and rateable value as the Guardians did, they simply al- lowed one-sixth on all sarts of buildings, and one-twelfth on land. The Guardians allowed 5 per cent. on land, 15 per cent. on houses, and 3.31 per cent. on werks.—The CHAIR- MAN suggested that the Board should ask the overseers to enter an appeal against„.the rateable value of Widnes.—The CLERK remarked that the rateable value of the railways in Widnes had been increased £20,000, whilst the works had also been considerably increased. It was decided that as many members as possible should attend the vestry meeting.

div.head: BOLLEITION OF ROWER'S BROOK.
div.p: THE BOLLEITION OF ROWER'S BROOK.

The CHAIRMAN said the members would be aware that Mr. Gossage bad been endeavouring to make an arrange- ment between the manufacturers and the London and North- Western Railway Company to keep Bower's Brook clean. A letter, dated November 3, had been received from Mr. Worthington, agreeing, on behalf of the company, to a tem- porary arrangement, by which the company would pay and the manufacturers I of the cost of cleaning the brook, on the understanding that the company did not assume any liability through the existing state of things. The commu- nication was referred to Mr. Gossage. GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.

The minutes °Obis committee stated that the water in stock on the 17th October was 7,486,538 gallons. The rain- fall for the month had been 483 inches. The water pumped during the five weeks ending the 17th nisi= was 56,820,940 gallons, and the water delivered was 58,099,555 gallons, an increase of over 10 million gallons on the cor- responding period last year. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 16 62 candles.— It was recommended that a Bray lamp (150 light) be sub- stituted for the present lamp at Anderson's Corner.—On the 2nd November, Mr. Carr wrote to the committee stating that he had now been a year in the Board's service and applying for an increase of salary.—lt was recommended that Mr. Carr's salary be increased £5O per annum.

div.head: AN INCREASE OF SALARY.-THE GAS ENGINEER
div.p: AN INCREASE OF SALARY.-THE GAS ENGINEER
EULOGISED

Mr. PANEHURST moved the contirmetion of the Gas Com- mittee's minutes, and referring to the proposed ine-. Mr. Carr's salary, said that gentleman durie— ' ease of had effected a saving of over £770 the past year ' general workmen, which he imr ii the wages paid to sufficient testimony t ....r.-Pankburst) thought was a o of changes ha • .is abilities as manager. A number the e-- ueen made in the plant at tee works daring petiod, which bad added to the economy and erticioncy of the undertalking. The new system of car- bonising had preyed a great success, and would save yearly, principally in coke, at least £6OO, besides being much more substantial and durable than the previous setting. Mr. Carr had prevented to a greet extent the waste of water which had been taking place, and the water department was in a much better position than it hail been for many years past. He would remind the Board that when Mr. Carr was engaged his salary Was to commence at £2OO. and it was understood that an increase would be given if the reseal: Otis work was satisfactory. This the committee believed to be so and was thoroughly unanimous in making that recommendation to the Boird.—Mr. WRIGHT seconded the motion —Mr. DUT- TON thought it was very early for a servant to ask for an increase in his salary. He had scarcely had time to develop his abilitits. He was perfectly satisded from his own ob- servation apd the reports of the Gas Committee that Mr. Carr had rendered efficient service, but that WAS what the Board expected and what they had paid for. He waisafraid that the man whose voice they had most of them heard very often at that Board was getting very silent, to wit the ratepayers. He (Mr. Dutton) did not agree with the increase recommended, and begged to move that that portion of the minutes referring thereto be expunged.—Mr. WEnsues wanted to know what Mr. Dut- ton meant by the ratepayer. (Hear, hear.)—The Cstein- mete : If there is no seconder to the amendment it falls to the ground.—Mr. Burrow There will be no seconder; they won't dolt in the interest of their gas bills.—Mr. HINDLY said they must all acknowledge that the salary paid to the engineer was a small one considering the important under- takings he had under "his management. He knew companies in the neighbourhood, with less extensive works, who paid their managers much higher salaries than Mr. Carr received, and if the Board wished to keep a good man they would have to pay him a sufficient salary. He referred to the many improvements which Mr. Carr had introduced, boat at the gas and water works, and said he had great pleasure in supporting the recommendation of the committee.—Mr. KERSHAW also paid a tribute to Mr. Carr's abilities. The labour was worthy of his hire. Mr. Carr was worthy of art increase, end he ter one should support the recommendation. —Mr. WRIOHT said Mr. Dutton had insinuated that certain people had made certain promises before they came to the Board. He did not know whether Mr. Dutton meant him- self or not, but he could tell that gentleman he had mule no promises nor brokem any. He went there as a member to do his duty, and when he could not do that he would re- sign his seat; or if the ratepayers said they had bad enough he could say the same. He referred to Mr. Carr's efficient management.—The mo'ion was then carried by 7 votes to 4. HIGHWAY COMMITTEE. -- -
Letters were read from Mr. S. B. Stringer and Mr. J

Bennett, complaining about sewage wate-r btcking into their cell Ars. The Surveyor was instructed to put a flip" on branch drains at the expense of complainants. Mrs. A, Lightfoot complained of a drain being stopped and ctusing her cellar to be flooded._ The Surveyor. reported

that Messrs Greenall and Company had given instructions to put in a " flap " at their expense. The Surveyor was instructed to do the work. Mr. Worthington (L. it N.-W. Railway Co.) wrote proposing to mike a road 24 feet wide instead of 18 feet, from Lugs- dale-road to the Tharsis Works, if the Board would adopt it as a public road.—The committee recommended that the proposal be not accepted.—Mr. Thomas Hughes applied for an increase of salary; and the commiteee recommended that an in itacrease of ss. per week he give.—Mr. MIDWOJD moved, and Mr. SADLER seconded the confirmation of the minutes, which were adopted.

div.p: THE SEWE- RAGE COMMI7TER.

This committee had applied to the owners of the Leigh Estate for an extension of twelve months time in which to complete the sewer. The resident engineer was instructed to proceed with the preparations of plans northwards from Simms' Cross and eastwards from Kent's lamp.—The CHAIRMAN moved, and Mr. MrDwoon seconded. the mfirmation of the minutes.—ln answer to a question, the CHAIRMAN said the committee had asked Mr. Copeland to prepare the plans because be bad been intimately connected with the sewerage scheme, but as a matter of course these plans would be submitted to the surveyor for approval 'be- fore being presented to the Bean—Mr. WEBSTER : I under- stood the resident engineer was under number one contract, and not number two. I think it is the duty of the Board to put the plans in Mr. Higginson's hands with the assistance of Mr. Copeland.—The CHAIRMAN said the idea of putting Mr. Copeland over the bead of Mr. Higgieson was never dreamt of for one moment. Mr. Copeland was still the assis- tant of Mr. Higginson as regarded the sewerage scheme.— The minutes were passed. THE SNIALL-PDX EPIDEMIC. WIIBN DOCTORS DIFFER, WHO SHALL DECIDE ?" The minutes of the Health Committee contained the medical oflicer'e report for October, which stated that the births numbered 98 and the deaths 50, being at the rate re- spectively of 47.04 and 24.00 per 1.000. Fourteen deaths occurred between children under one year, and 15 batween children between one and five years. ZyMotic diseases accounted for ten deaths. Mr. bicksen, the nuisance in- spector, recorded that four cases of scarlet fever had been reported, ar d also two deaths. One death bad occurred fiom typhoid fever in Vine-street. Since the let• October four new cases of small-pox bad been reported, making 26 cases during the present outbreak; four deaths were also reported. [he vaccination returns from the let July, 1882. to 31st ieptember, 1883, showed that tbe number of births regis- tered was 552. Of these .children 411. were successfully

vaccinated; 69 died unvaccinated, Se, were pestpeced by medical certificate, and 29 could not be found.—i'he Market Superintendent reported that the receipts for October amounted to £39 9s 2d, being an increase of 4314 145 4d as compared with the corresponding month last year. A memorial from Mrs. J. Smith and other stall-keepers had been presented to the committee complaining about people being allowed to " hand-sell" outside the 'market. The Clerk was inetructed Is reply that the committee c :aild not recom- mend any alteration from the present system. iii consequence of Die. McLennan aed MeD.mnell refusing to attend any cases at the Hospital Tents, the Medical Officer of Health was instructed to ettend ti any patients in the hospital not having a inedie4l attendant until the 13th instant, at the Board's expense. It was recommended that the question of medical attendauce at the II; spital Tents be determined by the Board. The commi'tee beeng en- gaged a matron at the rate of £3O per annum, and a general servant at £1 per month, recommended that these engage- ments be confirmed. It was recommereled that the mana- gers of schools be written to suggestieg the advisability of disinfecting the schools daily.—Dr. 0 KEEFFE moved the adoption of the minutes, which WAS seconded by Mr. HOT:GHTON.—Dr. OUCREFFE said there were at present eight cases in the hospital. Three were very acute cases, one being indeed very severe, and there were five convalescent patients. He was glad to say that all the patients were satis- fied with the arrangements Made for their confort. He had visited the hospital nearly every day in miler to aecertain whether the patients were treated in a campetent manner, and the reply in all cases had been saisfactory. They got everything they le quired, and the nereing was good. The tenta had stood the late storms admirably. Of course the committee when they found .the storms coming, _pro.

cored additional ropes in which they stayed the tents an au excellent manner. They had an old sailmaker with them, who was exceedingly useful, The I,toperature of the tents had been very satisfactory except on the previous night when the air was very frosty, and they had to provide ad- ditional stoves for heating purposes. Gas stoves were much cleaner and easier worked than when coal was used, and the committee adopting them thought th ,y would also be con- ferring a benefit upon the Gas Convoittee. The cooking stores performed their work with great perfection, and the nurse was highly pleased. There had been three fatal cases of small-pox since the outbreak, but none had occurred in the hospital, although he anticipated a fatal termination to one patient's illness. With regard to the distance of the hospital from any honses,there was not the slightest danger a whatever, because when Dr. Parsons was in Widnes he said that forty feet from any highway or dwelling-houses was quite enough for any infectious hospital, • and instead of the tent being 40ft. distact, it Was at least 600 yalds. So that there was not the slightest necessity for any person, property owner or other- wise, to anticipate danger. The Board were in a great fix for the want of a site—had they ban able to get one -sooner he believed there would not have becu any fatal cases—un- til Major Cross kindly offered the site which they had at present. Major Cross had shown himself a benefactor to the public, and he (Dr. O'Keeffe) had great pleasure in pro- posing that the thanks of the Bond and pf the inhabitants of the township be conveyed to him.—ln answer to Mr. Dutton, Dr, O'KERFFE said the temperature of the tents on one occasion was 58 degrees, and daring the gale it reached 65 degrees. He should be glad to /Alava any gentleman round the tents who liked to go. (Loud laaghter.)—Mr. Durroot : No, thank you, doctor. (Laughter.)—Mr. WRIGHT, who had paid a visit to the hospital tents on Friday, spoke favourably of the arrangements.—Dr. O'KEEFFH said he was sorry that there appeared in t'let agenda the names of two medical gentlemen who reflood point blank to attend any Case in the hospital, even though they had attended their patients themselves otits:de And recommended their removal to the hospital. It Was very painful for him to have to • say as, but as long as he occupied the position he did, there shoald be no complaint that he had not done his duty. He (Dr. O'Keeffe) offered to attend'the patients himself, but the committee thought it best to make temporary prorislan for attendance on the

_ patients at the hospital by reconnneriding that they beat- tended by the substitute of the Medical Officer of Health until that day, at the expense of the ratepayers. It was for the Board to make further arrangements for medical attend- ance on the patients. At the commencement he thought that they could carry out the rime practice they had at the accident hospital, viz., that each medical man would attend his own patieats. 'That was what they ought to have done, but he was sorry to say that the philanthropy of the pro- fession had given way under the dread of their being, as they said, called "smallpox doctors," and thus 'nil& their private practice. At the same time he was aware that one of the doctors mentioned in the agenda was at..tricirEg a smallpox case, and was still doing so, and irk he declined to go to the hospital. He (the doctorl, tad-no more fear of going there if there were 50 1157.0n5 congregated together than he had of going l" ' —Mr. DurrON *. inhale the pure breezes of Pex-hill, youdisinfectedyourself, doctor d ? -AFFR said he always took precautions. He had never .et conveyed infection from one person to another. He was not afraid of conveying it to his own family, and he was glad to say that he had given some hostages to fortune. He had as many children as any other medal man in Widnes, and he was not afraid of giving the disease to any of them. —The minutes were then passed.—Mr. HANDLEY in suitable terms then seconded the vote of thanks to Major Cress.— The motion was carried unanimously.—Mr. Dorrost moved, in eulogistic language, a vote of thanks to Dr. O'Keeffe for his arduous serv.ces in connection with the hospital, and far attending the patients when the other medical men refused.—Mr. Houarrroet had great pleasure in seconding the propoeitiou, referring to the doctor's offer to atteni the patients free of charge.—Mr. SADLER supported the motion. which was carried by acclainatlon..—The Board then con- si.lered what should be done as regarded attendance on the patients.—The CHAIRAIAN said when he heard of Dr. McDonnell's refusal he wrote asking what he proposed to do with regard to the works, for he was the medical attendant at Messrs. Gas- hell Deacon's Workmen's Club. Dr. McDorinell instructed him to say to the Board that he did not intend to convey to the committee in his interview with them that he would not undertake to attend any of his patients. What he meant to say was that he personally did not wish to at- tend small-pox cases either in the hospital er outside, and he had made arrangements for his patients to he attended by one of his duly qaalified medical assistants—Dr. Mc Cambridge; and that any of his patients who went to the hospital, whether private or club patients would be attended to by him or his deputy, Dr. McCarnbride.e, same as they did at the Accident Hospital. Dr. O'KEEFFE : Ile said positively that he nor any of his assistants would attend at the hospital. . (Hear, hear.) Mr. HOUGHTON : I think Dr. McDonnell was car. carried by the influence of Dr. McLennan.—The CHAIRMAN I think it probable That the doctors will each attend their own patients.—Mr. Durrox asked if the public understood the circumstances under which they entered the hospitu:, and the medical attendance and charges. The CHAIRMAN understood that - unless the patients were in receipt of parish relief they were expected to pay their own medical attendant the same as they did at the accident hospital. They were simply nursed at the hospital for the benefit of the public health and their own speedy recovery. The Board provided nur4- I ing and food, and the patients paid for nothing beyond I their medical attendant.—Mr. DUTTON: Has anyone ob- jected to go in the hospital.—Dr. OICERFFE replied in the negative. There was one patient outside the hospital, but she was entirely isolated, there being only herself and the nurse in the hones, and no danger was anticipated. The doctor asked that the committee should be empowered to obtain an ambulance. He could obtain a all, which would do, for £lo.—The Caaigstare moved that in the event of the medical men further refusing to attend the hospita:, the Health Committee be empowered to deal with the matter, and that the committee be also empowered to pur- chase an ainbulance.—Mr. Houarezore seconded the motion. which was carried. PROPOSED NEW PUBLIC OFFICES.

The Finance Committee recommended that designs far public offices, at a cost not exceeding £3,500, be advertised far.—ln moving the adoption of this recommendation, Mr. HANDLEY said the surveyor had drawn ground plans of the proposed new building, and the School Board had agreed to take part of the place at an annual rent of £7O It was very necessary that this matter should go on, as the Board's lease for the present premises expired in September next —Mr. SA.DLER seconded the motion.—ln answer to the Chairman, Mr. HANDLEY said it was not intended to erect a town hall, but offices suitable for the Local Board, the School Board, and probably the overseers—The CHMRMAN siid it was highly desirable that something of the kind should be done. but he wished to know if thee designs which the committee contemplated were to be such that were capable of being made use of by-and-bye for a more extensive building. for 801110 day they might have a town hall. It was desirable that whatever they did now should be built so that it could form part of a future town hall, and not he in:any way wasted.—Mr. HANDLEY said the site was at the corner of the street in which the present offices were, aad no doubt the proposed offices would form part of a to" hall.—Mr. WEBSTER thought it would be best to get designs of a town hall, and then erect a portion for public offices, and conclude the other portion at some future oeriod.—Mr. Drrrom asked what financial advantage was to be derived from the proposed town ball. They would epepd About £5O in advertising, and probably after that do nwleter. Better for them to stay where they were. He thooc',., e9nsideri.ng the unprofitable nature of the market, thez• letd better utilise that for their purposes. (Laughter.)—Mr. Itenseem agreed with Mr. Dutton. He thought the Bo rd bad spent enough upon public offices already, both at, the gas works andat the present place.—Mr. MIDWOOD: iioo.—Mr. Ran- seneelv thought that with slight alterations the present efhces made suitable. He pointed out that the could be Board had already obtained designs . fer a town ball, and he asked if these had been taken into considera- tion. In his opinion the Board ought to attend to the sewering of the town before entering into any expense for public offices or town hall. It was a disgrce to the Izeal Board, considering the period it had been in CXISI.CDCE te have the town a mere "slutch hole" with F c,o-cely a sewer in it.—Mr. HANDLEY argued that the proposal eicee would not cost the Board more than they were p tvirzat preq.e-. If they expended £3,500 on public offices iher- would 'her'- row the money at 4 per cent, which would Cost £l4O per year. Of that they should receive £7O f-em the School Board, and £BO the Board was at present paving made £350. So that it would not cost the ratepayers a Penny more tbau it did now.—Mr. Drerrow : There be the -principal Mr. HANDLEY :We shall have the building for it. Nr• Handley remarked upon the unsuitability of the present offices, and the minutes were then passed.. The Board then rose, after sitting over three hottre.

"FOOTBALL NOTES."

Sii,—A3 an old football player, and one who takes great interest in the game in this district, I desire to express an opinion about "Fairplay's " %marks. He says "Leather Hunter" made an incorrect statement, namely, that the Temperance team " charged " too much. Strange to say, " Fairplay " within the next dozen lines states, " I admit the game was wet and rough," thus proving Leather Hunt-zr's" information to he the truth, and involving him- self ("Fairplay") in a contradiction so plain as to make his statement appear more. than ridiculous. The simple fact is that both charging and rough play was indulged in, as all who saw the match must admit, if they are not led astray by partial judgment. " Fairplay " makes another 'unfortunate remark when he refers to the match at Stack- steads, for the idea has got abroad from it that the match played at Haydock was some sort of retaliation or revenge for the roughness received away. .Being one who rejoices at the spread of temperance in all its various forms,' regret that " Fairplay " rushed into print with such rash and ran- dom statements, which do more hurt than he is aware of, for it is well known the Temperance team show more vigour sometimes than is necessary. I trust a word to the wise will be sufficient. If a match be lost through playing a more friendly game the team will be able to say that they were defeated but not disgraced, which is far more honour- able than winning by rough or unfair play. Though not a member of, or much known by, either the Earlestown, Hay. dock, or Golborne clubs, I would like to write a litre shout the disturbance on the ground of the latter at Golborne. I would say all honour io the Earlestown team for not retali- ating with foul play. Believing honourable and scientific play will always bring the reward of satisfaction and often success, and hoping all three clubs will find their way into the third round of the Lancashire cup competition, I remain yours, &c., TEMPERANCE-

HIGHWAY ASSAULT AND _ROBBERY

_ AT WARRINGTON. . A WIDNES MAN "ON THE SPREE." At the Warrington Borough Court, on Tuesday, Daniel Houneesey, Thomas Garritty, and Jane nviin no orioue characters, were in custody on the charge of com-nittine a highway assault on Michael Garritty, furnaceman, of 25, Pear-street, Widnes, and stealisg 13s d of his money.—lt appeared from the statement of the Chief-Constable and the evidence of witnesses that on the previous day prosecutor came to Warrington "on the spree," and took lodgings at No. 5, Hill-street, where he met the three prisoners. The two G.J„Lri,tys were not related in any way. Prosecutor had about ns 9d or las in silver and copper in his right-hand trOnsers pocket, and he took from this is, which he gave to the female prisoner to fetch him half a pound of beef steak. She did so, and brought him the change. After his meal prosecutor expressed a desire to see the attractions of War- rington, an asked to be shoes to a place of amusement. The three prisoners accordingly went out with him and ad- journed to the Bear's Paw publichouse, where prosecutor paid for two pints of ale and two glasses of rum. Shoraly afterwards they proceeded further, and next visited the Mill Stone, Sankey-street, where they each had two pennyworth of rum, for which prosecutor paid. They stayed-here about minutes when the landlord, thinking his customers were getting a bit too lively, "bundled out the whole four," to use the Chief-Constable's words. They then walked along the street, the male prisenera being on each Bide of him an.i Paying him every attention, the woman being in the rear. When in Golborne-street the female pritoner came up and placed her hand in his trousers pocket, and extracted his money, some of which rolled on the ground. One of the men then knocked him down and both (iarritty and Hennessey kicked him violently. Prosecutor got up, when the three prisoner.s ran away.. He followed them into Bold-street, where a rather desperate struggle en- sued between him and the prisoner Garrittv. All thp prisoners subsequently turned up Itylands-etre;t, and prose- cutor in again following them met P.C. MeLarcn, to whom he gave information of what bad taken place They then with Serge Ant Bowen went in search of the pri,,,mera, when _ in they found Hennessey and Flynn at a mate; Market Gate, and they took them to the house at 5, Hill-street, where they discovered Garrity. wh,n about to be taken into custody all the three prisoners were very rough. Bowen, on alernpting to :rarch Hennessey was met with much resistance, Henuessey Hoe- ing him in the stomach and closing with the police-officer. Something was heard to jingle in the lining of Hennesiey's trousers, and 3s. in silver and bronze subsequently fell out. lienneseey refused to walk when outside the house and he bad to he carried to the lock-up.—ln reply to the magis- trate., Hennessey sad" I had nothing to (In with it. That nseney (meaning the 35.) is mitte."—Gar/itty pleaded not guilty. and Flynn said he admitted haying hod a drink with prosecutor but dd not steal his rooney.—Prisoners were committed for trial at tic Liverpool assizes,

CLIAPTER XL.—TEtz Ricer. During the last few weeks the Fe'nian agitation, which had been supposed to have ceas‘d, had been renewed with increased fury. Rumours of all kinds were flying .about as to the nature and extent of the movement. By one set of reporters they were merely held to be local and trifling., and that only made so much noise because the Fenians took care to give them publicity, with added circumstances of exaggeration that quite falsified their true character, as simply agrariaa dis- turbances. But others took a darker view, and thought the Fenian policy very different, and much more subtle and dangerous. They considered the Fenians really originated the seeming riots; desiring to cover a great part of Ireland with similar centres of actiya disaffection, under the disguise of local affairs; so that, without exciting the suspicions of the Government, they might go on unmolested as insurrection- ists till they were ripe for action, and then strike. News reached the.camp the day before the one in question that a riot of this dubious character had broken out at a place a few miles distant, and a detachment of troops were ordered off under the commatad of Captain Etheridge, Stephen being in the ranks. The troops started early in the evening, marched the whole night, which was dark, but pleasant, and only as thy began came in sight of the place where the riot was said to have broken oat. If so, they all thought it must be over, and the rioters abed, for they saw not a living person, heard not a sound, till on turning a corner they found themselves before a vast crowd of men, mingling with whom were some women. They had evidently waited the approach of the soldiers in silence, and then at the monient of the appearance of the troops hurled a felrful volley of stones upon them. Several of the men were knocked down, and the remainder were about to fire, but Captain Etheredge, in advance with lifted hands, forbad, and bade them advance slowly withthe bayonet. " Disperse them, but do no more if you can possibly help. f - _ _

AL . Again came t'ne storm of heavy stones, and the blood o the soldiers was at fever heat, as they levelled bayonets, and advanced. But the crowd, which greatly out-numbered them, now closed with them, raising wild, unearthly cries. And then for some minutes a hand-to-hand fight took place. The rioters using all sorts of weapons—clubs, old swords, guns, newly-made pikes, and the women, shrieking and cursing like demons, mingled in the bloody struggle with imple- ments drawn from the domestic hearth. Stephen got a sharp blow on the cheek, which for a moment confused him, and seemed to fill his eyes with gore. • But the sight of both his immediate superiors, the Cor- poral and the Sergeant, lying senseless on the ground, nerved him to fresh exertions. • Assuming command without waiting for a word or a second I in saying why he did so, he rallied the men about him, and headed them in an attack upon a body of rioters that were near, and a little apart from the chief body who were engaged with the Captain. He struck so effectually that they dispersed on all sides— those at least who were able to get away. Then seeing the position of the Captain he called the notice of the men, who were snatching a moment to breathe more freely, and to dress their wounds, to his danger; and with a few excited and exciting sentences brought them into order and led them with fresh ardour and a loud hurrah against the mab of rioters. These, knowing not the number of the new body, began to fall back fighting at each step; till see- ing their chanoe of escape through the fatigue of the sol- diery, and the injuries many had received, they followed the example of their companions, and dispersed rapidly by so many ways, seeking cover as they went, that pursuit was practically impossible; taking with them their killed and wounded. The object of the expedition had been achieved, but at heavy cost, which they were not as yet able to estimate. No one was actually dead, and that was all that could be thought of as comforting. And now there remained for the troops, including the wounded, some in extreme danger, no resource but to march back to the camp. That march home was by common con- sent always afterwards spoken of as the worst part of the whole affair. Such had been the efforts, and such was the state of the men, who now came back to the camp.; but with no music to cheer the men, their pace that of a funeral march, their appearance a striking and fearful contrast to the troops that had gone out but a little time before. And as that body may be said to have typified in a super- ficial sense the glory of war, so did these troops suggest all the misery and ruin and degradation that too often lies be- yond or beneath the "glory." Almost to a man they were covered with mud, and Stains of gore. As to the wounded the impromptu manner in which alone their hurts could be attended to in their march home, caused heads to be tied 141 p with parti-coloured hand- kerchiefs, that made the pale faces and dried up gore all the more hideous and ghastly. Limbs, too, were bandaged with whatever ligature came first to hand. Such was the spectacle which met the eyes of a deeply- interested observer. Gentleman Jack, whose mental comment was worthy of him— "Catch me in that sort of fun if you can !" But he, like the otter men off duty, helped to take the weapons from those of the exhausted soldiery, who still had managed to struggle alorg with them; and to relieve those who were carrying not only their own arms, but those of comrades to helpless to bear anything but them- selves. Then, too, they had to succour others who could not have marched at all without the aid of comrades only a little less exhausted ; and lastly, to set free the litter bearers, for two soldiers, severely wounded, were borne along on a framework made by muskets and great coats. These first steps in the way of relief to all concerned, be- rg accomplished, and the whole of the returning men ba- ng arranged, wi:h a slight attempt at formation the Captain

addressed them. " Men," said be, and then stopped for a moment, as if to seek fresh strength before he could go on. It was no wonder. He bad endured a more than common share of the efforts and suff-aring of the last few hour!, ending in that march home, under a sun of such uncommon beat as us man among them remembered before in October, and such as only his spirit and sense of responsibility could have carried. him through. "Men," he began for the second Ulna, "the courage and devotion you have shown in quelling this formidable riot, which at times threatened, I fear, to become an insurrec- tion, demand my warm acknowledgments." He paused, looked round, as in search of someone, then cried, "Stephen Shand ! " " Here,' Captain," was the redly ; and Stephen stepped out of the ranks, and moved to the front in obedience to the Captain's call and gesture. Eagerly Gentleman Jack bent forward to see if it was his old 4 friend;' but so changed was the man he saw, by his military aspect on the one hand, and the injuries he bad just received on the other, that even his old acquaintance scarcely recognised Lam. The loss of his long hair aad moustache, the darkening of his features hy exposure to the sun of the last few, weeks the dreaa at once so showy, so dirty, and so disorderly, , the spots on his face, and the exhaustion, that made it a severe trial to stand there upright and steady with the aid of his musket as a staff, all these were ob- stacles to recognition. "Is that your swell ?" whispered Gentleman Jack to Tommy Atkins, whose ordinarily sullen features became more characteristic as he guessed what was impending, and was too envious and malignant to condescend to reply. But when Gentleman Jack nadged him' and rep2stel the question, he did condescend to nod an affirination. "Stephen Shand," said the Captain, "Your behaviour must not pass without official recognition. At a critical I moment you took the place of your immediate superiors, aided in re-organising many of your comrades under a deadly and exasperating shower of stones from overwhelm- ing numbers, and in dispersing them. You then came to your captain's aid, acd sub,eqecattly joined in a gene •al charge that swept all before us. Your conduct on the march home has been no less conspicuous. Wounded and worn out like all the rest, you seem to have thought only of your comrades. Your merits will not be overlooked. Men, you are now dismissed." And then he waited their departure tat hold a little private , conversation with Stephen.

The bait took speedily; the coast was clear. And then Gentleman Jack, advancing with an air that seemed to say he knew how glad Stephen would be of the opportunity, said to him, with a laugh— " We are alone at last." "IL seems you won't let me be alone," retorted • Stephen. • " What an unkind remark to one who has paid flying visits to some half-at-dozen regiments in search of you, and found you at last—a private soldier !" "I advised you in London to turn over a new leaf, and I chose to follow my own prescription." "And how do you like it ?" queried Gentleman Jack. "That deiruds upon how it will answer its purpose. And you, Jack ?" "I've only as yet got a few glimpses into the vocation ; and I mean in double-quick time to get out of it. Officers and men are all rank Philistines." "Then hadn't you bitter stay?" asked Stephen, "and be the Samsew to smite them."

So Stephen was awakened, and for a brief time found amusement in listening to the gossip, end in comparing mentally the actual truth, according to his own experience, with the fabulous reports caught up and improved upon bx the bystanders. Among the things said were some that deeply interested

him, and threw a new colour on the late Etr144;12. It appeared from them that the peasantry were under the belief that the military were only the advance guard of the Sheriff, with a lot of officers and bailiffs corning to evict them wholesale from their farms. Facts, too, were mentioned showing how severe had been their sufferings during the last few years, durinc, which the arrears had accumulated, for which the landlord's agents had threatened to turn them all out if the recta were not paid by a certain day. This expired three days bdure the march of the soldiery. LAstly, their mistake was attributed to the acts of the Venians, who wanted to create everywhere bad blood be- .. .

" What, with the same glorious weapon—the jawbone of an as 3 ?" said Gentleman Jack. And Stephen could not resist a hearty laugh. Presently, however, he took occasion to say " Now, Jack, I can't at present help you, and you can do nothing for me, except to keep aloof from me, and from my affairs in all respects." "I am not a leech, wanting to stick," wis the answer. To which Stephen responded by a significant, Hem !" "And if I am, ain't leeches good thin2ts "Occasionally, Jack; occasionally. het me tell you I have lately been studying a. character." I "Nut mine, should hope. I hate such ways." "Judge for yourself from its traits. A gentleman born, yet with so little pride as to live upon people poorer than himself." "That's savage !" "Gifted with talent, yet content to use his talent only to adorn, if such a thing is poasible, one of the most con- temptible of lives." "That's downright wicked," remonstrated Gentleman Jack, with imperturbable good humour. "But stop! I've an idea. I'm going to sketch your face." And he pre- tended to be drawing on the back of a letter. "Now mind, please; the month quite stmt.". Stephen did manage to resist a laugh, and continue his critical analysis— " Strong, healthy, having taste and talent fit for anything and everything, yet refusing to pay the little price that all these things demand for ensuring a manly and useful life !"

tween their countrymen and the English. Stephen, however, thought that remained to be proved. Considerateness, in view of Stephen's E tire, on the part of Tommy Atkins, now drew his actention away. Tummy had a can of beer in his hand. This he offered to Stephen, saying, "I've fetched this for you from the canteen." "I'm greatly obliged," said Stephen warmly, and be drank with zest, and felt at once greatly refreshed. " That's worth a Jew's eye, as they say. But the precise value of that article I never could learn." " Whatdo you say to another tussle with me now ?" asked Tommy. " 'rnat's a likely game !" roared out a soldier close by. "And why not" demanded Tommy. "He's tired. So am I. Been in a heavy fatigue job. What do you say, Shand ?''

"Well, I should have preferred your asking me to-mor- row. But if you can wait till I have rested, got something to eat, and had a good wash—" "And done half a hundred things beside, I suppose ! I guessed how it would be. You won by a fluke the other day, and you don't mean to lose by a fair tussle!" " Help me up," said Stephen coolly; and with Tommy Atkins' help he got up awl faced his challenger. "Fair pity, bays !" called out ona of the crowd of redcoats that speedily gathered in a ring about the pair. " Ay, ay! we'll see to that," cried the others. Tommy Atkins was a bigger man altogether than Stephen, and therefore the more dangerous if he should manage what was said to be an old trick of his—namely, that if he suc- ceeded in throwing his man, to fall upon him also, as if accidentally, and so settle him. He was also fairly skilful, and well acquainted with all technical feints and dodges, the advances and retreats, which may be brought into play, to catch the antagonist at an unguarded moment, then suddenly close with, and throw him before he has time to resist. But in this as in so many other physical exercises, the brain—the head—is of more consequence than the muscle, the brute power, and the deceptive art. So was it now. Stephen was an accomplished oarsman, fencer, runner, and leaper. Athletic exercises had been the media through which in his London life he passed off and drove away whatever was most dangerous in his enforced idleness, and latent discontent. He found, too, in them means to satisfy his ambition, his love of power, and his self-solacing belief that he was still good for something. Tommy Atkins, who had not the sense to see or suspect the vital difference between himself and the "Swell," even after his first defeat, was now to be furnished with means for—and to be made to see the necessity of—at ence begin- ning with the study of those differences if he meant to ven- ture a third trial. Stephen reflected that if in his present state he gave his antagonist time to prolong the struggle, he would in all pro- bability be himself beaten by the strength, weight, and en- durance natural to the other; and which had in no notice- able degree been lessened by his "fatigue" labour. He de- termined, therefore, to run any risk but that. The struggle began. Wary on both aides for a time, though Tommy Atkins kept presslng on, confident if he could once get a firm grip the business would soon be brought to an end. The business was settled even sooner than Tommy Atkins hoped and believed. Getting tired of Stephen's Parthian mode of combat, he made a bold faint which Stephen had carefully invited. It failed, and instantly he was himielf caught by a feint on Stephen's part. A moment later he was in the air, his feet just lifted from the ground, and then, instead of instantly recovering, as he thought, terra firma, he found he had got too much terra firma, for he was lying at full length upon it. And then to sap the unpleasantness of Tommy Atkins' position came the shouts of the soldiery, announcing for the second time the triumph of the Swell.

CHAPTER XLlT..—Ovrn HUNDRED POUNDS REWARD. Stephen generously offered his hand to Tommy Atkins to help him to his feet; but the beaten man looked as if he could spit upon it, if he dared, turned away, rose by the aid of his own hands to his knees, and then gained an erect posture. Finding himself a good deal shaken, he took the , offered arms of two of the soldiers, and went away followed by most of those present. And then Stephen once more lay down and disposed him- self for sleep; feeling he could neither eat nor drink or do anything else whatever for his comfort or decency of ap- pearance till he had obtained refreshment from that "sore labour's bath," of which Macbeth speaks. But he 1143 again interrupted. Gentleman Jack, seeing few of the soldiers about, and none very near, came and lay down close by Stephen, and stared him full in the face. Stephen stared in return at this seemingly impaient stranger recruit, put him out of countenance .by his stern imperturbability, lighted his pipe, and took ao more notice than if he were quite atone. "Comrade!" at last says Gentleman Jack. "Well ? " replied Stephen in a tone somewhat differing from his natural one. Gentleman Jack's answer was to thrust before his eyes a newspaper, and point with his finger at a particular part. "Want me to read it for you?" said Stephen, as if sup- posing the recruit could not read it for himself. "If you wouldn't mind," said Gentleman Jack. The passage pointed at was an advertisement, beaded with the words in full capitals— "ONE HUNDRED POUNDS REWARD." Stephen's rapid glance soon took in the nature of the ad- vertisement; but he showed no sign of being at all inter- „ested, and began to read aloud in a hard, artificially-sound- ing voice as follows : "ONE HUNDRED POUNDS RRWARD.--Stephen C. F. is most earnestly requested to come to or communicate with hie aged, possibly dying mother, who has to make known a matter of the utmost interest and importance to him per- sonally."

" The foregoing having appeared fruitlessly for several weeks, the reward mow prefixed will be paid to anyone, who knowing or guessing the name of the gentleman referred to, and his present abode, can and will furnish the information required, to Messrs. Brandon and Cobb, solicitors, Lincoln's Inn. It is supposed he has enlL•ted." "Well ?" queried Gentleman Jack, at the close of the reading. " Well ?" responded Stephen, and again he looked at Gentleman Jack so steadily, and apparently so unconscious of any cause why he should not, that the latter's confidence was shaken ; and he went away, for- getting the newspaper, which Stephen was glad to retain, if only for a second perusal. "A terrible message," he thought to himself, "for one who has no longer the power to respond. lam chimed here."
His face saddened as he thought of his mother's state, her anxiety for his presence, and the possible hope that she meant to hold out, of something pleasing to him regarding Miss Vandeleur.

But would his mother know of what had passed just be- fore his departure? Or would she only partially know, and therefore fancy a reconciliation was still possible if he would but come? Such thoughts revived vividly his past relations with Miss Vandeleur, and his own sense of dissatisfaction with the sevreity of his judgtnent, and the more than severity of the punishment he had in- flicted.

He sighed, but again went back to his former saying— "l am chained here, and must abide whatever bdall in consequence." Seeing Gentleman Jack was coming i),AC'4, whom he had instantly recognised, while determining not to be recognised in his turn, if be could help it, he hurriedly tore off a piece of the newspaper, from that tore the adver- tisement which be slipped into a pocket; and used the rest of the piece to clear away the mud from his clothes and boots.

"1 forgot mv paper," said Gentleman Jack, as he again came cl.)se to Stephen. "Paper ! What paper ?" ejaculated the latter dreamily as if his thoughts were far away. "My newspaper !" said Gentleman Jack, c irefully i;;Elor- ing the wreck of it which he saw on the ground. " Newspaper ? Oh yes. There it is !" and Stephen pointed to the mutilated sheet. Gentleman Jack took it up, and at once cried—. " Why, it's torn out !" "What's torn out ?"
"The advertisement I got you to read for me." There w:ts an exatruition of regret fro.a Stephen, who presently added—

He rose in sullen silence. And Stephen rose too, to add a few words that might mitigate the pain without impairing the force of what he had seen it vitally necessary to say. _ _

"And now, Jack, since you see at last the true state of the case between us, I have only further to tell you that if you do obey my injunction, and keep absoluasitence about me, my family, and my residence here, it will, in all prob- ability be only necessary for a few months, or perhaps a year or so at the outside. And then you shall be the first to in- form my mother, and get the reward." "Ay, but suppose they find out where you are without my help ?" said Gentleman Jack, with a wonderfully suj- den recovery of. his spirits.
"Then it-shall be Illy task to tell the Countess; you might have earned it, but lost the chance to please me.". "And will it please you if I do now determinedly lose it ?" "Yes."

"Then I'm your man. I will do it, and be happy, because it pleases you." This was a great relief to Stephen. He saw what a dis- reputable companion Gentleman Jack must be for a man like himself, in such a place, aiming high, and unable to explain the circumstances in which the acquaintance originated. But what he had been most anxious about was the assured certainty in Ms own mind that Gentleman Jack would not lose an hour in bringing down hil friends upon him, for the sake of bringing down a shower of gold upon himself.
Well, he had settled both questions, he thought, satis- ,letorily; and would again be able to breathe and work in freedotn.

A man under "Pack Drill" carries forty rounds of ammunition, his thick great coat, his kit, i.e., knapsack, with shirt, socks, comb, black- ing brushes, pipeclay brush, button cleaner, knife, fork, and spoon, his tin panikin used for food, and for all sorts of other puposss, towel, razor, forage cap, heavy boots; and then to add to the burden of the body for the chance of lightening the spirit—the Bible, understood to be the Queen's present.

Yet that was the burden under which Stephen saw this nnfortunate soldier in a•warm day going through all the prolonged business of the drill, in attitudes that made the effect of the burden fearfully severe. _ As he approached nearer he saw it was Gentleman Jack.

The charge against the proprietor and publisher of Judy of libelling the "Central News" was proceeded with at the London Mansion House on Monday. The Lord Mayor thought the libel complained of was of a trivial nature, and he suggested th.At he should be allowed to deal summarily with the case. The defendants, however, expressed their preference for going before a jury, and they were committed. for trial.

SERIOUS GAS EXPLOSION AT SHEFFIRLD.—A gas explo- sion, by which three children were seriously injured, oc- curred in Sheffield on Sunday night soon after six o'clock, at the house of Jeremiah Siincutt, hosier, Attercliffe. A loud report as if dynamite had exploded was heard, and on the neighbours rushing to the house they found that the partition wall between the dwelling room and the passage had been blown down. Further search revealed the uncon- scious (elms of two of the cbildren,Annie Elizabeth and Her- bert Henry, who were severely burnt on the face, bands, and logs. The other child was not so badly burnt, but all thre2 are unsler medical treatment. It was ascertained that the gas main ne a the house had burst, and it is believed it ignited at the kitchen fire.
