DISTRICT NEWS. BURTON WOOD. CAUTION TO PARENTS —At the Newton Petty S2ssionp, On Saturday, John Turton and William Robinson, both of Burtonwoo-d, were fined ss. each for neglectiw,; to send their children to school, as required by the Elementary Education Act.—Joseph Stock was also summoned for a similar offence, bat the Bench dismissed the summons on the de- fendants wife promising to see that the child attended school.

CAD'S FIEAD. Two excellent discoerses on behalf of foreign missions were preached in the Wesleyan Chapel, Cadisbead, on Sun- day. The following Tuesday a public meeting was held. The attendance was good, considering the inclemency of the weather. The chair was occupied by Mr. Horrocks, of War- rington, whose opening address was of a stirring character. A brief report of mission work was read by the Rev. R. Dillon. This was followed by a thoughtful and a suggestive address from Mr. Hopewell. The deputation, the Rev. J. Ham- mond, of Manchester, late missionary in the West Indies, addressed the meeting in a speech remarkable for its force and excellence, replete with missionary facts ef a very gratifying character. This brought to a close a missionary meetibg which will be long remembered by the friends. The collections upon the whole were good. _ CRONTON.

MISSIONARY MEETING—The annual meeting of the Cronton Branch of the Wesleyan Missionary Society was held on Thursday night week, in the chapel, Cronton. Mr. Thomas Robinson was in the chair, but on account of the unpropitious weather there was only a small attendance. The amount contributed by the eronton Branch was st tted b' the Secretary to be .£l7 85 lid, showing an incraase on the previous year. Missionary addresses were delivered by the Rev. J. Hothersall, and Messrs. Peter Glovtr and Hew- son.

FRODSIIAM. LUTHER COMMEMORATION.—A special thanksgiving ser- vice in commemoration of the 400th anniversary of the birth of 'Luther was held in the Trinity Chapel, Frodsham, on Thursday evening. A highly interesting and eloquent address was given by the Rev. G. Lupton Allen, resident minister, on the life of Martin Luther, and the choir rendered a selection of hymns and music of the Reformation period in a tasteful manner.

HEATLEY. ALL ABOUT Doos.—John Bradbury, Broom Edge, was summoned to the Lymm Petty Sessions, yesterday, for be- ing drunk on licensed premises and refusing to quit.— Sergeant Harrington and P.C. Antrobus were in Heattey on the 7th inst., when they were called to the Railway Hotel, kept by Mr. Traverse. They there found the defendant resisting a man named Simpson, who was endeavouring to eject him. The officers requested him ta leave and he refused, and they had to eject him three times by physical force.—The defendant was drunk, and from his statement to the magistrates it seeme4 that a quarrel had arisen between him and a man named Wrigley abut their dogs, the defen- dant saying that his dog was better than Wrigley's, and Wrigley saying that his dog was better than the defendant's. Wrigley said that his dog would take the hat off man's head, and Bradbury bet him a half-crown that it could not. The dog was fetched, and a quarrel arose about the way in which it took the hat off.—The defendant was fined 40s and costies ed. KINGSLEY. FlRE.—About twelve o'clock, on Thursday night 'week, it was discovered that a fire had broken out at the lockup shop of Mr. S. Brown, Kingsley. Instantly an alarm was raised, and a number of people endeavoured to extinguish the fire and save the building and valuable stock from des- truction. Meantime a mounted messenger was sent to Run- corn for the fire brigade, and the bell at the market was rung rung shortly before two o'clock. The brigade turned out very promptly, the men being under the charge of Superin- tendent Wright. The engine left Runcorn shortly after two o'clock, arriving at the scene of the conflagration at 3-20. At that hour the building was completely gutted, only the walls remaining standing, so that the services of the brigade were not required. The damage to the building and stock is very considerable.

LTA' ff. LYAEW UNITED BANDS OF HOPE.—Next Monday week, the first of a series of demonstrations under the auspices of the Lymm United Bands of Hope, will be given in the Mission Hall; particulars of which will be found among the an- nouncements.

LY3OI LIBERAL ASSOCIATION: PUBLIC LECTURE.-110 lecture on " The representation of the people," by W. Clarke, Esq., M.A., to be given in the Plough Hotel Assembly- room. Lymm, on Monday evening next, will no doubt prove an instructive one, and we hope there will be a good atten- dance of the Liberals of the district. Mr. E. Brewtnall will preside. Further particulars will belound in our advertis- ing columns. ENTBRTAINMENT.—An entertainment, under the auspices of the Lymm Branch of the Church of England Temperance Society, was held in the c laurels School, Lymm, on Tuesday. The Rev. G. W. Guest presided, and there was a large attendance. A capital programme was gone through, in :Lich the following ladiea and gentlemen took part :—Mr. Talbot, of Manchester, who delivered an address; Mrs. Addenbrooke, Mrs. Hall, Miss Pearson, Mr. G. Hall, Mr. J. E. Blakemore, Mr. W. Joyn- son, Mr. J. E. Smith, and the Rev. G. W. Guest. Ftais AT BOLLINGTON.—A destructive fire to3k place on Saturday, on the farm of Martha Sutton, Bollington, two stacks being burnt to the ground, and damage done to the amount of £l4O. A grandson of Mrs. Sutton's had been playing with matches near the stacks, which were by this means set on fire. In the m irvellously short time of 35 minutes from the moment the fire broke out, the Altrincham fire brigade, under Sup. Leighton, was on the scene of he conflagration. Despite their efforts, however, the fire was not extinguished until damage was done to the amount stated.

A Max KILLED NEAR LYDIXt.—An inquest was held at Warrington, on Tuesday, concerning the death of John Nixon, 32 years of age, assistant linesman in the service of the Cheshire Lines Committee. On Saturday evening last, decrased was walking on the Loudon aad North-Western Railway near Lynun, where he lived, and was knocked down by a train. At a quarter-past six he was found with his legs and feet terribly injured. He was taken to the Warring- ton Infirmary, where he died a few days ago.--The Coroner said deceased was a • trespasser on the line, as he was not connected with that company. Sometimes railway servants , went " mooning" along the line, never thinking about the ' trains, and a man who would walk in such a dangerous place must have his wits about him.—A verdict of " Acci- I den,al death" was returned.

ILLEGALLY TARING WATER AT LYMlL—Yesterday, at Lymm Petty Sessions, a respectably-dressed young woman named Gaynor Locker, of Newfield, Lymm, was summoned for taking water belonging to the Lymm Waterworks Com- pany, she not having agreed to be supplied with the same. —Mr. Cameron, who is secretary to the company, said there was a pipe fixed outside a building at a row of cottages at Newfield, about 50 or 80 yards from where the defendant lived. The defendant had got no authority to take the water from the pipe' she not being supplied with water from the company. The company had had considerable trouble with people taking water from this particular pipe when they had no right to do r.o.—P.C. Chatterton said that on the 13th inst. he met the defendant going to the pipe with a bucket, and he asked her if she knew she had no right to the water, and she replied that she did. She, however, went on to the tap and filled her bucket, which she took home.—The defendant said that the pump from which she was supplied had been out of order for some time, and that was the reason she had used the water.—Mr. Cameron said the company did not wish to inflict a heavy fine, bat they desired the case to act as a warning to others.—The case was dismissed on the defendant paying the costs. OVER.

SERVICH OF SONG.—The Wesle-vans gave a service of song in Over Board Schools on Saturday night, entitled "Uncle Tom," illustarted by Mr. Leigh, of Marston, eifith his magic lantern, who, at the close, elicited much enjoy- ment by his funny exhibition. The Rev. B. Murphy gave the reading in explanation, and the choir did the singing in as effective way. It was their "benefit night," but rain rather damaged it.

div.head: PALRTINGTON.
div.p: PALRTINGTON.

UNJUST WEIGHTS.—WiIIiam Pollard, Partington, was summoned to the Lymm Petty Sessions, yesterday, for hav- ing in his possession two weights, both of which were unjust and one unstamped.—Superintendent Leighton, in company with a constable, visited the defendant's shop on the 29th ult., and there found a lib and a ill) weight, both of which were light, and the ilb weight was unstamped.— The defendant: I was not aware they would come upon me so soon; I have only just got them. I didn't 5411 any- thing but sweets, and I thought the weights were all right.—The Bench ordered him to pay the costs, 7s ad in each case.,

div.head: WESTON POINT.
div.p: WESTON POINT.

Nhw Doc.—. The excavations for anew dock at Weston Point have been commenced. The dock, of which the present "church gut "will form a part. will be between the old basin and Delatnere dock, and will be 225 feet in length and 130 feet wide. Accommodation for a large number of vessels will be provided, while every facility for loading and discharging will be afforded. There will be ample wharfage, and the work when completed will give an impetus to the Staffordshire trade, which has been on the increase for some time, WINSFORD.

Mr. Knowles continues to improve but very slowly. LUTHER CELEBRATION.—At the Wesleyan Chapel, on Monday night, the Rev. E. Murphy delivered a lecture on " Martin Luther and the Protestant Reformation," and there was a good attendanca. OPENING OF A NEW LIBERAL CLUB AT WINSFOIID.— A new Liberal club was opened at Winsford on Friday after- noon, under very auspicious circumstances. A large public meeting was held in the Town Hall in the evening, undPr the presidency of Mr. Wilbraham, of Delamere House. Ad- dresses were delivered by Mr. James Tomkinson, Willington Hall, and Mr. David Duncan, Liberal candidate for 'Nes Cheshire. Resolutions were passed. thanking the Govern- ment forthe Agricultural Holdings Act and other measures, and urging them to extend the franchise. Th3ference was made by Mr. Tomkinson ti the growth of Liberalism in the division, and the prospects of both candidates were cl,clibed as most sati,3fzictory and encouraging. ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS. 1.31t0-'rm. Munnrm IN CHEt•utaF..—On Satur(lav night an old man, named Roggan, was drinking in a beerhousa in Wallasey, when he got into an altercation with a ycurhz man named Clough. Clough left, but appears to hav, waited for Roggan and to have assailed him, breaking his

leg in three place, innict7n!: Other irj,7o-1", and l'eaving him smSeless in a ditc:J. Itoggan was cli..3uvered the nest morning and taken to th..) Wallasey Hospital, where hiS leg was amputated. He died oo Mondsy, having pre- viously recovered comciousness and given the name of his assailant.

LONG SERVICE AND GOOD COZ, DUCT IN LLNCASIIIILE AND CHrSHIIiB REGIMEN'S.—On the rec4mnlend,:tion of the Field Marshal Commanding in Chief, the to'hier-men- tioned non-cormoissioned officers ene. men of the Livcashire and Cheshire regiments have been awarded silver medalS, with gratuities, "for long service and good cJoduct," the list being made up to the Ist inst.:—,...ancashire Artillery Volunteers (staff): Sgt. J.Wylie. Royal Lancaster Regiment: Private.T. Green. Cheshire Regiment: Privates J. AsburY and J. C.-ward. Est lancashire : Sergeant R. Hunt and Private D. Nichols. North Lancashire Regiment : Corporal J. Geary. Manchester Regiment: Quartermaster Sergeant J. Cahill, Arinourer Sergeant R. Uarpen:er, and Private H. Hoggtr. York and LaLcaster Regiment: Private T. Ryan.

CHESHIRE AGRICULTI7RAL SOCIETY.—A meeting of the committee of this society was held at Crewe on Thursday, Mr. H. J. Tollemaclie, M.P., presiding. The annual report was submitted for approval. It expressed regret that 3 violent outbreak of foot and mouth disease a few weeks be' fore holding the late show entirely prohibited the exhibition of horned stock, sheep, and pigs. However, notwithstand- ing this great drawbick. the financial results had not suf- fered, a' balance of £403 14s 5d being carried to next year'S account. The entries at the last show exceeded those of an)" year of the society's existence. The teport was agreed to. As to the place of meeting for next year, the secretary said that that could not be decidel until it was known whether the Royal would go to Chester. Some said that the Man- chester and Liverpool were going to Stockport. In that case it would not be desirable for the Cheslif e Society to go to Macclesfield. Several protests were then considered. Mr. Bowers, of Nantwich, was disqualified from takinw second prize in the jtimoing competition because the rider of his horse did not weigh. The prize therefore goes to Mr. Dods - worth.

div.head: POLITICAL.
div.p: POLITICAL.

Mr. Gladstone, replying to a resolution from the Council of Chambers of Agriculture regarding foot-and-inouth disease. suggests that the matter should be referred to the Lord President of the Council, who will, be feels sure. see to the fulfilment of the engaaeinents on this sub- ject, into which the Government entered in Parliament last session.

On Thursday night, a crowded Liberal meeting was held at Reading, at which an address was presented to Mr. Shaw-Lefevre to commemorate his twentieth year of ser- vice as member for the borough. He spoke of the impor- tance of improving the dwellings of the poor, but thought it could be best done by private entcrpiise, controlled and assisted by the State. Referring to Ireland, he said the Laud Act was not a concession to agitation, but a proper answer to the just demands of moderate men. The county franchise must be dealt with at once, and until it was the agricultural labourers' condition could not be improved. Mr. Fawcett, who also addressed the meeting. spoke of the necessity of securing open spaces for the recreation of the people, and said much more remained to be done in that direction. He urged them to closely consider the problems which awaited settlement, particularly county franchise and redistribution; but warned them against the principal Of equal electoral districts, believing many smaller borougbis should be retained.

TRH ORDER OF BusINESS NEXT SESSION.—The secretall of the National Liberal Club has received the following letter front Mr. Gladstone :--" 10, Downing-street, Whiter- hall, November 9, 1883.—My Dear Sir,—Mr. Gladstone is obliged to you for forwarding to him the resolutions which! were passed at the meeting of the General Committee 0, the National Liberal Club held on Wednesday, urging the importanoe of dealing next session with the question of London Municipal Reform.. In acknowledging these reso- lutions, he desires me to say that they will not fail te receive due and full examination from Her Majesty's Government, who will consider with, great care, both of what measures it may be proper to advise the introduction, and in what order they should be taken.—l remain, irY , dear air, yours very faithfully, E. W. LIAMILTOII.—W• ' Digby, Esq."—The following is the resolution referred to "That this committee earnestly hopes that the Govern- ment, while dealing with the question of the county frau' chise next session, will also, in the interests alike of the metropolis and the whole country, introduce a measure deal'

lug with London municipal reform." " COLSTON DAY."—Tuesday was "Colston Day" ,at Bristol, and there were the usual party banquets. At tbat given by the Anchor Society, which is supported by the Liberals, Lord Northbrook, who was the principal speaker, referred to the difficult task Lord Spencer had been called upon to undertake. He had shown that he had not oral desired to accord to the people of Ireland every justice which was their due, but his determination to see law aild order enforced in that country, and not to allow outrageS which were a disgrace to the United Kingdom to continue in Ireland, The right hon. gentleman addressed himself specially to the Ilbert Bill, which he said had been intro- &iced by the Government of India with the full support of Her Majesty's Ministers for the purpose of removing a die qualification under which all native judges and magistrate now lay inregard to the exercise of criminal jurisdiction over Englishmen in the rural districts of India. He contended that if a difference of race and religion were to be accepted as a valid reason for establishing separate jurisdiction 3, the) whole fabric of Indian legal procedure must be recoil': struc'ed. Lord Northbrook explained the various modifier tions made in tile bill since its introdumion. At the gather. lug of ale Dolphin Society, Mr. Jainei Luwther, waS the principal speaker.
iSTRANGE. FREAKS OF A. MADMAN
AT ST. HELENS.

A great commotion was caused in Parr on Friday after noon last by the freaks of a madman named Jam s Fogarty'. Foga' ty, who lived in Traverse-street, bad, it is said, bed' suffering from inflammation of the lungs for some time, ap" been confined to his room. On Friday afternoon he cow ducted himself in a strange and restless manner, and at one time fastened his room door by drawing the bed rebind R- ile afterwards got through the room window on to an Wit" house, and f,heace to the ground. He then walked along the street with only his night dress on, ultimately going to! beerhouse near the railway, and getting through a window on to an outhouse, on the roof of which he commenced togs" ticulate, to shout, and to pray in the most eccentric fashir; A large crowd soon assembled around the building. 30u, Fogarty commenced to tear up the slates and throw them a'' the people below. Father Egger, of Holy Cross Church, earns up at the time, and was struck with a piece of slate op the lip, which was cat through, arid a tooth knocked oot Fogarty, after remaining on this elevated position for a cote siderable time, came down and sat on a wall, and while tiler! a person came up behind and pushed him off. A nurobqr 01 man then closed in upon him, and he was secured. On th 4 same day be was conducted to Prescat Workhouse, and later on to Rainhill Asylum.

AN OBSTRITCTIVE CAB-DRIVER AT NEWTON. : t‘t be . Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Richard Hutt, a cab' drivee, was charged with obstructing Mill-lane.—The defect- dant pleaded not guilty.—P.C. Spencer deposed that on the 25th October, one of the H..ydock Park coursing days, he saw the defendant draw out from a line of cabs standing In Mill-lane. Jackson re- marked that there were between 50 and 60 cabs, ant it eras a necessity upon the police to preserve order. The Zrqinds of the action brought by plaintiff were that the otchlent he met with was occasioned by the defective state tk the saw, bench, and fence. As to the saw, he contended teat no defective condition within the meaning of the Act ,s'IM been shown, and with regard to the fence, he submitted aintiff had not brought that part of the case within sub- ption 3of section 2 of the 6.ct, and as to the whole case, „L'at the plaintiff had not shown that the defect caused the jreonal injury. With respect to defects in the condition bt Machinery, Judge Woodford had a similar case before rill at the Derby County Court, and he found that the defect ttel the machinery did not come within the meaning of sub- .. ction 3, because there a defect in machinery tTleant something which had arisen in consequence of some wegleet or misuser or something by which thd machinery hall incapable of doing its work as originally set up. With O'gard to this saw the defect was not uccasioned„by neglect: ,r Misuse ; if there was a defect at all it was a defect in the nufactured article, and that was not a defect in the con- 'rim of machinery, coming within the meaning of the Act. ett order to prove the case within the meaning of the Act, considered it must be shown that the fault in the saw, if hu,eit be any, was occasioned by some negligence on the rt of the employer or his managers, and it had not been lilggesteu that the fault was occasioned in any such way. there was a defect it was inherent in the nature of the 1,7 itself. As to the other point Ii c scientific evidence showed that the accident could not Dlit happened through the mere play of the fence, and solved conslusively that it must have canted.—His Honour 4.. id that if-the defect in the saw arose in the course of use, 0:4 owing to the negligence of the employer or superior irzant, although discovered had not been remedied, then teheanle within the moaning of the Act. On resuming Way at half time, the home team, with the wind in their favour, set to work in high expectation of very soon equalising :matters, but greatly to their surprise, under the combined play of the visitors, they were severely pressed during the whole of the play, and at the close of , I the game the Temperance team were victors by seven, goal, . ..

Earleetown, arranged to play a match on the ground of the Earlestown Association Club at Wargrave, on daturday last. Unfortunately the bitterly cold weather, coupled with the powerful wind blowing across the field, deterred many from witnessing the game. There was, however, a pretty fair attend- anee of spectators. The gurus needs little description, as with the exception of one or two men on each side, the players were entire novices. The result was a victory for the Fitters by two goals to none. The umpires were J. Whalley and J elmm (of the Barlestwn P.O ), add Mr. P. nestle (of the Earles- town P.C.) officiated as Referee. An excellent and substantial dinmer was afterwards partaken of at the Sunbeam Inn, the "spread" reflecting credit upon the host and hostess. The evening was spent in a convivial manner. EARLESTOWN V. PRESTON PARISH CHITECH.—A somewhat hastily a.•rangel much between the Eariestewn and Preston Parish Oburch clubs was played on the ground of the former . .

on Saturday afterno ,n. The visitors turned up with a strong 6:even ; while the home team were two men short—their goal- keepee, Appleton. and Mather, right wing player. T. Cham- pion and J. Green ably filled their places. however. The home team won the toss, and for the first half chose to play with the wind against them. ~Tne visitors accordingly kicked off with the wind in their favour. Immedialely the leather was started it, was run into the home quarters, and after a short scrimmage the visitors sec ',red an easy goal through a mis-kick by one of the lixne backs, &hint one minute from the start. This early sueces encouraged the Prestonians to further exertions, but the. Earlestonians infused new energy into th:lir play, and tile game became a little exciting. The visitors held a slight advent a._;e, however, and before half time th. y scored wiother goal. On the change of ends the home team were two goals to the bad. but they elinms‘neoil in a manner likely to win. The Prastonians were severely pressed, and af er a few minutes' play Dagnall kicked a goat for Baxlessown. The visitors strove hard to prevent their opponents from gett'ng on an equality, but they could not pre- vent the Earlestonians from seriously endangering their up- rights. 'C'everal scrimmages occurred right in front of the goal and during one of these the leather was forced between and the scare equalised amid app ause. The play was afterwards in favour of the home team, but when time was called no alteration in the yore had been made and the result was a draw —two goals each. Doxnury ; left wig. J. chnm and J. Ogden.

div.head: MAYOR AND CORPORATION AT CHURCH.
div.p: THE MAYOR AND CORPORATION AT CHURCH.

According to custom, the newly-elected Mayor of War- rington (Alderman Joseph Harrison) and most of the mem- bers of the Corporation attended service at the Parish Church on Sunday morning. The Mayor, Council, and friends assembled at the Town Hall at ten o'clock, the I police under the direction of the Chief Constable, heading I the procession to the church. Then came the members of of the Fire Brigade followed by the Mayor's carraige (which containehia Worship and Mr. H. B. White), drawn by a couple of greys, the aldermen and councillors coming last. There was a large congregation at the church. An appropriate sermon was preached by the Rector (the Rev. W. Quekett, M. A.) from the words "Take you wise men and understanding, and known among your tribes, and I will make them rulers over you." (Dent. I. XIII.) In the course of an address marked as usual with plain common sense, the reverend gentleman referred to the duties of magistrates and proceeded: And if there ever was a time calling for the especial consideration of the magistracy in putting the law in force to abate a prevailing crime existing here that time is our own. The daily papers call attention to the fact, and the remarks of the magistrates are hawked about in our streets and where is the remedy ? I believe the great cause of this state of things is the wretched abodes in which the lower orders live. Paisful are the sights in our own courts and alleys. The small ill-conditioned houses, the wretched ventilation and sanitary arrangements, the narrow passages and alleys, in which the light of the sun in some never shines, much less a good example seen, homes crowded with old and young huddled together, when this state of things exists can you be surprised at the pain- ful results? Hundreds of these abodes ought to be pulled , down. I hope I may yet live to see the Labourers' Dwelling Act carried out in our town Goad sites may be found *here thousands may be accommodated in blocks of buildings,' with well-arranged apartments of all sizes and prices, and all the modern 'improvements which will add to the comfort and health of the inmates. We want at once a large indus- trial school for the waifs and strays. These matters deserve the consideration of the chief magistrate, who ought not to shrink from his duty. Though the great, the rich, and the powerful may be in league against him, he will be undis- mayed; he will bid defiance to all attempts at intimidation; and strong in the power of his God, he will perform his duty through both evil and good report. He will execute his several functions, neither swayed by private affection nor ambitious to purchase a short-lived popularity at the expense of the approbation of his own con- science. But though he acknowledges no fear of man, yet will he be conspicuous for the fear of his God. Such were the qualities for which Moses of old required the rulers of Israel to be eminent and distinguished amongst their tribes, and it will be found that the same qualifications should adorn the characters of magis- trates in every age; and may 0-od in His mercy put it into the heart of all your tribes to look out and provide a succes- sion ef able and understanding magistrates; who, when ad- vanced to the highest office, shall, like your late chief ruler, approve themselves conscientious and faithful in the dis- charge of their public duties. And it is pleasant to reflect that his good deeds require no eulogium from me. The past will prove the best example for the future, and when our present chief magistrate retires from his elevated position riles, the conscicusness of his exertions-to uphold the dignity of his office, and to promote the welfare of his fellow towns- men, increase the happiness of his domestic life; and when at length he shall be summoned to another world may it be to bear the approving sentence, "Well done, thou good and faithful servant, enter thou into the joy of thy Lord." div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATITEDAY, NOVEMBER 17, 1883.
THE WARRINGTON WATCH ROBBERIES. commirrAL OF THE PRISONER.

Maurice Jones, journeyman watchmaker, was brought up on remand at the Walrington Through Court, on Tuesday, charged with stealing a silver lever hunting watch, value £O, the properly of George Tomlin, watchmaker. Butter- o arket-street.— he facts of the case were reported in last week's Exantince.—Mr. Jenkins, who prosecuted, said he thought there was sufficient evidence against prisoner to warrant the magistrates in committing him for trial.—The Chief Constable said he was not aware of all the particulars, but he knew that five or six different watches had been re- covered since the last bearing, and which the prisoner had been found dealing with unlawfully.—The magistrates asked whether there was a sufficient case against prisoner to commit him for trial.—The Chief Constable: Quite so. I think there are five different cases against him.—Mr. ! Jenkins: We only propose to take three.—The evidence relating to the watch belonging to Mrs. Shaw, of Padgate, ' which was pawned by prisoner whilst in the employ of Mr. Tomlin was then taken.—The following cases were then gone into.—George Hatton. painter, 56, Mersey-street, stated that about even months since he handed prisoner a silver lever watch to regulate. Prisoner was at that time in the employ of Mr. Tomlin, but he took this watch as a private -job. About a fortnight afterwards prisoner brought the Watch home, but as it would not go witness returned it to him. Witness had not seen the ticker from that time until it was shown him by P.C. Neill. He had asked him for it frequently, but each time some excuse was given for its detention. Witness identified the watch pro- duced as his property, and valued it at £S.—P.C. Neill proved that on the ffth November he searched prisoner's lodgings, and found in his bedroom the pawnticket relating to the last witness's watch, and which he found had been pawned at Mrs. Jackson's, Church-street. In answer to the charge of stealing this watch prisoner said, "Yes, it is George Hatton's.—Herbert Jackson, assistant to his mother, a pawnbroker, deposed to prisoner having pledged the watch produced for 12s 3d.—Samuel Wheeler, blacksmith and wheelwright, of 62, Legh-street, said that in February last he handed the prisoner two Geneva watches to clean and put in repair. One was a hunter with a closed face, and worth £3, and the other an open-faced watch, valued at 50s. He had many times askei prisoner for the watches, but he gave various excuses, such as they were not quite finished, wanted regulating, Jac. The watches produced witness identified as his property. He had not authorised prisoner to deal with the watches in any way.—Benedict Tyro, assistant to Mr. Morton, pawnbroker, Winwick-street, preduced the duplicate ticket relating to the bunter watch, identified by Wheeler as belonging to him, and which pri- soner had pledged with witness for Ts o.l.—James Tierney, another assistant to Mrs. Jackson, produced Wheeler's open- faced watch, pledged by the prisoner. Previous to making the advance witness asked prisoner if he was a dealer in watches, and he replied in the affirmative. Having con- fidence in him, witness then advanced 5s on the watch.— P.C. Neill also gave evidence respecting the robbery, and said that when prisoner was asked in the first instance how he had obtained possession of three of the watches he said one was his own, which he usually wore, and the others had been given to him to sell.---Prisoner, who said he had no statement to make and no witnesses to call, was committed for trial on all the charges,

VESTRY MEETING AT WIDNES.

TEE COUNTY RATE. Yesterday afternof n a vestry meeting was I,eld in the overseers' Wave Victoria-road, Widnes, to consider the basis or steuelard. for county rate as recently prepared by the Committee of Justices appoined for that purpose. On the niotioc of Mr. T. Handley, Mr. J. W. Wareing (the senior overseer; was veted tf the chair. There were also present Maur., John :NI ithews, A. Cowley, 8. Sadler, J. W. Carlile, S. B. stringer, S. Owen, J. T. Allen (clerk to the Local Board', and John Gaff (eeeistant overseer).—Mr. ALLEN said the heels simply showed what was the valuations of the various townships in 1876, and what they were increased to in 1853 ev the present basis. It gave no information. They saw that the rateable value of Widnes had lefen gare)ee Whet they wanted was some right of inquiring into this increased basis. The justices he Inderetood got the gross value; they then took one-twelfth eee laud, and one-sixth off buildings. In Widnes a great proportion of the rateable value was made up from large chemical works, and he did not consider that one-sixth was a fair discount from the gross value to get at the rateable value of these buildings. This view was borne out by the overseers' action in past years. He understood that at pre- sent the overseers took the gross valuation. 'rhey then took five per cent. off lands, tithes, canals, &c.; 15 p-r cent. off house property, and 33;4 per cent, off chemical works. If the overseers, who were local men with a full knowledge of the township, considered this was a fair basis, then teat of the justices was not. Then there was another thing. They had no particulars given of what Widnes was paying to the county for. He saw from the last year's returns of the Prescot Union that Widnes paid the county .£2,852. What they should like to know was how much of this was for pubic bridges, &c. He thought the ratepayers of Widnes would be considerably astonished when they found bow if was made out—Me. T. HANDLEY retaareed that the Local Board had appointed Mr. Allen to attend and ask the overeeers to appeal against the basis.—The CHAIRMAN re- marked that owing to the representations of Mn. Guff, the assistant overseer, at the meeting of justices at St. George's Hall, the gross rental of Widnes was reduced £l,OOO in con- sideration of the deterioration of chemical works.—Mr. Aveis pointed out that between the rateable value of Widnes fixed by the overseers and that fixed by the county jestrces there was a difference of £7,000, and it was there- fore incumbent upon the reprepresentatives of the town- ship to get some reduction in the rateable value. This great increase in the rateable value of the towu was caused by the chemical works and railways. They knew that ap- peals were pending against these assessments, and if they werirreduced by £20,000, and they got no redress from the county, they might have to go on plying the county fur the next seven years on a wrong basis. If Gaskell, Deacon and' Co. were successful in their appeal there was no doubt the other chemical companies would follow suit.— Mr. HANDLEY then moved "That this meeting requests the overseers to appeal against the county- valuations for the purpose of pointing out the appeal; now pending against the valuations by railway companies and chemical works, and also for the purpose of ascertaining the particulars of the various rates included in the precept against the township. That any cost incurred by the overseers be a charge upon the rates of the town- ship."—Mr. WRIGHT seconded the motion, and it was car- ried unanimously.—lt was also decided that. Mr. Wareing, Mr. J. TA lien, and Mr. J. Goff form a deputation to wait upon the county justices at Preston.—A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Wareing for presiding. THANES TO FATHER FINEGAN. Mr. Owes said he observed from that morning's news- papers that Father Finegan had displayed much ability and tact at the meeting of Prescut Guardians on the previous day in connection with the proposed increase of the clerk's salary, and be thought the ratepayers owed him a debt of gratitude. (Hear, hear.) He moved that their hest thanks be accorded .to him.—Mr. CARLILE observed that he thought the time had arrived when the Guardians should make another attempt to obtain two more representatives for the township.—Mr. ALLEN pointed out that whilst Widnes had 12 per cent. of the representation it supplied 19 per cent. of the expendi- ture of the Union. That was a very nice going up. Laughter.) The Widnes Guardians each represnoted £26,00, while some guardians in thelanion represented as low as £4l,ooo.—Mr. COWLEY : Well, they cannot send less than one.—Mr. WAREING: I should like to ask what will be the nee of the extra guardians if you get them.—Mr. CARLILE: There would be six votes instead ef four.—Mr. OWENS If separation is within the range of probability, we had better agitate for that.—Mr. ALLEN: I don't think there is at present.—Mr. WARRING (to Mr Owena)n You want to go in for Home Rule, do you ?—Mr. WRIGHT seconded Mr. Owens' motion, remarking that the ratepayers had long wished to know bow the salary of the clerk to the Guardians was made up. Perhape they would get it now after the Rev. Father Finegan's action.—The proposition was carried unanimously, and the meeting separated.

MR. BANTOCK PIERPOINT'S CONCERT, RUNCORN. The fourth annual grand concert orgenieed by Mr. Ban- tack Pierpoint took place at Runcorn Public Hall on Tues- day evening. A fashionable company assembled, but the concert, although an unqualified success from a musical standpoint, failed to attract so large an audience as on former occasions, and we fear that Mr. Pier point's enterprise did not receive that financial return it deserved. No doubt the con- dition of the weather exerci4ed a prejudicial influence, for to a cold and chilling atmosphere there was the added dis- comfort of a dense fog. The conc,rt was unusually interent- ing from the fact that t‘eo arcistcs-31ise Thudichutu and Mr. Chilley—were to appear who bad not made the acquaint- ance of the Runcorn public, but of whote vocal abilities dattering accounts had been received. They proved them- selves worthy of the reputation they have gained, and quickly ingratiated themselves into the favours of the audi- ence. Miss Thudichum p.,ssessee a soprano voice of flue tone and great power, and be dillicalties in the pieces she had chosen were sermee -teel in apparent ease. The sweet ballad, "Let me dream 1.1 in," received from her a charming interpretation, and she was re-ealled. The rest of her selections lost one half of their charms to the audience through being sang in a foreign tongues and although the-excellent quali- ties of her vocaiisatien were very noticeable, Miss Thudi- chum was not so enthusiastically applauded as on the first occasion. She, however, received a hearty encore for her rendering of "Es war em n traurn " and 'Du bist wie eine blume," when she favoured the audience with "Robin Adair." Miss Emilie Lloyd is a Warm favourite with Run- corn audiencee, and she received a most flattering reception on coming forward to sing "Never to part." Her voice had lost none of its charms. Her pere tones and exquisite modulation entitle her to high rank as a singer, and etch of her efforts was enthusiastically encored. She sang " A winter story," "The Quaker's daughter," "Auntie," and "Darby and Joan." Mr. Charles Chilley is a tenor of rising fame. He possesses a voice of great power, which he uses to the beat advantage; end although he was evidently suffering from a celd, en Tuesday, his singing was heartily enjoyed. He was equally successful in singing the sentimental ballad " All in all," or the some- what rollicking song "The Biy of Biscay.' He was tOlce recalled, and in response sing "The lass that loved a sailor." He also sang "Good night, iseloved," and in con- nection with Mr. Pierppint the duet "Excelsior," a most auccessful and interesting piece of vocalisation. 'Of our townsman, Mr. Pierpoint, we can only speak in terms of praise. His voice seemed to have gained a greater richness of quality than formerly, and was as full and resonant as ever. His enunciation has also considerably improved, and he may look forward to scoring many successes in the musical world. He WRS perhaps heard at his best in "The Vicar's Song." for which he was encored, and rendered the Cavalier's song "Here's health unto Her Majesty ; " but the "Bedroom love song" and "The devout lover" re- ceived happy interpretations. The violin solos of Mr. Frank Arnold were a feature in the evening's entertainment, and his performances proclaim him to be a genius. He was twice encored. The concert concluded with the part song, "Oh were I but a drop of dew," in which all the vocalists took part. b.

INFECTIOUS HOSPITAL FOR PRESCOT UNION. CONFERENCE AT IVHISTON, On Thursday afternoon, a conference was held in the Workhouse of the Prescot Union, at Wbiston, for the pur- pose of considering the advisability of establishing a joint hospital fer infectious clies for the whole of the Union. There were present deputation from the various sanitary authorities in the Union, including St. Helens, Widnes, Prescot, Huyton, Rainford, Stc., and the Local Govern- ment Beard was represented by Dr. Thorne, their medical officer, and Mr. Smith, their architect. Mr. W. Tyrer, chair- man of the the Prescet Board of Guardians, was elected to the chair. Mr. Hartley (clerk to the Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority) read a statement he had prepared setting forth the various circumstances which had led up to the Con- ference, and als3 giving a return of the population and rate- aa4e value of the different districts of which the Union is composed. Of St. Helens, the population was 57,234, rateable value, £231,860; Widnes, population 24,918. rateable value £123,721; Huyton, population 4,060, rateable value £13,929; Much Woottoe, population 4,539, rateeble value £22,068; Rainford, population 3,745, rateable value £21,740; Little Wootton, population 1,159, rateable v due £15,923; Prescot, p)pulation 6,418, rateable value £l4 232 ; Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority dis- tr c', population 15865, rateable value £148,213 ; t, oat pout ati en, 127 933 ; total rateable value, £621 753 He (Mr. Hartley) estimated that a hospital providing accommodation for 50 beds could be built for £5,000, vvhicn sum could be borrowed at the rate of 4 per cent., and p aid back at the rate of £289 133 4d, in- cluding interest, and he further estimated that the general working expenses would be £2lO per annum, making a total of £5OO a year, which on tae basis of the rates!-le value jnst stated would be contributed to as follows :—St. Helens Corporation, £lB6 .ss; WiJues, £99 103; Huyton, £35; Much Wootton. £lB 103 ; Rainford, £l7 lOs ; Little Woot- ton, £l2 15e ; Prescot, £ll 103 ; Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority, £ll9. The St. Helens Corporation had already made some provision for their own patients, and if they did not feel inclined to join the scheme the cost to the other authorities would be, per annum, as follows :—Widnes, £153 103 ; Hayton, £56 103; Much Woolton, £2B 103; Rain- ford £2B; Little Wooltou, £2O lOs ; Prescot, £lB ss; Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority, £lB9 15s. In the event of neither St. Helens or sNidnes joining in the scheme, the cost to the remaining authorities, per annum, would be : Huyton; £B2 103; Much Wootton, £4l 10s; Rainford, £4O 15s; Little Wootton, £29 15s; Prescot, £2O 15e; Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority, £278 15s. Each authority over and above this regular contribution would have to pay for the maintenance, &o, of its own patients. It was also proposed that the hospital should be made as attractive as possible, and should not be known by the name of "fever hospi'll " or " smallpox hrepital," but the less objectionable name of "sanatorium."—Dr. THORNE then addressed the meeting, and in the outset of his remarks pointed out that it was not the duty of the Guardians to provide for non-pauper infec- tious cases, but of the respective sanitary authorities, and this had been done by a large number of those authorities throughout the kingdom. If the several sanitary authorities of the Prescot Union did this there would have to be eight hospitals provided, which would be greatly more expensive than the building of one by the combined authorities. There was, he said, an immense saving by a proper combination. It would be for them to consider in case of combination whether they would have one bospital or whether they would have two, one for the northern division of the Union and one for the southern. He also strongly impressed upon those present the advisability of providing a hospital before a serious emergency arose. Hospitals which were built in a panic he had generally found were of little use afterwards. The sanitary authorities, he said, ought to look on the building of a hospital as an insurance premium against the spread of disease. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. R. PILICINOTON (St. Helens) said he had not come to pledge the Corporation of St. Helens to anything, but he was quite sure the Corporation, although they had provided a hospital of their own, would be quite willing to entertain, as one of the authorities of the Union, any suggestion that might be made. The different autho- rities were bound to help each other in these things, and 1 St. Helens, although perhaps the only authority in the ' Union which had made any provision for itself, would be glad to give any assistance that was proper. He hoped the result of the conference would be that proper hospital ac- commodation was provided. (Hear. hear.)—Mr. CARRY (Widnes) said he and his colleagues had come more to listen than anything else. The ideas entertained by the Widnes Local Board lately were of having a hospital of their own, as they had rather a large township, covered a large area, and had an increasing population. They thought of making their hospital in such a part of their township that it would be useful to some of the neighbouring townships, such as Ditton and Cronton. If they joined in the general hospi- tal scheme, and the hospital was built, say near the work- house, they would have to bring their patients a distance of five or six miles, which might not be a very good arrange- ment.-Dr. THORNE slid he had generally found that patients did not like to be removed from urban to rural districts, but they would go from village into towns. With regard to the removal, if patients wore rem wed at an early stage of the attack they could be carried a distance of 8 or 10 miles without danger. He also pointed out that the hospital was not provided for epidemics but to prevent them.—The Rev. T. Cruelness (Halewood) hoped it would be agreed to at once erect a hospital.—Dr. O'Keuva (Widnes) said be was not aware that the old Poor Law had been repealed by which every township in that Union had the right of sending infectious disease cases to the hospital at the workhouse.—Dr.THOßNß said there never was such a right. It rested with the Guardi ins whether they would even rec-ive the pauper cises, and with regard to the non-pauper cases they had not only no right, but it was absolutely illegal to receive them. i —Mr. R. PILKINOTON said the sanitary authorities could not afford to be selfish in that matter. It wee to their in- terest that no infection arose in an outside but adjoining their boundaries, so that it miglft not spread within. He would move that the clerk to the Union be loguNsted to write to the various local authori- ties in the Union, asking that a representative may be sent to act upon a joint committee to consider and re- port what steps, if any, should be taken for the provision of proper and efficient hospital accommodation for the treat- ment of infectious diseases for all the sanitary districts of the Union.—Mr. Mnanows (Rural Sanitary Authority) secondel this preposal.—Mr. HILL, who represented Much Wootton Local Beard, said that some of the members of that Board were opposed to the scheme because they thought the hospital would be a greater distance than other places into which they could get their patients by paying. —Mr. Focio (Prescot) said the question about the powers of the Sanitary Authorities to compel people to go to the hospital had not bsen touched upon by Dr. Thorne. He mentioned that the Prescot Local Board had once established a hospital but could get ne one to go into it.—Dr. Taming said the Public Heaith Act provided that the Sanitary Authorities could by getting an order from the magistrates to compel patients to go into the hospital, but he strongly dieadvised this course. If a hospital, he said, was Properly conducted and made attractive people would go into it without being forced.—Dr. McNicolor. (St. Helens) was also of this opinion. In St. Helens, he said, they had no difficulty in getting patients to go into the hospital there. He had known a place where the people would not go into the hospital provided, but then the leading men and medical men of that place were in the habit of denouncing it.—Mr. Pilkingtoe's resolution was then put and carried, and on the motion of Mr. MEADOWS, the time for the meeting of the representatives of each of the authorities was fixed to he the 13th December.—The conference then ended.

div.head: MRS. BARFOOT'S CONCERT AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: MRS. BARFOOT'S CONCERT AT ST. HELENS.

MrP. Barfoot. gay: the sixth of her pleasant annual re- unions in the Town Hall on Tuesday evening, and it was, as on fortner occasions, liberally patronised. The assembly- room was tilled from and to end, and the gallery had also to be thrown open before the whole of the audience could be accommodated. The distinguishing feature of this concert was, of course, as in the case of those which have preceded It, the musical performances of the children, pupils of Mrs. Barfoot. Not that these were the only attractions of the evening as the efforts of the young people were sup- plemented by those of Mr. Fred. Walla, of Bristol, and Mr. J. H. Greenwood, of Manchester, the former of whom gave several highly appreciated exhibitions of his skill in the use of the violin as well as other instruments, and the latter was extremely successful in rendering comic songs and sketches. Mr. Greenwood's sketch of "Silver wedding" was particularly amusing, being replete with humour, whilst free from buffoonery, and full of excellent mimicry. His "Showman" also excited the risibilities of the audience, and in response to a persistent encore, Mr. Greenwood gave the "Sleepy man." The bulk of the programme was, however, as we have said, made up of pianoforte , pieces and songs by Mn. Barfoot's pupils, which were all lendered with notable precision and in so satisfactory a way ' as to clearly indicate a great amount of painstaking care on the part of the tutors; and, it may perhaps be added, no little aptness an the side of the pupils. The most notice- able of the contributions by the pupils were the songs by Miss Kate Williams, who revealed the possession of a singularly pleasing and penetrating voice. "Y Girtiotes Fach," a Welsh song, which she sung, was deservedly en- cored, and in response to the continued applause of her next song, "Little birdie, mine," she bowed her acknow- ledgments. Miss Nellie Barfoot, a very young girl, also showed very commendable skill in a pianoforte solo witich she played. The pieces which were sung by a large num- ber of children collectively, were a collection of Nursery Rhymes and selections Irma "Pinafore." The Misses I:tarfoot, whose musicsl accomplishments are well known in St. Helens, likewise contributed in no small degree to the suceess of the concert by their performance on the violin, zither, harp, pianoforte.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The ordinary fortnightly meeting of this Board was held in Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday. There were present —Mr. W. Tyrer (in the chair) ; Messrs. J. T. Hall, H. Leigh, T. F. Hill, H. Tuson, J. Fisher, J. Fidler, W. Tyrer, T. Sadler, W. Gerrard, J. Matthews, T. Eatock, Jno. Lowe, W. Birchen, Edward Syder, J. Leatherbarrow, W. Gilbody, W. Swift, Jos. Griffith, Jne. Kenwright, P. Longton, and Buckley; the Revs. J. Barnacle, T. Finegan, and T. Muni- bora ; and Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk).

div.head: ', ' 111.49TRR 3 REPORT.
div.p: ', ' 111.49TRR 3 REPORT.

The WORKHOIISH ifeerrs"---n-re—p—o-rieTihat there were 450 inmates in the Workhouse, as compared witb 454 last week, and 478 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 175 boys and girls in the Kirkdale Schools. Thirty- four vagrants had been relieved, as compared with 101 in the corresponding period of last year.

div.head: WIDNf,I 4VD ITS DETRACTORS.
div.p: WIDNf,I 4VD ITS DETRACTORS.

The CLERIC suggested that he should be empowered to distribute notices in the township of Widnes giving inst. t C tioas to the people of the town as to reoraccination. Sm 11. pox, he said, had been in Widnes for some time, and it was well known that re-vaccination was a preventive of this diseas3.—Mr. SADLER thought it would be better to let the ti•ing riot.. Mr. MA.7-rllnwo maid a groat doal moro hal been said about the small-pox in Widnes than was necessary. It would be better for the tradesmen of that town if les3 were said.—Mr. SADLER pointed out that there had only been three deaths returned in the whole of Widnes. and that he thought was not excessive in a population of 26,000. —rile Rev. Mr. FINHOAN concurred in what had been amid by Mr Matthews and Mr. Sadler, and he said he had not heard of a new case for the last 10 days. He was of opinion the alarm was passed.—Mr. MIILDOWS thought the Guar- dians ought to take all precaelions which wire thought eeceseary.—lt was agreed, however, in deference to tbe opinions of the representatives of Widnes, that no action should be taken with regtrd to the distribution of notices.

div.head: SCARLET FEVER 111 TILE WORKHOUSE.
div.p: SCARLET FEVER 111 TILE WORKHOUSE.

It was stated that the lavtlical officer had reported an out- break of scirlet fever in the workhouse. It appeared that the fever had started in the infant department. As to the citlle, the 'ltalical officer had not been able to satisfactorily tccount for it, and he could not say whether it had started de novo from the drains, or had been brought in by fresh arrivals in the workhouse.

div.head: ST. lIELENS VAGRANT WARD.
div.p: THE ST. lIELENS VAGRANT WARD.

The Visiting Committee reported that tbny hyl 11-1 ler con- sideration an application from the St. Helens Corporation for the ent‘blishment of a vagrant ward in that town. It had ben moved by Mr. Meadows, and seconded by Mr. Hall, that the St. Helms Corporation be informed that the committee could not, in view of the decrtase in vagrancy, recommend the Guardians to provide a vagrant ward in St. Helens. The committee would, however, be glad to meet a deputation of the Corporation at the Work- house, and hear their views on the subject. These minutes , were continued.

div.head: TrIE CLERK'S SALARY.
div.p: TrIE CLERK'S SALARY.

In regafd to the application from the Clerk for an increase of sliary to pay for office assistance, the Finance Com- mittee reoommended, after consideriog a statenawnt sub- mitted by the Clerk, and being satisfied that there had been a considerable increase in the duties of the office, that the salary be increased by £2OO a year for office assistance.— The Rev. Father FINEGAN thought the statement which hal the Finance Committee to this conclusion ought to be submitted to the whole Board. Before that increase was voted the Board should be furnished with a statement of everything he received during the twelve months. (Hear, hear.)—After some discussion the state- ment referred to SIMI read over by the Chairman of the Finance Committee, Mr. Leatherbarrow. It was of consi- derable length, and set forth the increase of duties and other circumstances which supported the application.—Mr. LEATNEREARROW mentioned that a return had been pre- pared by which it was shown that the average of salaries paid by the several Unions of similar size to the Prescot Union was about £430 or £440. Out of the salary of £250 paid to the Clerk by the Guardians Ihe had to pay for office assistance, which ab- sorbed all the £2so.—The Rev. T. FINEGAN said the £250 was for the clerkship to the Guardians alone, but he wished to know how much bad been paid to the cterk by the various committees. Ile himself knew that within the last six or eight months the clerk had received from some of the committees more than £lOO, and he believed what he received from one of them was nearly S2oo.—Mr. FIDLER said that the most the clerk received was from the Assess- ment Committee last year, and that was £l5O for extra work.—Mr. Earocx said the Board had a right to take everything into account. It would be better for the clerk to give them all the information.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS thought the Guardians had no right to ask for the clerk's income from the committeee. They might as well, he said, inquire into his private means, such as what property he had with his wife, or what he expected from his great grandmother.—The Rev. T. FINEGAN: That does not come from the rates.—Mr. LHATHERDARROW gave notice that he wonld move at the next meeting that , the clerk's salary be increased by £200.-I'he Rev. T. Frxi.:(tax moved that the clerk furnish each member of the Board with a Nil statement of everything he received from the rates in coniaection with the Guardians.—Mr. SADLER seconded this motion.-1 his motion on being put was careierl by a small inajority.—This concluded the business.

Radcliffe said that from what he had been told he stepped the defendant when driving a shandry along Higher Parr-street on the Sunday morning previous, and on looking under the saddle of the pony in the shandry he found a raw wound on the hick from which matter was exuding.—A fine of 5s and costs was imposed. AN INCIPIENT " JACK SREPIIABD."—A lad named Richard Jones was on Monday charged at the St. Helens Polls° Court with having stolen two pigeons, the property of Daniel Cottrell, a shoemaker, living at 7, Queen-street, on the evening of the Bth inst. On the evening of the 9th inst. prosecutor missed two of his pigeons from his cote, and in consequence gave information to the police, who made inquiries and ascertained that the prisoner had t.ried to sell the two pigeons to Joseph Blanchard, a pigeon dealer in Westfield-street, who, however, refused to bny them. The prisoner, who was only 14 years of age, had been twice before convicted, and once sent to gaol for a month for stealing pigeons. He was again sent to gaol for one month's hard labour.

c.,;IOUTHPORT CONVALESCENT HOSPITAL AND BEA-BATHING INFIRMARY. The Board of Governors wish particularly to call the atten- tion of the Public, and the Committees of Management of Hospitals and Infirmaries, to the advantages to be obtained by Convalescent Patients in this Institution. A handsome addi- tion to the old Hospital, capable of accommodating 160 patients, and fitted with every modern appliance for heating and venti- lation has recently been erected by the Committee of the Cotton Districts Convalesoent Fund, and the total number of beds in the new and old buildings now amounts to 370. During the winter months especially the dry bracing air of Southport is considered very beneficial in cases of incipient Phthisis. Bronchitis, Rheumatism, and Debility; an the Governors are anxious that the benefits to be derived by these classes of patients from a short stay in this 11 °vital shall be widely known. Recommendations entitling patients to receive board and lodging, baths, medial' advice, and medicine for three weeks, for the sum of 365.. may be obtained from the local agents in Warrington, Messrs. G. and W. Fell, or from the Master. MR. J. G. ANDREWS, Convalescent Hospital, Southport.

LATEST . NEWS. BATTLE IN SOUTH AMERICA: 700 INDIANS KILLED.— Mail advices received from Lima state that a column of Chilian troops, on its way to Ayacucho, encountered a hirely of 4,000 Indians, of whom 700 were killed in an engagement which ensued. GALES ON THE AMERICAN LAKES.—Further gales, at- tendei by loss of life, are reported from the Western Lakes. Several vessels were lost with their crews. A violent gale has swept over the State of Maine, causing the destruction of much valuable timber. THE STALEyBRIDGE CHILD MURDER.-At the Liverpool Assizes, yesterday, before Mr. Justice Denman, in the Crown Court, Emma Elizabeth Scott (30), housekeeper, was charged with murdering her child on the 21st August, and sentence of death was passed. THE ALTurat COLLIERY ExrDosloN.—Two more deaths were reported yesterday morning, making a total of 66. The two who have succumbed to their injuries daring the night are Timothy Yates, of Church-lane, and a boy named Os- baldeston, of Quarry-street, whose father was killed. Both lived in Clayton-le-Moors. Two or three other miners Injured are in a precarious condition. DEPRESSION IN THU SCOTCH IRON TRADE. --• The out. look for the malleable iron and steel trades of the West of Scotland is extremely unfavourable, and appears to be be. coining more so every day. 'Reports from Coatbridge and the middle ward as to the condition generally of the malle- able ironworks are regarded as very disheartening. Some large works are clearing off their last orders, and unless more are placed before the end of the year no alternative seems possible but to suspend operations.
